hand/real-analysis.html:
Metric Spaces and Completeness

A metric space is a set X equipped with a distance function d : X × X → ℝ satisfying positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. The real line ℝ with the usual distance d(x,y) = |x−y| is the prototype. A sequence (xₙ) in a metric space is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there exists N such that for all m,n ≥ N, d(xₘ,xₙ) < ε. The space is called complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space. ℝ is complete; ℚ is not because a Cauchy sequence of rationals can converge to an irrational limit. Completeness is the analytic counterpart of the least‑upper‑bound property and underpins the existence of limits for iterative processes such as Newton’s method or the contraction mapping principle. In a complete metric space, the Banach fixed‑point theorem guarantees a unique fixed point for any contraction mapping, a tool used repeatedly in differential equations and numerical analysis.

Important examples of complete metric spaces include ℝⁿ with the Euclidean metric, the space ℓ² of square‑summable sequences, and the space C([a,b]) of continuous functions on a closed interval with the supremum norm. Incomplete spaces arise naturally: the space of polynomials on [0,1] with the supremum norm is not complete; its completion is C([0,1]). The process of completing a metric space by adding limits of all Cauchy sequences yields a complete space unique up to isometry. This construction mirrors the passage from ℚ to ℝ and shows that completeness is not a peculiarity of the real numbers but a structural property that can be imposed on any metric space.

Compactness in ℝⁿ

Compactness captures the idea that a set is “small” in a topological sense while retaining the completeness of closed bounded intervals. In ℝⁿ the Heine‑Borel theorem states that a subset is compact iff it is closed and bounded. Equivalently, every open cover admits a finite subcover. Sequential compactness — every sequence has a convergent subsequence — coincides with the covering definition in metric spaces. The Bolzano‑Weierstrass theorem is the one‑dimensional incarnation: every bounded sequence in ℝ has a convergent subsequence. Compactness is preserved under continuous images: if f is continuous and K is compact, then f(K) is compact. Consequently a continuous real‑valued function on a compact set attains its maximum and minimum (extreme value theorem) and is uniformly continuous (Heine‑Cantor theorem). These facts are the backbone of many existence proofs in optimisation and the calculus of variations.

In infinite‑dimensional normed spaces closed and bounded no longer implies compact; the unit ball of ℓ² is closed and bounded but not compact. This failure motivates the study of weak topologies and the notion of relative compactness. The Arzelà‑Ascoli theorem characterises compact subsets of C([a,b]) as those that are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. It provides a practical criterion for extracting convergent subsequences from families of functions, a technique essential in the proof of the Peano existence theorem for ordinary differential equations and in the theory of integral equations.

Worked Example: Uniform Convergence on a Compact Set
Let fₙ(x) = xⁿ on [0,1]. Show that (fₙ) converges pointwise but not uniformly. Then prove that on any compact subinterval [0,a] with 0 ≤ a < 1 the convergence is uniform.
Pointwise limit: for x ∈ [0,1) we have xⁿ → 0; for x = 1 we have 1ⁿ = 1. Hence the pointwise limit function f(x) is 0 on [0,1) and 1 at x = 1. This limit is not continuous, so the convergence cannot be uniform on [0,1] (uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous). On [0,a] with a < 1, supx∈[0,a] |xⁿ−0| = aⁿ → 0 as n → ∞. Given ε > 0 choose N such that aᴺ < ε; then for all n ≥ N and all x ∈ [0,a], |fₙ(x)−0| ≤ aⁿ < ε. Thus convergence is uniform on [0,a].
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about uniform convergence, first check continuity of the pointwise limit. If the limit is discontinuous on a compact domain, uniform convergence is impossible. For positive results, bound the supremum of the difference by a quantity independent of x; the Weierstrass M‑test is the standard tool for series of functions.

The Baire Category Theorem

The Baire category theorem is a cornerstone of modern analysis. In a complete metric space (or a locally compact Hausdorff space) the intersection of countably many dense open sets is dense. Equivalently, a non‑empty complete metric space cannot be expressed as a countable union of nowhere‑dense closed sets. A set is nowhere dense if its closure has empty interior. The theorem implies that “most” points of a complete space belong to a residual set (a countable intersection of dense open sets). This abstract statement has concrete consequences: the set of continuous nowhere‑differentiable functions is residual in C([0,1]); the set of points where a separately continuous function fails to be jointly continuous is of first category. The proof uses a nested‑ball construction: given dense open sets Uₖ, pick a closed ball B₁ ⊂ U₁, then B₂ ⊂ U₂ ∩ interior(B₁) with radius halved, and so on. Completeness guarantees the intersection of the balls contains a point belonging to all Uₖ.

Applications extend to functional analysis. The uniform boundedness principle (Banach‑Steinhaus) follows from Baire: if a family of continuous linear operators is pointwise bounded on a Banach space, it is uniformly bounded on some neighbourhood. The open mapping theorem and the closed graph theorem are also derived via Baire category arguments. In measure theory, the theorem shows that a non‑empty complete metric space without isolated points is uncountable, providing a topological proof that ℝ is uncountable without diagonalisation.

Differentiation of Integrals and the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem

The Lebesgue differentiation theorem states that for any locally integrable function f on ℝⁿ, the average value of f over balls centred at x converges to f(x) for almost every x as the radius tends to zero. Formally, limr→0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) f(y) dy = f(x) a.e. This result generalises the fundamental theorem of calculus to the Lebesgue setting and shows that the indefinite integral of an L¹ function is differentiable almost everywhere with derivative equal to the original function. The proof relies on the Hardy‑Littlewood maximal function Mf(x) = supr>0 (1/|B(x,r)|) ∫B(x,r) |f(y)| dy and the weak‑type (1,1) inequality |{x : Mf(x) > λ}| ≤ Cₙ ‖f‖₁ / λ. The maximal inequality controls the set where the averages deviate significantly from f, allowing a covering argument (Vitali covering lemma) to establish almost‑everywhere convergence.

Consequences include the Lebesgue density theorem: for any measurable set E ⊂ ℝⁿ, almost every point of E has density 1, and almost every point of the complement has density 0. This underpins the structure theory of sets of finite perimeter and the theory of functions of bounded variation. In probability, the differentiation theorem justifies the almost‑sure convergence of conditional expectations with respect to a filtration generated by shrinking σ‑algebras. The theorem fails for the Riemann integral because Riemann integrable functions need not be defined on a set of full measure; the Lebesgue framework is essential.

Common Traps

  • Confusing completeness of a metric space with closedness of a subset; a closed subset of a complete space is complete, but a complete subset need not be closed in a larger incomplete space.
  • Assuming that closed and bounded implies compact in every metric space; this holds only in ℝⁿ (Heine‑Borel) and fails in infinite‑dimensional normed spaces.
  • Thinking pointwise convergence of continuous functions preserves continuity; uniform convergence is required, and the limit of a pointwise convergent sequence of continuous functions can be highly discontinuous.
  • Misapplying the Baire category theorem to non‑complete spaces; the conclusion can fail dramatically, e.g., ℚ is a countable union of singletons, each nowhere dense in ℚ.
  • Believing the Lebesgue differentiation theorem holds for every point; it holds only almost everywhere, and counterexamples exist on sets of measure zero.
  • Using the Riemann integral to differentiate under the integral sign without verifying uniform convergence of the difference quotients; the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem provides the correct hypothesis.
  • Overlooking that the Hardy‑Littlewood maximal function is not integrable even when f ∈ L¹, which is why the weak‑type estimate is the sharp available bound.

The Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem — Compactness in Function Spaces

The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem characterises relatively compact subsets of the space C(K) of continuous real‑valued functions on a compact metric space K, equipped with the uniform norm. A subset F ⊂ C(K) is relatively compact (its closure is compact) if and only if it is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Uniform boundedness means there exists M > 0 such that |f(x)| ≤ M for all f ∈ F and all x ∈ K. Equicontinuity means for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that for all f ∈ F and all x, y ∈ K with d(x, y) < δ we have |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. The proof proceeds by a diagonal extraction argument: from a sequence in F one first extracts a subsequence converging on a countable dense subset of K using the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem and the uniform bound; equicontinuity then upgrades pointwise convergence on the dense set to uniform convergence on all of K. The theorem is indispensable in the study of integral equations, where solution operators often map bounded sets into equicontinuous families, guaranteeing the existence of convergent subsequences. It also underlies the compactness of the embedding of Hölder spaces C0,α(K) into C(K) for α > 0, and it is a key step in the proof of the Peano existence theorem for ordinary differential equations. In the context of metric spaces, the theorem extends to C(X, Y) where X is compact and Y is a complete metric space, provided the family is pointwise relatively compact in Y and equicontinuous. The Arzelà–Ascoli criterion fails if either hypothesis is dropped: the sequence f_n(x) = x^n on [0,1] is uniformly bounded but not equicontinuous at x = 1, and its only possible uniform limit would be discontinuous; the sequence f_n(x) = n on [0,1] is equicontinuous but not uniformly bounded, and it has no uniformly convergent subsequence.

The Stone–Weierstrass Theorem — Uniform Approximation by Algebras

The Stone–Weierstrass theorem generalises the classical Weierstrass approximation theorem (polynomials are dense in C([a,b])) to arbitrary compact Hausdorff spaces. Let X be a compact Hausdorff space and let A be a subalgebra of C(X, ℝ) that contains the constant functions and separates points (for any distinct x, y ∈ X there exists f ∈ A with f(x) ≠ f(y)). Then A is dense in C(X, ℝ) with respect to the uniform norm. The complex version requires additionally that A be closed under complex conjugation. The proof uses the lattice version of the theorem: the set of functions obtained by taking finite maxima and minima of elements of A is also dense; one then approximates the absolute value function by polynomials to show that the uniform closure of A is a lattice, and finally applies the Kakutani–Stone representation or a direct Urysohn‑type argument. Applications are ubiquitous: trigonometric polynomials form an algebra separating points on the circle, giving density in C(𝕋) and justifying Fourier series approximation in the uniform norm; the algebra generated by exponentials eλx with λ in a set having an accumulation point is dense in C([0,1]) by the Müntz–Szász theorem, a corollary of Stone–Weierstrass. In functional analysis, the theorem implies that the Gelfand transform of a commutative C*‑algebra is an isometric *‑isomorphism onto C(Δ) where Δ is the maximal ideal space. A common pitfall is to forget the separation condition: the algebra of even polynomials on [−1,1] does not separate x and −x, so its uniform closure consists only of even functions. Another subtlety is that the theorem does not hold for non‑compact spaces without additional hypotheses (e.g., the algebra of polynomials on ℝ is not dense in C_b(ℝ) because polynomials are unbounded).

Worked Example: Applying Stone–Weierstrass
Let X = [0,1] × [0,1] and let A be the algebra generated by functions of the form f(x)g(y) where f, g ∈ C([0,1]). Show that A is dense in C(X).
The algebra A contains constants (take f ≡ 1, g ≡ 1). To separate points, let (x₁,y₁) ≠ (x₂,y₂). If x₁ ≠ x₂, choose f ∈ C([0,1]) with f(x₁) ≠ f(x₂) and set g ≡ 1; then f(x₁)g(y₁) ≠ f(x₂)g(y₂). If x₁ = x₂ but y₁ ≠ y₂, choose g with g(y₁) ≠ g(y₂) and f ≡ 1. Thus A separates points. By the Stone–Weierstrass theorem, A is uniformly dense in C(X). This result is the foundation of the tensor‑product approximation used in multivariate numerical analysis.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks whether a given family of functions is dense in C(K), first check if the family is an algebra containing constants. If it is, verify the separation condition explicitly; constructing a separating function for an arbitrary pair of points is often the decisive step. If the family is not an algebra, consider its generated algebra or use the lattice version. Remember that the complex version requires self‑adjointness (closure under conjugation).

The Riesz Representation Theorem — Dual of Continuous Functions

The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem identifies the continuous dual of C₀(X), the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on a locally compact Hausdorff space X, with the space of regular complex Borel measures on X. For a compact Hausdorff space X, the dual of C(X) is the space of regular complex Borel measures with the total variation norm. The theorem states that every bounded linear functional Λ on C₀(X) can be represented as Λ(f) = ∫_X f dμ for a unique regular complex Borel measure μ, and ‖Λ‖ = |μ|(X). The construction proceeds by first defining a positive linear functional on the subspace of non‑negative functions, extending it to a positive functional on all of C₀(X) via the Jordan decomposition, and then using the Daniell–Stone or Carathéodory extension to obtain a measure on the Borel σ‑algebra. Regularity (inner regularity by compact sets and outer regularity by open sets) follows from Urysohn’s lemma and the properties of the functional. The theorem is the bridge between functional analysis and measure theory: it turns abstract linear functionals into concrete integrals, enabling the use of measure‑theoretic tools (dominated convergence, Fubini) in the study of C(X)*. In probability, it shows that the dual of C_b(ℝ) (bounded continuous functions) consists of finitely additive measures, while the dual of C₀(ℝ) consists of countably additive measures. A frequent mistake is to assume the representing measure is always positive; the theorem yields a signed or complex measure, and positivity of the functional corresponds to positivity of the measure. Another subtlety: the theorem fails for non‑locally‑compact spaces (e.g., the dual of C([0,1]^ℕ) is not represented by Borel measures on the product space).

The Banach Fixed Point Theorem — Contraction Mappings and Applications

The Banach contraction principle states that if (X, d) is a non‑empty complete metric space and T : X → X is a contraction (there exists 0 ≤ k < 1 such that d(Tx, Ty) ≤ k d(x, y) for all x, y ∈ X), then T has a unique fixed point x* ∈ X, and for any starting point x₀ the iterates xn+1 = T x_n converge to x* with the error estimate d(x_n, x*) ≤ k^n/(1−k) d(x₁, x₀). The proof constructs the Cauchy sequence of iterates and uses completeness. The theorem is a cornerstone of nonlinear analysis: it guarantees existence and uniqueness for ordinary differential equations via the Picard–Lindelöf iteration (the integral operator is a contraction on a suitable Banach space of continuous functions for small time intervals), for integral equations of Volterra type, and for the implicit function theorem in Banach spaces. It also underlies the convergence of Newton’s method under a Lipschitz condition on the derivative (the Kantorovich theorem). In numerical analysis, the theorem justifies iterative solvers for linear systems (e.g., Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel) when the iteration matrix has spectral radius < 1. The contraction constant k need not be uniform; a mapping that is a contraction on each ball of a covering can still have a unique fixed point if the space is complete and the mapping is a global contraction in the sense of Rakotch. A common error is to apply the theorem to a map that is only non‑expansive (k = 1); such maps may have no fixed points (e.g., translation on ℝ) or infinitely many (e.g., identity). The theorem also fails if completeness is dropped: the map x ↦ x/2 on (0,1) is a contraction with no fixed point in the space.

The Implicit Function Theorem — Local Solvability of Nonlinear Systems

The implicit function theorem gives conditions under which a relation F(x, y) = 0 can be solved locally for y as a function of x. Let F : U ⊂ ℝn+m → ℝ^m be continuously differentiable, and let (a, b) ∈ U satisfy F(a, b) = 0. If the m × m Jacobian matrix D_y F(a, b) is invertible, then there exist neighbourhoods V of a and W of b and a unique continuously differentiable function g : V → W such that g(a) = b and F(x, g(x)) = 0 for all x ∈ V. Moreover, the derivative of g is given by Dg(x) = −[D_y F(x, g(x))]-1 D_x F(x, g(x)). The proof uses the contraction mapping principle on the map Φ(y) = y − [D_y F(a, b)]-1 F(x, y) for x near a. The theorem extends to Banach spaces: if F : X × Y → Z is C1 and D_y F(x₀, y₀) is a bounded linear isomorphism, then a local implicit function exists. Applications include the proof of the inverse function theorem (set F(x, y) = f(x) − y), the derivation of Lagrange multipliers in constrained optimisation, and the regularity of level sets (the preimage of a regular value is a C1 submanifold). In differential geometry, the theorem shows that a submersion locally looks like a projection. A frequent trap is to assume the theorem holds when D_y F is merely injective or surjective; invertibility (bijectivity) is essential. Another is to forget that the theorem only guarantees a local solution; global solvability requires additional topological arguments (e.g., degree theory). The constant rank theorem generalises the implicit function theorem to the case where D_y F has constant rank r < m, yielding a local parametrisation of the solution set as a product of a manifold and a linear subspace.

  • Confusing the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem with the Heine–Borel theorem; the former characterises compactness in function spaces, the latter in ℝⁿ.
  • Assuming the Stone–Weierstrass theorem applies to non‑compact domains without a vanishing‑at‑infinity condition.
  • Thinking the Riesz representation theorem yields a positive measure for every bounded linear functional; the measure may be signed or complex.
  • Applying the Banach fixed point theorem to a map with Lipschitz constant 1 (non‑expansive) and expecting a fixed point.
  • Using the implicit function theorem when the partial Jacobian is singular; the theorem requires invertibility, not just non‑zero determinant of a submatrix.
  • Neglecting the regularity hypothesis (C¹) in the implicit function theorem; mere continuity of F is insufficient.
  • Believing the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem holds for pointwise bounded but not equicontinuous families; equicontinuity is indispensable.

These advanced theorems form the backbone of modern analysis and are essential for solving problems that go beyond routine calculus.

hand/symplectic-topology.html:
Hamiltonian Dynamics and the Hofer Metric

The group of Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms Ham(M, ω) consists of time‑1 maps of Hamiltonian flows generated by smooth, time‑dependent functions Hₜ with zero mean (on closed manifolds) or compact support (on open ones). The Hofer norm of a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism φ is defined as the infimum of the L¹,∞ norm of generating Hamiltonians: ‖φ‖ₕ = inf{∫₀¹ (max Hₜ − min Hₜ) dt : φ = φᴴ}. This norm descends to a bi‑invariant metric dₕ(φ, ψ) = ‖φ⁻¹ψ‖ₕ on Ham(M, ω). The metric is non‑degenerate (Lalonde–McDuff, 1995) and induces a topology strictly finer than the C⁰ topology. A central invariant derived from the Hofer metric is the displacement energy e(U) of a subset U ⊂ M: the minimal Hofer norm needed to move U off itself by a Hamiltonian isotopy. Gromov’s non‑squeezing theorem implies e(B²ⁿ(r)) = πr² for a standard ball, while for a symplectic cylinder Z²ⁿ(R) = B²(R) × ℝ²ⁿ⁻² the displacement energy is infinite, reflecting the rigidity of symplectic embeddings. The Hofer metric also controls the growth of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms: the asymptotic Hofer norm ‖φᵏ‖ₕ/k converges to the stable norm, which is related to spectral invariants from Floer homology. In particular, the spectral invariant c([M], H) equals the action of the maximal fixed point and satisfies the triangle inequality, making it a quasi‑morphism on the universal cover of Ham(M, ω). These tools have resolved long‑standing questions such as the C⁰‑rigidity of Hamiltonian flows (Buhovsky–Humilière–Seyfaddini, 2012) and the existence of infinitely many periodic orbits for Hamiltonians on certain symplectic manifolds.

Symplectic Capacities and Embedding Problems

A symplectic capacity is a function c that assigns to each symplectic manifold (M, ω) a number c(M, ω) ∈ [0, ∞] satisfying three axioms: monotonicity (if there exists a symplectic embedding (M₁, ω₁) → (M₂, ω₂) then c(M₁) ≤ c(M₂)), conformality (c(M, λω) = λ c(M, ω) for λ > 0), and non‑triviality (c(B²ⁿ(1)) = c(Z²ⁿ(1)) = π). The first capacity, introduced by Gromov, is the Gromov width w_G(M) = sup{πr² : B²ⁿ(r) symplectically embeds into M}. Ekeland and Hofer constructed a sequence of capacities cₖᴱᴴ for convex domains in ℝ²ⁿ using the action functional on the loop space; these capacities are symplectic invariants and satisfy cₖᴱᴴ(B²ⁿ(R)) = πR² for all k, while cₖᴱᴴ(Z²ⁿ(R)) = ∞ for k ≥ 2. For an ellipsoid E(a₁,…,aₙ) = {∑ |zᵢ|²/aᵢ < 1} the Ekeland–Hofer capacities are the numbers π aᵢ arranged in non‑decreasing order with multiplicities. This explicit computation solves many embedding problems: an ellipsoid E(a₁,…,aₙ) embeds into a ball B²ⁿ(R) iff max aᵢ ≤ R, and into a polydisk P(r₁,…,rₙ) iff the sorted aᵢ are dominated by the sorted rᵢ. The notion of symplectic packing — placing disjoint equal balls into a given manifold — leads to the packing numbers pₖ(M) = sup{ k π r² / vol(M) : k disjoint balls of radius r embed }. For ℂℙⁿ the full packing stability was proved by Biran (1997) using symplectic blow‑ups and the Seidel representation. Capacities also detect the non‑existence of exact Lagrangian embeddings: if a Lagrangian L ⊂ ℝ²ⁿ is exact, then its displacement energy is zero, contradicting the non‑zero capacity of any neighbourhood. Thus capacities provide a bridge between rigid symplectic geometry and flexible topological constructions.

Computing the Gromov width of an ellipsoid
Let E(1,4) = { |z₁|² + |z₂|²/4 < 1 } ⊂ ℝ⁴ with the standard symplectic form. Determine the Gromov width w_G(E(1,4)).
The Gromov width is the supremum of πr² such that a ball B⁴(r) symplectically embeds into E(1,4). By the monotonicity and conformality of capacities, w_G(E) equals the smallest Ekeland–Hofer capacity of E. The capacities of E(1,4) are π·1, π·4, π·4, … (the sequence of aᵢ with multiplicities). The smallest is π·1 = π. Hence w_G(E(1,4)) = π. Equivalently, the largest ball that fits has radius 1, so π·1² = π.
Exam‑day strategy
When a problem asks for a symplectic embedding obstruction, first list the relevant capacities (Gromov width, Ekeland–Hofer, Hofer–Zehnder). Check monotonicity: if the target has a smaller capacity than the source, the embedding is impossible. For ellipsoids and polydisks, remember that the Ekeland–Hofer capacities are just the defining parameters with multiplicities; this makes comparisons a simple ordering exercise.

Lagrangian Intersection Theory and the Arnold Conjecture in Higher Dimensions

Two Lagrangian submanifolds L₀, L₁ in a symplectic manifold (M, ω) intersect generically in isolated points when they are transverse. The Arnold conjecture for Lagrangian intersections asserts that the number of intersection points is at least the sum of Betti numbers of L₀ (with coefficients in a suitable field) provided L₀ and L₁ are Hamiltonian isotopic. Floer’s original construction defined a chain complex CF*(L₀, L₁) generated by intersection points, with differential counting pseudoholomorphic strips with boundary on L₀ and L₁. The homology HF*(L₀, L₁) is invariant under Hamiltonian isotopy and, when L₀ = L₁, is isomorphic to the singular cohomology H*(L; Λ) where Λ is a Novikov ring accounting for area of discs. The proof of the Arnold conjecture for general Lagrangians required overcoming transversality issues for multiply covered curves; this was achieved by Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono (2009) using Kuranishi structures and virtual fundamental cycles. Their machinery also yields the spectral sequence from the pearl complex (Morse theory on L combined with holomorphic discs) to Floer homology, which computes the quantum cohomology of M when L is a Lagrangian sphere. A striking application is the non‑displaceability of the Clifford torus in ℂℙⁿ: its Floer homology is non‑zero, so it cannot be displaced by any Hamiltonian isotopy. In the monotone setting, the minimal Maslov number N_L controls the grading; if N_L ≥ 2 the Floer differential squares to zero without Novikov coefficients. The theory extends to immersed Lagrangians and to the wrapped Fukaya category of Liouville domains, where the endomorphisms of a Lagrangian are given by its wrapped Floer cohomology, linking symplectic topology to homological mirror symmetry.

Symplectic Field Theory and the Compactness Theorem

Symplectic Field Theory (SFT), introduced by Eliashberg–Givental–Hofer (2000), is a unified framework for Gromov–Witten invariants, contact homology, and Legendrian contact homology. The basic geometric object is a symplectic cobordism (W, ω) between contact manifolds (Y₋, ξ₋) and (Y₊, ξ₊). One considers pseudoholomorphic curves in the completion Ŵ = (−∞,0]×Y₋ ∪ W ∪ [0,∞)×Y₊ with asymptotics to Reeb orbits on the ends. The SFT compactness theorem (Bourgeois–Eliashberg–Hofer–Wysocki–Zehnder, 2003) states that a sequence of such curves with bounded energy and genus has a subsequence converging to a holomorphic building — a collection of curves in the symplectizations ℝ×Y₋, ℝ×Y₊ and in W, joined at Reeb orbits. This generalizes Gromov’s compactness for closed curves and the compactness for curves with Legendrian boundary. The theorem is the analytical backbone of SFT: it ensures that the differential in the contact homology chain complex squares to zero, because the boundary of the 1‑dimensional moduli space consists of broken buildings corresponding to the differential applied twice. The compactness proof uses the Hofer energy bound, the monotonicity lemma for pseudoholomorphic curves, and a delicate analysis of neck‑stretching near Reeb orbits. Applications include the computation of contact homology of Brieskorn manifolds (Ustilovsky, 1999), the proof of the Weinstein conjecture for many contact manifolds via Taubes’s isomorphism with Seiberg–Witten Floer homology, and the definition of the rational SFT invariants of symplectic fillings. The compactness theorem also underlies the functoriality of SFT under exact symplectic cobordisms, leading to the notion of an SFT algebra and its relation to the wrapped Fukaya category of the filling.

Applications to Mirror Symmetry and Topological Strings

Mirror symmetry predicts an equivalence between the symplectic geometry of a Calabi–Yau manifold (M, ω) and the complex geometry of its mirror (M̌, J). The homological mirror symmetry conjecture (Kontsevich, 1994) states that the derived Fukaya category D^πFuk(M) is equivalent to the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves D^bCoh(M̌). The Fukaya category has objects given by Lagrangian submanifolds equipped with local systems, and morphism spaces given by Floer cohomology groups HF*(L₀, L₁). The A∞‑structure on this category encodes counts of pseudoholomorphic polygons with boundary on a sequence of Lagrangians. On the B‑side, the category of coherent sheaves is algebraic and accessible via sheaf cohomology. The SYZ conjecture (Strominger–Yau–Zaslow, 1996) provides a geometric construction: M should admit a special Lagrangian torus fibration, and M̌ is obtained by dualizing the fibres. This picture explains the exchange of symplectic and complex moduli and predicts that Gromov–Witten invariants of M (counts of pseudoholomorphic spheres) equal period integrals on M̌. In topological string theory, the A‑model topological string computes Gromov–Witten invariants, while the B‑model computes variations of Hodge structure. The open‑closed string map relates the Hochschild homology of the Fukaya category to quantum cohomology, and the closed‑open map relates quantum cohomology to the endomorphisms of the unit object. These structures have been rigorously established for toric Calabi–Yau manifolds (Chan–Lau–Leung–Tseng, 2011) and for the quintic threefold (Sheridan, 2015). The interplay between symplectic topology and mirror symmetry continues to drive advances in both fields, from the classification of Lagrangian tori to the computation of higher genus Gromov–Witten invariants via the holomorphic anomaly equations.

  • Confusing the Hofer metric with the C⁰ metric; the Hofer metric is strictly finer and non‑degenerate on Ham(M, ω).
  • Assuming all symplectic capacities coincide; different capacities (Gromov width, Ekeland–Hofer, Hofer–Zehnder) can give distinct values and detect different phenomena.
  • Neglecting the Novikov ring in Floer homology for non‑monotone Lagrangians; without it the differential may not square to zero.
  • Overlooking the role of the minimal Maslov number in grading Floer complexes; it determines whether the grading is ℤ or ℤ₂.
  • Treating SFT compactness as identical to Gromov compactness; SFT allows breaking at Reeb orbits, producing holomorphic buildings with multiple levels.
  • Confusing the A‑model and B‑model in mirror symmetry; the A‑model is symplectic (Fukaya category), the B‑model is complex (coherent sheaves).
  • Forgetting that the Arnold conjecture for Lagrangian intersections requires Hamiltonian isotopy, not just any symplectic isotopy.

The advanced topics above illustrate how symplectic topology connects dynamics, rigidity, and algebraic structures across dimensions.

Quantum Homology and the Seidel Representation

Quantum homology QH_*(M,ω) is a deformation of the ordinary singular homology of a closed symplectic manifold (M,ω) obtained by counting pseudoholomorphic spheres. The product, called the quantum product, is defined on the Novikov ring Λ = Z[[q^A]] where A∈ H2(M;Z) and q^A records the symplectic area ∫_Aω. For homology classes a,b∈ H_*(M) the quantum product a*b is a sum over spherical classes A of Gromov–Witten invariants ⟨ a,b,·⟩0,3^A multiplied by q^A. Associativity follows from the gluing axiom for the moduli space of stable maps overline{M}0,3(M,A). The unit for this product is the fundamental class [M].

The Seidel representation is a group homomorphism Scolon π1(Ham(M,ω))→ QH2n(M)× from the fundamental group of the Hamiltonian diffeomorphism group to the group of invertible elements of top degree in quantum homology. Given a loop {φ_t}t∈ S1 in Ham(M,ω), one constructs a Hamiltonian fibration over S2 with fibre M and a section of minimal Chern number. Counting sections of this fibration weighted by their symplectic area yields an element S({φ_t})∈ QH2n(M). Seidel proved that this map is a homomorphism and that its image lies in the group of units. The representation detects non‑trivial loops in Ham(M,ω); for example, on CP^n it recovers the generator of π1(Ham(CP^n))congZ/(n+1). The Seidel element also controls the action of π1(Ham) on Floer homology via the Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz isomorphism, and it appears in the computation of the quantum cohomology ring of toric manifolds through the Batyrev presentation.

Important technical points: the Novikov ring must be completed with respect to the valuation nu(q^A)=∫_Aω to ensure convergence of infinite sums. The grading on QH_*(M) is Z-graded only when the minimal Chern number N_M≥ 2; otherwise one works with a Z2 grading. The Seidel representation is compatible with the quantum product in the sense that S(γ1·γ2)=S(γ1)*S(γ2). For monotone symplectic manifolds the representation can be computed using the quantum Chevalley formula for the action of divisor classes. In the non‑monotone case one must incorporate the Novikov variable for each spherical class, and the representation takes values in the completed quantum homology QH2n(M;Λ).

Wrapped Fukaya Categories and Stop Removal

The wrapped Fukaya category W(M,Λ) of a Liouville manifold (M,λ) with a chosen stop Λ⊂∂_∞ M (a Legendrian submanifold of the contact boundary) was introduced by Abouzaid and Seidel to capture the symplectic topology of non‑compact exact symplectic manifolds. Objects are exact Lagrangian submanifolds L⊂ M that are cylindrical over Legendrians disjoint from Λ at infinity. Morphism complexes CW^*(L0,L1) are generated by Hamiltonian chords from L0 to L1 that escape to the stop; the differential counts pseudoholomorphic strips with boundary on the Lagrangians and with asymptotic markers at the stop. The A_∞‑structure is defined by counting pseudoholomorphic polygons with one output and several inputs, again with stop‑boundary conditions.

Stop removal is a fundamental functoriality result: if Λ1⊂Λ2 are stops, there is a canonical fully faithful embedding W(M,Λ2)hookrightarrowW(M,Λ1) induced by allowing chords to end on the larger stop. Sylvan proved that the wrapped Fukaya category with empty stop W(M,∅) is equivalent to the category of modules over the endomorphism algebra of a single cotangent fibre, recovering the Nadler–Zaslow correspondence with constructible sheaves. The stop encodes a “boundary condition at infinity” that makes the category invariant under Liouville homotopies fixing the stop. For a Weinstein domain W with skeleton Sk(W), the wrapped Fukaya category with stop equal to the Legendrian link of the skeleton is generated by the cocores of the critical handles; this gives a combinatorial model for W(W) via the Legendrian contact homology algebra of the attaching spheres.

Key applications include the computation of W(T^*Q) for a closed manifold Q, where the stop is the unit cotangent bundle and the category is equivalent to the derived category of constructible sheaves on Q. The stop removal theorem also underlies the proof of the generation criterion: a collection of Lagrangians generates W(M,Λ) if and only if their images generate the category after stop removal to ∅. In mirror symmetry, the wrapped Fukaya category of a punctured Riemann surface with stop at the punctures is equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on the mirror Landau–Ginzburg model, providing a categorical formulation of homological mirror symmetry for log Calabi–Yau varieties.

Technique
Explain how the Seidel representation detects a non‑trivial loop in Ham(CP2) and compute its image in quantum homology.
The generator of π1(Ham(CP2))congZ/3 is represented by the loop φ_t([z0:z1:z2])=[e2π i tz0:z1:z2]. The associated Hamiltonian fibration over S2 is the projectivisation of OoplusO(1). Sections correspond to lines in the fibres; the minimal Chern number is 3. Counting sections of area k yields the quantum homology element qk[CP2]. The Seidel element is S=q[CP1][CP2]+q2[CP1][CP2]+[CP2]. In the quantum homology ring QH_*(CP2)=Λ[H]/(H3=q) with H the hyperplane class, this element equals (1+H+H2)[CP2], which is a unit because (1+H+H2)(1-H)=1-H3=1-q. Hence the loop is non‑trivial and its Seidel image is the unit (1+H+H2)[CP2].
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for the Seidel element of a specific loop, first identify the Hamiltonian fibration and its minimal Chern number. Write the quantum homology ring presentation (e.g., Batyrev for toric manifolds). Compute the count of sections by degree using the quantum Chevalley formula or known Gromov–Witten invariants. Express the result in the Novikov ring and verify it is a unit by finding its inverse using the quantum relation. For wrapped Fukaya categories, remember that stop removal is fully faithful and that the empty‑stop category is generated by a single cotangent fibre; use this to reduce generation questions to checking whether a set of Lagrangians splits generates the category after stop removal.

Legendrian Contact Homology and the Chekanov–Eliashberg DGA

Legendrian contact homology is an invariant of Legendrian submanifolds Λ in a contact manifold (Y,xi=kerα) introduced by Chekanov and Eliashberg. The invariant takes the form of a differential graded algebra (DGA) (A(Λ),∂) over Z2 (or Z with signs after a choice of coherent orientations). The algebra A(Λ) is the free unital tensor algebra generated by the Reeb chords of Λ — integral curves of the Reeb vector field R_α that start and end on Λ. The grading of a chord c is given by the Conley–Zehnder index μCZ(c) shifted by n-3 where dim Y=2n-1. The differential ∂ counts rigid pseudoholomorphic disks in the symplectization R× Y with boundary on R×Λ and with one positive puncture asymptotic to a chord c and several negative punctures asymptotic to chords c1,…,c_k; the term contributed is ± c1⋯ c_k. The count is performed in the moduli space of such disks modulo R-translation, and the differential squares to zero because the boundary of the 1‑dimensional moduli space consists of broken configurations corresponding to ∂2.

The Chekanov–Eliashberg DGA is invariant under Legendrian isotopy up to stable tame isomorphism, which allows adding or removing pairs of generators with differential ∂ a=b. Augmentations varepsiloncolonA(Λ)toZ2 (DGA maps to the ground ring) give rise to linearized contact homology LCH_*^varepsilon(Λ), a graded vector space that is easier to compute and often distinguishes Legendrian knots with the same classical invariants (Thurston–Bennequin number and rotation number). For Legendrian knots in R3 with the standard contact structure, the DGA can be computed combinatorially from the front projection using the Ng resolution; the differential counts immersed polygons with corners at the cusps and crossings. The existence of an augmentation is equivalent to the existence of a graded normal ruling of the front diagram, a purely combinatorial condition. Higher order invariants such as the A_∞‑structure on the linearized complex and the Legendrian contact homology of satellites have been developed by Ekholm, Etnyre, Ng, and Sullivan.

Applications include the classification of Legendrian knots up to Legendrian isotopy in R3 and in the 1‑jet space J1(S1). The DGA also provides obstructions to exact Lagrangian fillings: if a Legendrian Λ bounds an exact Lagrangian L in the symplectization, then the DGA of Λ admits an augmentation induced by the Floer homology of L. Conversely, the non‑existence of augmentations proves non‑fillability. The Chekanov–Eliashberg DGA is functorial under exact Lagrangian cobordisms: a cobordism from Λ_- to Λ_+ induces a DGA map A(Λ_+)toA(Λ_-). This functoriality underlies the construction of the Legendrian contact homology category and its relation to the wrapped Fukaya category of the filling.

The Giroux Correspondence and Open Book Decompositions

The Giroux correspondence establishes a bijection between contact structures on a closed oriented 3‑manifold Y up to isotopy and open book decompositions of Y up to positive stabilization. An open book decomposition of Y is a pair (B,π) where B⊂ Y is a link (the binding) and πcolon Y∖ B→ S1 is a fibration whose fibres (the pages) are compact oriented surfaces with boundary B. The monodromy of the fibration is a diffeomorphism φ of a page Σ fixing the boundary; the open book is determined by the mapping class of φ in the mapping class group MCG(Σ,∂Σ). A positive stabilization adds a 1‑handle to the page and composes the monodromy with a right‑handed Dehn twist along a curve that runs once over the new handle. Giroux proved that two open books define isotopic contact structures if and only if they become isotopic after a sequence of positive stabilizations.

The contact structure xi associated to an open book (Σ,φ) is constructed by taking a neighbourhood of the binding modelled on ker(dθ+r2dφ) in cylindrical coordinates and extending over the pages as the kernel of a 1‑form that is dθ on the binding and dα on the pages, where α is a Liouville form on Σ with φ^*α-α=dH for a positive Hamiltonian H. The Reeb vector field is transverse to the pages and tangent to the binding. Conversely, given a contact structure xi, one can find a contact form α whose Reeb flow has a periodic orbit that serves as the binding; the pages are global surfaces of section for the Reeb flow, yielding an open book. The correspondence is natural with respect to contactomorphisms and mapping class group actions.

Key consequences: every contact 3‑manifold admits a compatible open book, so contact structures can be studied via mapping class groups. The classification of tight contact structures on a given 3‑manifold translates into the classification of open books up to positive stabilization. For example, the tight contact structure on S3 corresponds to the trivial open book with page a disk and monodromy the identity; overtwisted contact structures correspond to open books whose monodromy contains a left‑handed Dehn twist. The Giroux correspondence also underlies the proof of the Weinstein conjecture for all contact 3‑manifolds (Taubes, using Seiberg–Witten theory) because the existence of a Reeb orbit is equivalent to the existence of a binding in some open book. In higher dimensions, a generalization by Giroux and Mohsen replaces open books by “open book decompositions” with pages that are Liouville domains and monodromy a compactly supported symplectomorphism; the correspondence holds for contact manifolds of any dimension.

  • Confusing the quantum product with the ordinary cup product; the quantum product includes Novikov‑weighted Gromov–Witten invariants and is not graded‑commutative in the same way.
  • Assuming the Seidel representation lands in the ordinary homology; it lands in the top degree of quantum homology, which may be a non‑trivial unit only after Novikov completion.
  • Neglecting the role of the stop in the wrapped Fukaya category; changing the stop changes the category, and stop removal is not an equivalence in general.
  • Treating the Chekanov–Eliashberg DGA as an invariant of the underlying smooth knot; it is an invariant of the Legendrian isotopy class and can distinguish Legendrian knots with identical classical invariants.
  • Forgetting that augmentations of the DGA are required to define linearized contact homology; without an augmentation the linearized complex is not defined.
  • Misapplying the Giroux correspondence by ignoring positive stabilization; two open books may define the same contact structure only after a sequence of positive stabilizations.
  • Overlooking the distinction between tight and overtwisted contact structures in the open book picture; overtwisted structures correspond to monodromies containing left‑handed Dehn twists, which are not allowed for tight structures.

The advanced sections above provide the technical depth needed to tackle research‑level problems in symplectic topology and contact geometry.

hand/topology.html:
Covering Spaces and the Classification Theorem

A covering space of a topological space X is a space \~X together with a continuous surjection p: \~X → X such that every point x ∈ X has an open neighbourhood U whose preimage p⁻¹(U) is a disjoint union of open sets each mapped homeomorphically onto U by p. The classic example is the exponential map ℝ → S¹, t ↦ e2π i t, which makes ℝ the universal cover of the circle. The group of deck transformations (homeomorphisms \~X → \~X commuting with p) is isomorphic to the fundamental group π₁(X) when \~X is simply connected. The classification theorem states that for a path‑connected, locally path‑connected, semilocally simply connected space X, there is a bijection between isomorphism classes of connected covering spaces of X and conjugacy classes of subgroups of π₁(X). The universal cover corresponds to the trivial subgroup; the cover corresponding to a subgroup H ≤ π₁(X) has fundamental group isomorphic to H. This correspondence turns algebraic problems about subgroups into geometric problems about covering spaces, and it underlies the proof that every subgroup of a free group is free (the Nielsen–Schreier theorem). In practice, constructing the cover for a given subgroup often uses the Cayley graph of the group with respect to a generating set, where vertices are cosets and edges correspond to generators.

Higher Homotopy Groups and the Hurewicz Theorem

While the fundamental group π₁ captures 1‑dimensional holes, higher homotopy groups πₙ(X) for n ≥ 2 are defined using based maps from the n‑sphere Sⁿ into X, with homotopy as equivalence. Unlike π₁, all higher homotopy groups are abelian. For spheres, πₙ(Sⁿ) ≅ ℤ, generated by the identity map, while πₖ(Sⁿ) = 0 for k < n. The Hurewicz theorem provides a bridge to homology: if X is (n‑1)‑connected (i.e., πᵢ(X) = 0 for i < n), then the Hurewicz homomorphism h: πₙ(X) → Hₙ(X) is an isomorphism, and for i = n+1 it is an epimorphism. This allows computation of the first non‑trivial homotopy group via homology, which is often easier. For example, π₂(S²) ≅ H₂(S²) ≅ ℤ, and π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ (the Hopf fibration). The theorem also implies that a simply connected space with trivial homology groups up to dimension n is contractible up to that dimension (Whitehead's theorem). In algebraic topology exams, a typical question asks to compute π₃(S²) using the long exact sequence of the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² together with the Hurewicz isomorphism for S³.

Technique
Use the Hurewicz theorem and the long exact sequence of a fibration to compute π₃(S²).
The Hopf fibration gives a fiber sequence S¹ → S³ → S². The associated long exact sequence in homotopy contains … → π₃(S¹) → π₃(S³) → π₃(S²) → π₂(S¹) → … . Since π₃(S¹) = 0 and π₂(S¹) = 0, the map π₃(S³) → π₃(S²) is an isomorphism. By Hurewicz, π₃(S³) ≅ H₃(S³) ≅ ℤ. Hence π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ.
Strategy
When a problem asks for a higher homotopy group of a sphere or a fibration, first check whether the Hurewicz theorem applies (the space is sufficiently connected). Then write down the relevant long exact sequence of the fibration; many terms vanish because spheres have trivial homotopy groups in low dimensions. The remaining isomorphism often reduces the computation to a known homology group.

Cohomology Rings and the Cup Product

Cohomology groups Hⁿ(X; R) with coefficients in a ring R carry a graded‑commutative product called the cup product, ∪: Hᵖ(X) × Hᑫ(X) → Hᵖ⁺ᑫ(X). This turns the direct sum ⊕ₙ Hⁿ(X) into a ring, the cohomology ring H*(X). The cup product distinguishes spaces that have identical homology groups but different ring structures; for instance, the torus T² and the wedge S¹ ∨ S¹ ∨ S² have the same homology groups but different cup products (the torus has a non‑zero product in degree 2, the wedge does not). The Künneth formula for cohomology expresses H*(X × Y) as the tensor product of the cohomology rings of X and Y, up to a Tor term that vanishes over a field. Poincaré duality for a closed oriented n‑manifold M states that the cap product with the fundamental class [M] gives an isomorphism Hᵏ(M) ≅ Hₙ₋ₖ(M). In terms of cup product, this means the pairing Hᵏ(M) × Hⁿ⁻ᵏ(M) → Hⁿ(M) ≅ R is non‑degenerate. The ring structure is also essential for characteristic classes: Stiefel‑Whitney, Chern, and Pontryagin classes live in cohomology rings and their products encode geometric information about vector bundles. In examinations, a common task is to compute the cohomology ring of a product space such as ℂP² × S² using the known rings H*(ℂP²) ≅ ℤ[x]/(x³) (|x| = 2) and H*(S²) ≅ ℤ[y]/(y²) (|y| = 2), then apply the Künneth theorem to obtain H*(ℂP² × S²) ≅ ℤ[x, y]/(x³, y²).

Morse Theory and Critical Points

Morse theory relates the topology of a smooth manifold M to the critical points of a smooth function f: M → ℝ. A critical point p is non‑degenerate if the Hessian matrix of second derivatives at p is invertible; its index is the number of negative eigenvalues. The Morse lemma states that near a non‑degenerate critical point of index λ, there are coordinates in which f(x) = f(p) − x₁² − … − x_λ² + xλ+1² + … + x_n². The fundamental theorem of Morse theory says that as one passes a critical value, the sublevel set Mᵃ = f⁻¹(−∞, a] changes by attaching a λ‑cell. Consequently, M has the homotopy type of a CW complex with one cell of dimension λ for each critical point of index λ. The Morse inequalities relate the number of critical points of each index to the Betti numbers: for each k, the number of index‑k critical points is at least the k‑th Betti number bₖ. A perfect Morse function achieves equality, giving a minimal cell decomposition. The classic example is the height function on the torus standing vertically, which has four critical points (minimum, two saddles, maximum) matching the Betti numbers b₀ = 1, b₁ = 2, b₂ = 1. Morse theory also underlies the proof of the h‑cobordism theorem and the classification of high‑dimensional manifolds. In competitive exams, a typical question asks to determine the minimal number of critical points of a smooth function on a given manifold using the Morse inequalities and the Euler characteristic χ = Σ (−1)ᵏ bₖ.

Fixed Point Theorems: Brouwer, Lefschetz, and Applications

The Brouwer fixed point theorem states that every continuous map f: Dⁿ → Dⁿ from the closed n‑ball to itself has a fixed point. The proof uses homology: if f had no fixed point, one could construct a retraction r: Dⁿ → Sⁿ⁻¹, which would induce a surjection on Hₙ₋₁, contradicting Hₙ₋₁(Dⁿ) = 0. The Lefschetz fixed point theorem generalises this to compact polyhedra (or more generally compact ENRs): for a continuous map f: X → X, the Lefschetz number L(f) = Σ (−1)ᵏ tr(f*: Hₖ(X; ℚ) → Hₖ(X; ℚ)). If L(f) ≠ 0, then f has a fixed point. For the identity map, L(id) = χ(X), so any space with non‑zero Euler characteristic forces a fixed point for every map homotopic to the identity. The Lefschetz‑Hopf theorem refines this by expressing L(f) as a sum of indices of isolated fixed points. Applications include the Borsuk‑Ulam theorem (every continuous map Sⁿ → ℝⁿ identifies a pair of antipodal points) and the existence of equilibria in game theory (Nash equilibrium via Kakutani's fixed point theorem, a set‑valued generalisation). In examinations, a standard problem is to compute the Lefschetz number of a map on the torus T² induced by a linear map A ∈ GL(2, ℤ) on the universal cover ℝ²; the trace on H₁ is tr(A), on H₀ and H₂ it is 1, so L(f) = 2 − tr(A) + det(A). If this number is non‑zero, the map must have a fixed point.

  • Confusing the classification of covering spaces with the classification of subgroups of the fundamental group; the correspondence is up to conjugacy, not equality.
  • Assuming higher homotopy groups are non‑abelian; they are always abelian for n ≥ 2.
  • Neglecting the graded‑commutativity sign rule in cup product calculations, leading to incorrect ring structures.
  • Applying Morse inequalities without checking that the function is Morse (all critical points non‑degenerate).
  • Forgetting that the Lefschetz number uses rational coefficients; torsion in homology does not contribute.
  • Misidentifying the index of a critical point in Morse theory; the index equals the number of negative eigenvalues of the Hessian, not the dimension of the unstable manifold.
  • Overlooking that the Brouwer fixed point theorem fails for non‑compact or non‑convex domains, a common trap in applied problems.

Fiber Bundles and Vector Bundles — Local Triviality and Global Twisting

A fiber bundle consists of a total space E, a base space B, a projection π: E → B, and a fiber F such that every point b ∈ B has a neighborhood U with a homeomorphism φ: π⁻¹(U) → U × F satisfying π = pr₁ ∘ φ. The maps φ are local trivializations; on overlaps Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ they differ by transition functions gᵢⱼ: Uᵢ ∩ Uⱼ → Homeo(F) satisfying the cocycle condition gᵢⱼ gⱼₖ gₖᵢ = id. A vector bundle is a fiber bundle with fiber ℝⁿ (or ℂⁿ) and transition functions taking values in GL(n, ℝ) (or GL(n, ℂ)). The tangent bundle TM of a smooth manifold M is the canonical example; its transition functions are Jacobian matrices of coordinate changes. A section of a vector bundle is a continuous map s: B → E with π ∘ s = id; the zero section always exists. The Whitney sum E ⊕ F and tensor product E ⊗ F of vector bundles are defined fiberwise. A bundle is trivial if it is globally isomorphic to B × F; the obstruction to triviality is measured by characteristic classes. The clutching construction builds bundles over a suspension ΣX from a map X → GL(n); this gives a bijection between isomorphism classes of rank-n vector bundles over Sᵏ and homotopy classes [Sᵏ⁻¹, GL(n)]. For n large, πₖ₋₁(GL(n)) stabilizes to the topological K-theory group K⁻ᵏ(pt). The classifying space BO(n) (or BU(n)) has the property that isomorphism classes of rank-n vector bundles over a paracompact space X correspond to homotopy classes [X, BO(n)]. The universal bundle γⁿ → BO(n) pulls back to any bundle via its classifying map. In examinations, a standard problem asks to show that the tangent bundle of S² is non-trivial by computing its Euler class or by noting that a nowhere-zero section would contradict the hairy ball theorem.

Characteristic Classes — Measuring the Twisting of Bundles

Characteristic classes assign to each vector bundle E → B a cohomology class in H*(B; R) that vanishes if the bundle is trivial. They are natural: for a map f: B' → B, the class of the pullback bundle f*E is f* of the class of E. The four fundamental theories are Stiefel–Whitney classes wᵢ ∈ Hⁱ(B; ℤ/2) for real bundles, Chern classes cᵢ ∈ H²ⁱ(B; ℤ) for complex bundles, Pontryagin classes pᵢ ∈ H⁴ⁱ(B; ℤ) for real bundles (defined via pᵢ(E) = (−1)ⁱ c₂ᵢ(E ⊗ ℂ)), and the Euler class e ∈ Hⁿ(B; ℤ) for oriented rank-n real bundles. The total classes are w = 1 + w₁ + w₂ + …, c = 1 + c₁ + c₂ + …, p = 1 + p₁ + p₂ + …. They satisfy the Whitney sum formula: w(E ⊕ F) = w(E) ⌣ w(F), c(E ⊕ F) = c(E) ⌣ c(F), p(E ⊕ F) = p(E) ⌣ p(F) (mod 2-torsion). For a complex line bundle L, c₁(L) classifies it up to isomorphism: c₁: Pic(B) → H²(B; ℤ) is an isomorphism for paracompact B. The Euler class of an oriented rank-n bundle evaluates on the fundamental class of a closed oriented n-manifold to the Euler characteristic. The Thom isomorphism theorem states that for an oriented rank-n vector bundle π: E → B, the map Φ: Hᵏ(B) → Hᵏ⁺ⁿ(E, E B) given by Φ(x) = π*x ⌣ u is an isomorphism, where u ∈ Hⁿ(E, E B) is the Thom class; the Euler class is e = π*u|_B. The Wu formula expresses Stiefel–Whitney classes in terms of Steenrod squares: w = Sq(v) where v is the Wu class. For the tangent bundle of ℝPⁿ, w(TℝPⁿ) = (1 + a)ⁿ⁺¹ where a ∈ H¹(ℝPⁿ; ℤ/2) is the generator. In competitive exams, a typical question asks to compute the total Chern class of the tangent bundle of ℂPⁿ using the Euler sequence 0 → 𝒪 → 𝒪(1)ⁿ⁺¹ → TℂPⁿ → 0, yielding c(TℂPⁿ) = (1 + x)ⁿ⁺¹ where x = c₁(𝒪(1)) generates H²(ℂPⁿ; ℤ).

Worked Problem: Chern Classes of a Tensor Product
Let E and F be complex vector bundles of ranks 2 and 3 over a space X. Express the total Chern class c(E ⊗ F) in terms of the Chern roots of E and F.
Let the Chern roots of E be x₁, x₂ and those of F be y₁, y₂, y₃. Then c(E) = (1 + x₁)(1 + x₂) = 1 + c₁(E) + c₂(E) with c₁(E) = x₁ + x₂, c₂(E) = x₁x₂. Similarly c(F) = ∏(1 + yⱼ). The tensor product E ⊗ F has Chern roots xᵢ + yⱼ for i = 1,2, j = 1,2,3. Hence c(E ⊗ F) = ∏ᵢ∏ⱼ (1 + xᵢ + yⱼ). Expanding: the first Chern class is c₁(E ⊗ F) = 3c₁(E) + 2c₁(F). The second Chern class is c₂(E ⊗ F) = 3c₂(E) + 2c₂(F) + 4c₁(E)² + 3c₁(E)c₁(F) + c₁(F)² (derived by symmetric polynomial identities). In terms of the total Chern class, one writes c(E ⊗ F) = ∏ᵢ c(F)(xᵢ) where c(F)(t) = 1 + c₁(F)t + c₂(F)t² + c₃(F)t³ evaluated at t = xᵢ. This method using Chern roots (splitting principle) is the standard computational technique for characteristic classes of tensor products, exterior powers, and symmetric powers.
Exam Strategy: Splitting Principle
When asked to compute characteristic classes of constructed bundles (tensor products, duals, exterior powers), always invoke the splitting principle: pretend the bundle splits as a sum of line bundles with formal Chern roots. Compute the desired class as a symmetric polynomial in the roots, then rewrite in terms of the elementary symmetric polynomials (the actual Chern classes). This reduces every problem to algebra in the ring of symmetric functions. Memorise the formulas for c(E*), c(∧²E), c(Sym²E) in terms of Chern roots; they appear repeatedly in qualifying exams.

Spectral Sequences — Computing Homology of Fibrations

A spectral sequence is a sequence of differential graded modules (Eʳ, dʳ) with Eʳ⁺¹ = H(Eʳ, dʳ) converging to a graded module H* with a filtration. The Serre spectral sequence applies to a fibration F → E → B with B a path-connected CW complex and π₁(B) acting trivially on H*(F; R). Its E²-page is E²p,q = Hₚ(B; H_q(F; R)) (homology with local coefficients if the action is non-trivial), and it converges to Hp+q(E; R). The differential dʳ: Eʳp,q → Eʳp−r, q+r−1 has bidegree (−r, r−1). The edge homomorphisms give the maps Hₚ(E) → Hₚ(B) (projection) and H_q(F) → H_q(E) (inclusion) on the E^∞ page. The transgression τ: H_q(F) → Hq+1(B) is the differential dq+1 on the fiber column p = 0. For the path-loop fibration ΩX → PX → X with PX contractible, the Serre spectral sequence computes H*(ΩX) from H*(X) and yields the homology suspension isomorphism. The Eilenberg–Moore spectral sequence computes H*(F) from H*(E) and H*(B) for a pullback square. The Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes generalized homology E*(X) from ordinary homology H*(X; E*(pt)). In examinations, a classic problem is to compute H*(ΩSⁿ) using the Serre spectral sequence of ΩSⁿ → PSⁿ → Sⁿ: the E² page is Hₚ(Sⁿ; H_q(ΩSⁿ)) with only columns p = 0, n non-zero; the differential dₙ: Eⁿn, q → Eⁿ0, q+n−1 is an isomorphism for q > 0, yielding H_q(ΩSⁿ) ≅ Hq+n−1(Sⁿ) for q > 0, so H*(ΩSⁿ) ≅ ℤ[x] with |x| = n−1 (polynomial ring for n odd, divided power algebra for n even). Another standard exercise: use the Serre spectral sequence for S¹ → S²ⁿ⁺¹ → ℂPⁿ to recover the cohomology ring H*(ℂPⁿ) ≅ ℤ[x]/(xⁿ⁺¹).

Cobordism Theory and Surgery — Classifying Manifolds by Cutting and Pasting

Two closed n-manifolds M and N are cobordant if there exists a compact (n+1)-manifold W with ∂W = M ⊔ N. Cobordism is an equivalence relation; the set of cobordism classes forms the unoriented cobordism ring 𝔑* under disjoint union (addition) and Cartesian product (multiplication). Thom proved 𝔑* ⊗ ℚ = 0 and 𝔑* ≅ ℤ/2[x₂, x₄, x₅, x₆, x₈, …] where xᵢ is the class of a manifold with non-zero Stiefel–Whitney number wᵢ. The Pontryagin–Thom construction identifies 𝔑ₙ with the stable homotopy group πₙ(MO) of the Thom spectrum MO. Oriented cobordism Ω*SO is a polynomial ring ℤ[y₄, y₈, y₁₂, …] (generators in dimensions multiples of 4) after inverting 2; the signature and Pontryagin numbers classify oriented cobordism classes. Complex cobordism MU* is the universal complex-oriented cohomology theory; MU* ≅ ℤ[x₁, x₂, …] with |xᵢ| = 2i. Surgery is a technique to modify a manifold within its cobordism class: given an embedding Sᵏ × Dⁿ⁻ᵏ → M, remove Sᵏ × Dⁿ⁻ᵏ and glue in Dᵏ⁺¹ × Sⁿ⁻ᵏ⁻¹. The effect on homology is to kill a class in Hₖ(M) and create one in Hn−k−1(M). The s-cobordism theorem (Smale, Barden–Mazur–Stallings) states that an h-cobordism W between simply connected manifolds of dimension ≥ 5 is trivial (i.e., W ≅ M × I) iff its Whitehead torsion τ(W, M) ∈ Wh(π₁(M)) vanishes. This underlies the classification of high-dimensional manifolds: the surgery exact sequence relates the structure set 𝒮(M) (homotopy equivalences to M up to cobordism) to the normal invariants [M, G/O] and the L-groups L*(π₁(M)). In competitive exams, a typical question asks to show that ℂP² is not a boundary (i.e., not null-cobordant) by computing its Pontryagin number p₁[ℂP²] = 3 or its signature σ(ℂP²) = 1; since oriented cobordism invariants vanish on boundaries, ℂP² cannot bound an oriented 5-manifold.

Obstruction Theory and Postnikov Towers — Lifting Maps and Classifying Homotopy Types

Obstruction theory addresses the problem: given a map f: X → Y defined on the k-skeleton of a CW complex X, when does it extend to the (k+1)-skeleton? For each (k+1)-cell ek+1 with attaching map φ: Sᵏ → Xᵏ, the composition f ∘ φ: Sᵏ → Y defines an element of πₖ(Y). These elements assemble into a cochain ck+1(f) ∈ Ck+1(X; πₖ(Y)) (with local coefficients if Y is not simple). The obstruction to extending f is the cohomology class [ck+1(f)] ∈ Hk+1(X; πₖ(Y)). If it vanishes, extensions exist and are classified by Hᵏ(X; πₖ(Y)). The primary obstruction is the first non-zero one. For lifting problems f: X → B along a fibration p: E → B, the obstructions lie in Hk+1(X; πₖ(F)) where F is the fiber. Postnikov towers decompose a space Y into a tower of fibrations … → Yₙ → Yn−1 → … → Y₁ where Yₙ has the same homotopy groups as Y up to degree n and vanishing above. The k-invariant kₙ ∈ Hn+1(Yₙ; πₙ(Y)) classifies the fibration Yₙ → Yn−1 with fiber K(πₙ(Y), n). A space is determined up to weak equivalence by its homotopy groups and k-invariants. The Whitehead theorem states that a map inducing isomorphisms on all homotopy groups is a weak homotopy equivalence; for CW complexes it is a homotopy equivalence. The Hurewicz theorem relates the first non-vanishing homotopy group to homology: if Y is (n−1)-connected, πₙ(Y) ≅ Hₙ(Y) and πn+1(Y) → Hn+1(Y) is surjective with kernel the image of the Whitehead product. In examinations, a standard problem asks to compute the first k-invariant of S²: the Postnikov tower starts S² → K(ℤ, 2) = ℂP^∞ with fiber K(ℤ, 3); the k-invariant is the fundamental class ι ∈ H³(K(ℤ, 2); ℤ) corresponding to the generator of π₃(S²) ≅ ℤ. Another common question: show that any map f: ℂPⁿ → S²ⁿ is null-homotopic for n > 1 by obstruction theory — the primary obstruction lies in H²ⁿ(ℂPⁿ; π2n−1(S²ⁿ)) = 0 since π2n−1(S²ⁿ) = 0 for n > 1.

  • Confusing the Whitney sum formula for Pontryagin classes: p(E ⊕ F) = p(E) ⌣ p(F) holds only modulo 2-torsion; the correct formula involves the Chern classes of the complexification.
  • Misapplying the Serre spectral sequence when the action of π₁(B) on H*(F) is non-trivial; one must use homology with local coefficients, not ordinary homology.
  • Forgetting that the Euler class of an oriented bundle is defined only when the bundle is oriented; for non-orientable bundles one uses the twisted Euler class in cohomology with local coefficients.
  • Assuming that cobordism invariants (Stiefel–Whitney numbers, Pontryagin numbers, signature) are sufficient to classify manifolds up to diffeomorphism; they classify only up to cobordism, and exotic spheres show that diffeomorphism classification is strictly finer.
  • Neglecting the local coefficient system in obstruction theory when Y is not a simple space (i.e., π₁(Y) acts non-trivially on πₖ(Y)); the obstruction cochain lives in cohomology with twisted coefficients.
  • Misidentifying the k-invariant in a Postnikov tower: it lies in Hn+1(Yₙ; πₙ(Y)), not in Hn+1(Yn−1; πₙ(Y)); the fibration is classified by a map Yn−1 → K(πₙ(Y), n+1) whose pullback of the fundamental class gives the k-invariant.
  • Overlooking that the splitting principle for characteristic classes requires working in a ring where the Chern roots exist formally; one cannot simply "split" a bundle without passing to a suitable flag bundle or using the algebraic splitting principle.
The advanced tools of fiber bundles, characteristic classes, spectral sequences, cobordism, and obstruction theory form the backbone of modern geometric topology and are essential for solving the classification problems that appear in rigorous competitive examinations.
