hand/geometric-measure-theory.html:
Tangent Measures and Preiss's Rectifiability Theorem

The concept of tangent measures, introduced by Preiss in 1987, provides a powerful blow-up analysis tool for arbitrary Radon measures. Given a Radon measure μ on ℝⁿ and a point x ∈ spt μ, a tangent measure of μ at x is any weak limit of the rescaled measures μx,r(A) = r-k μ(x + rA) as r → 0, where k is a fixed scaling exponent. The set of all such limits is denoted Tan_k(μ, x). Preiss proved that if 0 < Θ^k(μ, x) < ∞ and Θ^k(μ, x) = Θ^k(μ, x) (the upper and lower k-densities coincide and are positive and finite), then every tangent measure in Tan_k(μ, x) is a k-uniform measure — a measure ν satisfying ν(A) = c H^k(A ∩ V) for some k-plane V and constant c > 0. The landmark Preiss Rectifiability Theorem (1987) states: if μ is a Radon measure on ℝⁿ with 0 < Θ^k(μ, x) < ∞ for μ-a.e. x, then μ is k-rectifiable if and only if for μ-a.e. x, every tangent measure in Tan_k(μ, x) is a flat measure (a constant multiple of H^k restricted to a k-plane). This characterization replaces the geometric definition of rectifiability (covering by Lipschitz images) with an infinitesimal, measure-theoretic condition. The proof uses the "density point" method and a delicate induction on dimension, exploiting the fact that tangent measures of tangent measures are again tangent measures. A key corollary: if μ is a Radon measure with positive finite k-density almost everywhere and all tangent measures are flat, then μ is absolutely continuous with respect to H^k restricted to a k-rectifiable set. This theorem resolved a long-standing question of Besicovitch and Federer and underpins the modern theory of quantitative rectifiability, including the David-Semmes theory of uniformly rectifiable sets and the recent solution of the Kakeya conjecture in ℝ³ by Guth and Katz.

Almgren's Stratification of Singular Sets and Dimension Reduction

Almgren's stratification theorem (1983, published 2000) provides a structural description of the singular set of area-minimizing integral currents (and more generally, stationary integral varifolds). For an integer rectifiable current T minimizing mass in its homology class, the singular set sing(T) = spt T reg(T) is the set of points where T fails to be a smooth embedded submanifold. Almgren proved that sing(T) can be decomposed into strata S^j(T) for j = 0, 1, ..., k-2, where S^j(T) consists of points x such that no tangent cone at x splits off a (j+1)-dimensional plane. Equivalently, the space of tangent cones at x contains no (j+1)-dimensional subspace of translations. The stratification satisfies dim_H(S^j(T)) ≤ j, where dim_H denotes Hausdorff dimension. The proof uses Federer's dimension reduction principle: if a tangent cone at x splits off a line, then the singular set near x is locally a product of a line with a lower-dimensional singular set. By induction on dimension, the top stratum Sk-2(T) has dimension at most k-2. For codimension-1 area-minimizing currents (hypersurfaces), the singular set has dimension at most k-7 by the Simons-Federer theorem, so Sk-8 is the highest nonempty stratum. In higher codimension, Almgren's big regularity paper (2000) showed that the singular set has dimension at most k-2, which is sharp (e.g., the holomorphic variety {z₁² + z₂² + z₃² = 0} in ℂ³ ≅ ℝ⁶ has an isolated singularity at 0). The stratification is effective: Cheeger-Naber (2015) proved quantitative versions with Minkowski content bounds, and Naber-Valtorta (2017) established rectifiable Reifenberg theorems for the strata. This stratification is the foundation for the partial regularity theory of harmonic maps, Yang-Mills connections, and the Navier-Stokes equations.

Worked Example: Stratification of a Cone
Consider the 2-dimensional cone C = {(x, y, z) ∈ ℝ³ : z = √(x² + y²)} as an integral current. Determine its singular set and Almgren stratification.
The cone C is a 2-dimensional area-minimizing integral current in ℝ³ (it is a minimizing hypersurface except at the vertex). The singular set is sing(C) = {(0, 0, 0)}, the vertex. At any point x ≠ 0, the tangent cone is a half-plane (smooth). At the vertex 0, the tangent cone is C itself. The tangent cone C does not split off any line (it is not a product ℝ × C' for any 1-dimensional cone C'), so the vertex belongs to S0(C). Since the singular set is a single point, dim_H(S0) = 0 ≤ 0, consistent with the stratification theorem. There are no higher strata S^j for j ≥ 1. This illustrates that for 2-dimensional area-minimizing currents in ℝ³, the singular set is isolated points (dimension 0 = k-2).
Exam Strategy: Stratification Dimensions
Memorize the key dimension bounds: for area-minimizing k-currents, singular set dimension ≤ k-2 (Almgren); for codimension-1 (hypersurfaces), singular set dimension ≤ k-7 (Simons-Federer). The stratum S^j has dimension ≤ j. In exam questions, identify the dimension k of the current and the codimension to apply the correct bound. A common trap is confusing the stratum index j with the dimension of the current k.

Sets of Finite Perimeter, Caccioppoli Sets, and the De Giorgi Structure Theorem

A set E ⊂ ℝⁿ has finite perimeter if its characteristic function χ_E is a function of bounded variation (BV), i.e., the distributional gradient Dχ_E is a finite Radon vector measure. The perimeter of E in an open set U is P(E, U) = |Dχ_E|(U) = sup{∫_E div φ dx : φ ∈ C_c^∞(U, ℝⁿ), |φ| ≤ 1}. Such sets are called Caccioppoli sets after De Giorgi (1954). The De Giorgi Structure Theorem states that for a set E of finite perimeter, the reduced boundary ∂*E — the set of points x where the measure-theoretic normal ν_E(x) = limr→0 Dχ_E(B(x,r)) / |Dχ_E|(B(x,r)) exists and has unit length — is (n-1)-rectifiable, and |Dχ_E| = Hn-1 ⌞ ∂*E. Moreover, at Hn-1-a.e. x ∈ ∂*E, the blow-up of E at x converges to a half-space {y : ⟨y - x, ν_E(x)⟩ > 0}. This means sets of finite perimeter have a well-defined measure-theoretic boundary with a normal vector almost everywhere, generalizing the classical boundary of C¹ domains. The Gauss-Green theorem holds: ∫_E div φ dx = -∫∂*E φ·ν_E dHn-1 for all φ ∈ C_c1(ℝⁿ, ℝⁿ). The isoperimetric inequality in ℝⁿ takes the sharp form P(E) ≥ n ω_n1/n |E|(n-1)/n, with equality iff E is a ball (up to measure zero). Sets of finite perimeter are the natural domain for the relaxed formulation of the Plateau problem and for the study of minimal surfaces via the direct method in the calculus of variations. The compactness theorem: if sup_i P(E_i) < ∞ and |E_i| ≤ C, then a subsequence converges in L1_loc to a set E of finite perimeter with P(E) ≤ liminf P(E_i). This underpins the existence of isoperimetric regions and solutions to the prescribed mean curvature problem.

Monotonicity Formulas: Huisken, Almgren Frequency, and Applications

Monotonicity formulas are the analytical backbone of regularity theory in GMT and geometric PDE. Huisken's monotonicity formula (1990) for mean curvature flow states: if Σ_t is a smooth MCF in ℝⁿ and ρx₀,t₀(x,t) = (4π(t₀-t))-k/2 exp(-|x-x₀|²/(4(t₀-t))) is the backward heat kernel, then d/dt ∫Σ_t ρx₀,t₀ dH^k = -∫Σ_t |H + (x-x₀)^⟂/(2(t₀-t))|² ρx₀,t₀ dH^k ≤ 0. The quantity Θ(Σ_t, (x₀,t₀)) = ∫Σ_t ρx₀,t₀ dH^k is non-increasing in t and its limit as t → t₀ is the Gaussian density of the flow at (x₀,t₀). This formula classifies Type I singularities as self-shrinkers (H = -x^⟂/2) and is essential for White's regularity theorem. Almgren's frequency function (1979) for harmonic functions (and more generally, for solutions of elliptic PDE) is N(r) = r ∫B_r |∇u|² / ∫∂B_r u². For u harmonic, N(r) is non-decreasing in r, and its limit as r → 0 is the order of vanishing of u at 0. This function controls the nodal set {u = 0} and proves its (n-1)-rectifiability and Minkowski content bounds. For stationary varifolds, the classical monotonicity formula is d/dr (r-k ||V||(B_r(x))) = r-k-1 ∫B_r(x) |(y-x)^⟂|² / |y-x|k+2 d||V||(y) ≥ 0, which implies the density Θ^k(||V||, x) exists and is upper semicontinuous. The almost-monotonicity formula for varifolds with bounded mean curvature (Allard, 1972) adds a term involving ∫ |H_V|. These formulas are the primary tools for blow-up analysis, dimension reduction, and the proof of ε-regularity theorems. In the quantitative stratification of Cheeger-Naber, the frequency function is replaced by a scale-invariant L² excess functional, and monotonicity of this excess yields effective Minkowski bounds on the singular strata.

The Deformation Theorem, Flat Chains, and Plateau's Problem in Higher Codimension

The Federer-Fleming deformation theorem (1960) is the combinatorial heart of GMT. It states: for any integer rectifiable k-current T in ℝⁿ with compact support and M(T) + M(∂T) < ∞, and for any ε > 0, there exists a polyhedral k-chain P (a finite sum of oriented k-simplices with integer multiplicities) such that F(T - P) < ε, M(P) ≤ C M(T), and M(∂P) ≤ C M(∂T), where F is the flat norm and C depends only on n, k. The proof uses a dyadic grid and a "pushing" argument that projects T onto the skeleta of the grid, controlling the mass increase at each step. This theorem implies that integer rectifiable currents can be approximated by polyhedral chains in the flat topology, which is the key compactness ingredient for the Federer-Fleming solution of Plateau's problem: the space of integral currents with bounded mass and boundary mass is compact in the flat norm, so a mass-minimizing sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit is an area-minimizing integral current. In higher codimension (n > k+1), the regularity of area-minimizing currents is much more subtle. Almgren's big regularity paper (2000, 1700 pages) proved that the singular set of an area-minimizing k-current in ℝⁿ has Hausdorff dimension at most k-2. The proof introduces the center manifold construction, a multi-valued function theory (Q-valued functions), and a delicate blow-up analysis using the frequency function. The deformation theorem also underlies the theory of flat chains with coefficients in a normed abelian group G (Federer, Fleming, White). For G = ℤ₂, flat chains mod 2 solve Plateau's problem without orientability assumptions. The flat norm F_G(T) = inf{M_G(R) + M_G(S) : T = R + ∂S} makes the space of G-flat chains a complete metric space. This framework is essential for the Almgren-Pitts min-max theory for minimal hypersurfaces, where the min-max limit is a stationary integral varifold obtained as a limit of flat chains.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the scaling exponent in tangent measures. The correct scaling for a k-dimensional measure is r-k, not r-n. Using r-n gives trivial limits (zero or infinite) for k < n.
  • Trap 2: Assuming Almgren's stratification bound k-2 applies to all stationary varifolds. It holds for area-minimizing currents; for general stationary varifolds, the singular set can have dimension k-1 (e.g., a union of two planes intersecting along a line).
  • Trap 3: Mixing up the reduced boundary ∂*E and the topological boundary ∂E for Caccioppoli sets. The reduced boundary is (n-1)-rectifiable and carries the perimeter measure; the topological boundary can be much larger (e.g., a dense open set with finite perimeter).
  • Trap 4: Forgetting that Huisken's monotonicity formula requires the backward heat kernel centered at the singular point (x₀, t₀). Using the forward heat kernel or a fixed center gives a different (non-monotone) quantity.
  • Trap 5: Stating that the deformation theorem approximates any current by polyhedral chains. It only holds for integer rectifiable currents (or flat chains with coefficients in a discrete group). General normal currents cannot be approximated in flat norm by polyhedral chains with mass control.
  • Trap 6: Confusing the frequency function N(r) for harmonic functions with the density Θ(r) for varifolds. N(r) is non-decreasing and measures vanishing order; Θ(r) is non-decreasing (for stationary varifolds) and measures density. They are related but distinct monotone quantities.
  • Trap 7: Assuming the isoperimetric inequality P(E) ≥ n ω_n1/n |E|(n-1)/n holds for all sets of finite perimeter without the condition that E has finite measure. Sets of infinite measure can have finite perimeter (e.g., a half-space) and violate the inequality.

hand/schramm-loewner.html:
Multifractal Spectrum and Intersection Exponents

The multifractal spectrum of an SLE curve quantifies how the harmonic measure scales near the trace. For chordal SLEκ in the upper half‑plane, the probability that the curve passes within distance ε of a boundary point x behaves like εα where α varies with the local geometry. The spectrum f(α) is obtained from the Legendre transform of the moment scaling exponents ξ(q) defined by E[|g′t(x)|q] ∼ t−ξ(q). Lawler, Schramm and Werner (2001) computed ξ(q) = ( (4+κ)q − κ q2 ) / (8κ) for q ≤ (4+κ)/κ, and showed that the spectrum is a concave parabola with maximum at α = 1 + κ/8. Intersection exponents describe the probability that two independent SLEκ curves avoid each other up to time t. For κ ≤ 4 the exponent is ξ2(κ) = (8−κ)(6−κ)/(2κ). These exponents enter the derivation of the Hausdorff dimension of the SLE trace, d = 1 + κ/8 for κ ≤ 8, and of the dimension of the set of double points, ddouble = 2 − (8−κ)(6−κ)/(2κ). The same formalism yields the multifractal spectrum of the harmonic measure on the SLE hull, which matches the predictions from conformal field theory with central charge c = (6−κ)(3κ−8)/(2κ). Understanding these exponents is essential for problems that ask for the scaling of crossing probabilities or the dimension of exceptional sets.

SLE Duality and Reversibility

SLE duality relates chordal SLEκ to chordal SLE16/κ through the outer boundary of the trace. For κ > 4 the trace is not simple; its outer boundary is a simple curve that has the law of SLE16/κ. This duality was proved by Zhan (2008) and Dubédat (2009) using the commutation relations of the Loewner flow. Reversibility, established by Zhan (2015) for κ ≤ 4 and by Miller and Sheffield (2016) for all κ ∈ (0,8), states that the time‑reversal of a chordal SLEκ curve from 0 to ∞ in the upper half‑plane has the same law as an SLEκ curve from ∞ to 0, up to a conformal automorphism. The proof uses the imaginary geometry coupling with the Gaussian free field and the fact that the GFF is invariant under reflection. Duality and reversibility together imply that the law of the SLE trace is symmetric under swapping the endpoints and under taking the outer boundary when κ > 4. These properties are frequently tested in questions that ask to identify the law of the boundary of an SLE6 cluster (answer: SLE8/3) or to argue that the scaling limit of the percolation exploration path is reversible.

Worked Example: Identifying the Dual Curve
A critical percolation exploration path on the triangular lattice converges to SLE6. What is the law of the outer boundary of this path in the scaling limit?
The outer boundary of an SLEκ trace for κ > 4 is known to be an SLE16/κ curve (Zhan 2008). Substituting κ = 6 gives 16/6 = 8/3. Therefore the outer boundary converges to chordal SLE8/3. This curve is simple and describes the scaling limit of the self‑avoiding walk, consistent with the prediction that the percolation hull boundary is in the same universality class as SAW.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “outer boundary” or “hull” of an SLE trace, immediately apply the κ → 16/κ duality. Memorise the pairs (2,8), (3,16/3), (4,4), (6,8/3), (8,2). For reversibility, recall that the time‑reversed curve has the same law for all κ ∈ (0,8); this fact is often used to simplify boundary condition arguments.

Imaginary Geometry and Flow Lines

Imaginary geometry, developed by Miller and Sheffield (2012‑2017), constructs SLEκ curves as flow lines of a complex Gaussian free field h + iχ, where χ = 2/√κ − √κ/2. The field h is a zero‑boundary GFF on a simply connected domain D. For a given angle θ, the flow line starting at a boundary point is the solution of the ordinary differential equation dz/dt = ei(θ + χ h(z)). The resulting random curve is an SLEκ(ρL, ρR) process with force points determined by the boundary data of h. When κ ≤ 4 the flow lines are simple and do not cross; for κ > 4 they can bounce off the boundary and merge, reflecting the non‑simple nature of SLEκ. The coupling of multiple flow lines with different angles yields a family of non‑crossing SLE curves that partition the domain, providing a geometric realisation of the conformal welding of quantum surfaces. This framework also gives a rigorous construction of the SLEκ branching tree (the “SLE fan”) and proves the locality property for κ = 6. Examiners often ask to identify the value of χ for a given κ or to explain why flow lines with angle difference π are the same curve traced in opposite directions.

Quantum Loewner Evolution and Conformal Welding

The quantum Loewner evolution (QLE) introduced by Miller and Sheffield (2016) describes the growth of a random curve on a Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface. Let γ ∈ (0,2) be the LQG parameter related to κ by γ = √κ for κ ≤ 4 and γ = 4/√κ for κ ≥ 4. The QLE(γ2, η) process grows a curve by adding quantum area at rate 1 and quantum boundary length at rate η. When η = 0 the curve is an SLEκ on a γ‑LQG surface; when η ≠ 0 the curve is an SLEκ(ρ) with force points. Conformal welding of two independent γ‑LQG surfaces along their boundaries produces a sphere decorated by an SLEκ curve, where κ = γ2 for γ ≤ √2 and κ = 16/γ2 for γ ≥ √2. This welding is the continuum analogue of the mating‑of‑trees bijection for random planar maps. The Sheffield bijection (peanosphere) identifies the pair of continuum random trees encoded by the Brownian excursion with the SLE8‑decorated LQG sphere. These results connect the scaling limits of random planar maps (the Brownian map) with SLE and LQG, and they are the basis for recent proofs of the convergence of uniform random triangulations to the Brownian map. Questions may ask to state the relation between γ and κ, or to explain why the welding of two γ‑LQG disks yields an SLEκ interface.

Numerical Simulation and Convergence Rates

Simulating SLE curves is essential for testing conjectures and for applications in image analysis. The standard algorithm discretises the Loewner equation using a time step Δt and updates the driving function Wt = √κ Bt where Bt is a Brownian motion. The conformal maps gt are approximated by the slit map composition method (the “zipper” algorithm) or by solving the Loewner PDE on a grid. Kennedy (2009) proved that the zipper algorithm converges with error O(Δt1/2) in the uniform metric for κ ≤ 4. For κ > 4 the trace self‑touches, and the convergence rate deteriorates; adaptive time‑stepping near hitting times restores O(Δt1/2) accuracy. The harmonic explorer and the discrete Gaussian free field provide alternative lattice‑based simulations that converge to SLE4 with rate O(a1/2) where a is the lattice spacing. Recent work by Johansson Viklund et al. (2020) shows that the Schramm‑Loewner evolution can be sampled exactly on a finite graph using the Wilson algorithm for uniform spanning trees, giving SLE8 without discretisation error. In examinations, you may be asked to compare the computational complexity of the zipper algorithm (O(N2) for N steps) with the PDE method (O(N3)) and to explain why the zipper method is preferred for high‑precision studies of the SLE trace geometry.

  • Confusing the duality exponent: the outer boundary of SLEκ is SLE16/κ, not SLEκ/16.
  • Assuming reversibility holds for κ ≥ 8; it is only proved for κ ∈ (0,8).
  • Mixing the γ–κ relation: γ = √κ for κ ≤ 4, but γ = 4/√κ for κ ≥ 4.
  • Stating that the multifractal spectrum is linear; it is a concave parabola derived from ξ(q).
  • Claiming the zipper algorithm converges with order Δt for all κ; the rate is Δt1/2 and requires adaptive steps for κ > 4.
  • Forgetting that the GFF coupling constant χ = 2/√κ − √κ/2 changes sign at κ = 4.
  • Misidentifying the scaling limit of the harmonic explorer as SLE2 instead of SLE4.

These advanced topics complete the theoretical toolkit needed to tackle research‑level problems and the most demanding examination questions on Schramm‑Loewner evolution.

hand/harmonic-analysis.html:
Carleson's Theorem and Pointwise Convergence of Fourier Series

Carleson's theorem (1966) settled a century‑old problem: the Fourier series of an L² function on the circle converges almost everywhere. The proof uses a delicate time‑frequency decomposition known as the Carleson operator, which dominates the partial sum operators S_N f(x) = Σ|n|≤N ĉ_n einx. The key estimate is the L² boundedness of the maximal Carleson operator C f(x) = sup_N |S_N f(x)|. Carleson introduced a stopping‑time argument that splits the frequency axis into tiles and controls the contribution of each tile by a tree‑selection lemma. Hunt later extended the result to L^p for 1 < p < ∞. The theorem fails at the endpoint p = 1; Kolmogorov constructed an L¹ function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere. The modern proof via the Lacey‑Thiele time‑frequency analysis replaces the original complex analytic methods with a combinatorial tile‑selection algorithm that is now standard in harmonic analysis courses.

An important corollary is the almost everywhere convergence of Fourier series for functions of bounded variation, which follows from the L² result and the fact that BV ⊂ L². The theorem also implies the pointwise convergence of the Fourier transform inversion formula for L² functions on ℝ, after a suitable periodization argument. Examiners often test the distinction between norm convergence (which holds in L^p for 1 < p < ∞) and pointwise convergence (which requires Carleson's theorem). A common trap is to claim that Fejér's theorem gives pointwise convergence for all continuous functions; Fejér only guarantees uniform convergence of Cesàro means, not of the original partial sums.

The T(b) Theorem and Multilinear Calderón‑Zygmund Theory

The T(b) theorem, proved by David, Journé, and Semmes in the 1980s, generalizes the T(1) theorem to operators that are not necessarily bounded on L² but satisfy testing conditions on accretive functions. A function b is accretive if Re b(x) ≥ c > 0 almost everywhere. The theorem states: let T be a Calderón‑Zygmund operator with kernel K satisfying the standard size |K(x,y)| ≤ C/|x−y|^n and smoothness |∇_x K(x,y)| + |∇_y K(x,y)| ≤ C/|x−y|n+1. If there exist accretive functions b₁, b₂ such that T(b₁) and T*(b₂) belong to BMO and T satisfies the weak boundedness property, then T extends to a bounded operator on L². The proof uses a corona decomposition of the space into regions where b₁ and b₂ are close to constants, reducing the problem to the T(1) theorem on each region.

Multilinear Calderón‑Zygmund theory extends these ideas to operators acting on several functions, such as the bilinear Hilbert transform BHT(f,g)(x) = p.v. ∫ f(x−t) g(x+t) dt/t. The boundedness of BHT from L^p × L^q to L^r (with 1/p + 1/q = 1/r) was established by Lacey and Thiele using a sophisticated time‑frequency analysis that combines the Carleson operator with a paraproduct decomposition. The multilinear T(b) theorem provides necessary and sufficient conditions for boundedness of multilinear singular integrals on product spaces. These results are central to modern harmonic analysis and appear in advanced problem sets on paraproducts, commutators, and the boundedness of the Cauchy integral on Lipschitz curves.

Technique: Verifying the T(b) hypotheses
Let T be a Calderón‑Zygmund operator with kernel K(x,y) = (x−y)/|x−y|n+1 (the Riesz transform). Choose b₁(x) = 1 + iε x₁ and b₂(x) = 1 − iε x₁ for a small ε > 0. Show that b₁ and b₂ are accretive and compute T(b₁), T*(b₂). Determine whether the T(b) theorem guarantees L² boundedness of T.
The functions b₁, b₂ have real part 1, so they are accretive with constant c = 1. The Riesz transform R_j is a Calderón‑Zygmund operator that is known to be bounded on L²; its adjoint is −R_j. Since R_j(1) = 0 and R_j(x₁) is a constant multiple of the identity, both R_j(b₁) and R_j*(b₂) are bounded functions, hence belong to BMO. The weak boundedness property holds because the kernel satisfies the standard estimates. Therefore all hypotheses of the T(b) theorem are satisfied, and the theorem confirms the L² boundedness of the Riesz transform — a result that can also be obtained directly from Fourier multiplier theory.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorize the three pillars of the T(b) theorem: accretivity of the testing functions, BMO membership of T(b) and T*(b), and the weak boundedness property. In multiple‑choice questions, distractors often replace accretivity with mere boundedness or omit the weak boundedness condition. Recognizing the exact phrasing saves time.

Wavelet Frames and Gabor Systems in Time‑Frequency Analysis

Wavelet frames provide stable, redundant expansions of L²(ℝ) functions with simultaneous localization in time and scale. A wavelet frame is generated by dilations and translations of a single function ψ: {ψj,k(x) = 2j/2 ψ(2^j x − k) : j,k ∈ ℤ}. The frame condition A‖f‖² ≤ Σ |⟨f, ψj,k⟩|² ≤ B‖f‖² holds for all f ∈ L² if and only if the Fourier transform ψ̂ satisfies the Calderón condition Σj∈ℤ |ψ̂(2^j ξ)|² ∈ [A,B] almost everywhere. Daubechies constructed compactly supported orthonormal wavelets; later work by Meyer, Lemarié‑Rieusset, and others produced smooth wavelets with arbitrary decay. Frames are more flexible than bases because they allow redundancy, which is crucial for applications such as denoising and sparse representation.

Gabor systems replace dilations by modulations: {gm,n(x) = e2πi m x g(x−n) : m,n ∈ ℤ}. The Balian‑Low theorem states that if g generates a Gabor frame with lattice density 1, then g cannot be both well‑localized in time and frequency; specifically, ∫ x²|g(x)|² dx · ∫ ξ²|ĝ(ξ)|² dξ = ∞. This obstruction does not exist for wavelet frames because the dilation group is non‑abelian. The theory of Gabor frames is deeply connected to the Heisenberg group and the metaplectic representation. Recent advances include the construction of Gabor frames with optimal time‑frequency concentration using Hermite functions and the solution of the Feichtinger conjecture for separable Hilbert spaces.

Sharp Weighted Estimates: The A₂ Theorem and Its Extensions

The A₂ theorem, proved by Hytönen in 2012, gives the sharp dependence of the operator norm of a Calderón‑Zygmund operator on the A₂ characteristic of a weight w. For a weight w ∈ A₂, the Hilbert transform H satisfies ‖H‖L²(w)→L²(w) ≤ C [w]A₂, where [w]A₂ = sup_Q (⨍_Q w)(⨍_Q w−1) is the A₂ constant. The linear bound is optimal; earlier estimates by Buckley gave a quadratic dependence. The proof uses a combination of the Bellman function method, the dyadic representation theorem, and a careful stopping‑time argument that reduces the problem to a sparse domination estimate. Sparse operators dominate a wide class of singular integrals, and their weighted norms are easier to compute.

Extensions include the A_p theorem for 1 < p < ∞, where the sharp bound is C [w]A_pmax(1,1/(p−1)), and the two‑weight problem, which asks for conditions on a pair (u,v) such that T : L²(u) → L²(v) is bounded. The two‑weight conjecture for the Hilbert transform was resolved by Lacey, Sawyer, Shen, and Uriarte‑Tuero using a testing condition involving the Poisson integral of the weights. These results have applications in the regularity theory of degenerate elliptic equations and in the study of the Cauchy integral on chord‑arc curves.

The Kato Square Root Problem and Its Resolution via Harmonic Analysis

The Kato square root problem, posed in 1961, asks whether the domain of the square root of an accretive elliptic operator L = −div(A∇) coincides with the Sobolev space H¹(ℝⁿ) when A is a bounded measurable matrix satisfying the ellipticity condition Re ⟨Aξ,ξ⟩ ≥ λ|ξ|². In other words, does ‖√L f‖₂ ≈ ‖∇f‖₂ hold for all f ∈ H¹? The problem remained open for four decades. The affirmative answer was given by Auscher, Hofmann, Lacey, McIntosh, and Tchamitchian in 2002 using a sophisticated blend of harmonic analysis techniques: the T(b) theorem, off‑diagonal estimates for the heat semigroup e−tL, and a Calderón‑Zygmund decomposition adapted to the operator L. The proof shows that the square root √L can be represented as a singular integral operator with kernel satisfying Calderón‑Zygmund estimates, and then applies the T(b) theorem with accretive test functions derived from the solutions of the elliptic equation.

This resolution has far‑reaching consequences. It implies the L² boundedness of the Riesz transform ∇L−1/2 associated with L, which in turn yields the solvability of the Dirichlet and Neumann problems for the elliptic equation in non‑smooth domains. The method has been extended to higher‑order operators, systems, and to the setting of differential forms. The Kato problem illustrates how abstract harmonic analysis — singular integrals, BMO, and the T(b) theorem — provides the tools to solve concrete PDE questions that are inaccessible by classical energy methods alone.

  • Confusing Carleson's theorem (pointwise a.e. convergence for L²) with Fejér's theorem (uniform convergence of Cesàro means for continuous functions).
  • Assuming the T(1) theorem applies without checking the weak boundedness property; the T(b) theorem requires it explicitly.
  • Believing that Gabor frames can achieve the same time‑frequency localization as wavelet frames; the Balian‑Low theorem forbids this at critical density.
  • Using the quadratic Buckley bound for the Hilbert transform on weighted L² spaces instead of the sharp linear A₂ bound.
  • Thinking the Kato square root problem is solved by a simple energy estimate; the proof fundamentally relies on the T(b) theorem and off‑diagonal heat kernel bounds.
  • Neglecting the accretivity condition when verifying T(b) hypotheses; boundedness alone is insufficient.
  • Overlooking that the A₂ characteristic [w]A₂ is defined via the supremum over all cubes, not just dyadic cubes, in the sharp weighted theory.

hand/diff-eq.html:
Sturm–Liouville Theory and Spectral Methods for Linear Operators

Sturm–Liouville theory provides the spectral foundation for a vast class of linear differential operators that appear after separation of variables in PDEs. A regular Sturm–Liouville problem on an interval a ≤ x ≤ b takes the form

−(p(x) y′)′ + q(x) y = λ w(x) y,

with boundary conditions α₁ y(a) + α₂ y′(a) = 0 and β₁ y(b) + β₂ y′(b) = 0, where p, q, w are real‑valued, p > 0, w > 0 on (a,b). The operator L y = (1/w)[−(p y′)′ + q y] is self‑adjoint in the weighted L² space with inner product ⟨u,v⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ u v w dx. Self‑adjointness guarantees a real, discrete spectrum λ₁ < λ₂ < … → ∞ and a complete orthogonal set of eigenfunctions {φₙ}. The Rayleigh quotient R[y] = ∫ₐᵇ (p y′² + q y²) dx / ∫ₐᵇ w y² dx yields the min‑max characterisation λₖ = mindim V=k max_{y∈V{0}} R[y].

Singular Sturm–Liouville problems arise when p vanishes or the interval is unbounded; classic examples are Bessel’s equation (p=x, q=ν²/x, w=x) on (0,1) and Legendre’s equation (p=1−x², q=0, w=1) on (−1,1). In both cases the spectrum may be continuous or discrete depending on boundary conditions at the singular endpoints. The completeness of eigenfunctions underlies Fourier–Bessel and Fourier–Legendre expansions, which are the spectral tools for solving the heat and wave equations in cylindrical and spherical geometries.

Spectral methods for numerical PDEs exploit this theory: the solution is expanded in the eigenbasis of the differential operator, turning the PDE into a system of ODEs for the modal coefficients. For periodic domains the Fourier basis diagonalises the Laplacian, giving exponential convergence for smooth data. For non‑periodic problems, Chebyshev or Legendre polynomials provide a similar diagonalisation after a suitable mapping. The key practical advantage is that the stiffness matrix becomes diagonal or block‑diagonal, eliminating the need for large linear solves at each time step.

Weak Solutions and Sobolev Spaces in the Modern Theory of PDEs

The classical requirement that a solution possess continuous derivatives up to the order of the equation is too restrictive for many physical problems. Distribution theory, introduced by Laurent Schwartz, extends differentiation to arbitrary locally integrable functions: the derivative of a distribution T is defined by ⟨∂ᵢT, φ⟩ = −⟨T, ∂ᵢφ⟩ for all test functions φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω). A weak solution of −Δu = f in Ω with u = 0 on ∂Ω is a function u ∈ H₀¹(Ω) such that ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx = ∫_Ω f v dx for every v ∈ H₀¹(Ω). Here H₀¹(Ω) is the closure of C_c^∞(Ω) in the Sobolev norm ‖u‖H¹² = ∫_Ω (|u|² + |∇u|²) dx.

Sobolev spaces Wk,p(Ω) consist of functions whose weak derivatives up to order k belong to L^p(Ω). The Sobolev embedding theorems describe when Wk,p embeds continuously or compactly into spaces of continuous functions or other L^q spaces. For example, if kp > n then Wk,p(Ω) ⊂ Ck−[n/p]−1,γ(Ω̄) (Morrey’s inequality). The Rellich–Kondrachov theorem guarantees compact embedding of H¹(Ω) into L²(Ω) for bounded Lipschitz domains, which is essential for proving existence of eigenvalues for the Laplacian.

The Lax–Milgram lemma provides a general existence and uniqueness result for linear elliptic problems: if a bilinear form a(u,v) is bounded and coercive on a Hilbert space V, then for every continuous linear functional F there exists a unique u ∈ V with a(u,v) = F(v) for all v ∈ V. Coercivity a(v,v) ≥ α‖v‖_V² follows from Poincaré’s inequality for the Dirichlet form a(u,v)=∫∇u·∇v on H₀¹. Regularity theory then upgrades weak solutions to classical ones when the data and domain are smooth: if f ∈ L² and ∂Ω is C², then u ∈ H²(Ω) and ‖u‖H² ≤ C‖f‖L².

Weak Formulation of the Poisson Equation
Derive the weak formulation of −Δu = f in Ω with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition u = 0 on ∂Ω, and identify the function space in which the solution is sought.
Multiply the equation by a test function v ∈ C_c^∞(Ω) and integrate over Ω: ∫_Ω (−Δu) v dx = ∫_Ω f v dx. Integrate by parts using Green’s identity: ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx − ∫∂Ω (∂u/∂n) v ds = ∫_Ω f v dx. Since v vanishes on ∂Ω, the boundary term disappears, yielding ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v dx = ∫_Ω f v dx for all v ∈ C_c^∞(Ω). By density, this holds for all v ∈ H₀¹(Ω). The weak solution is u ∈ H₀¹(Ω) satisfying this identity. Existence and uniqueness follow from the Lax–Milgram lemma because the bilinear form a(u,v)=∫∇u·∇v is coercive on H₀¹(Ω) by the Poincaré inequality and bounded by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
Exam Strategy for Functional Analytic PDEs
When a question asks for a weak formulation, first state the test space (usually H₀¹ for Dirichlet problems). Write the integration‑by‑parts step explicitly, show the boundary term vanishes, and then cite Lax–Milgram with the two required properties: boundedness and coercivity. For eigenvalue problems, recall that compact embedding of H¹ into L² yields a discrete spectrum and an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions.

Geometric Mechanics: Hamiltonian Systems, Symplectic Structure, and Integrability

Hamiltonian mechanics reformulates Newtonian dynamics on a symplectic manifold (M, ω), where ω is a closed, non‑degenerate 2‑form. In canonical coordinates (q,p) on the cotangent bundle T*Q, ω = ∑ dp_i ∧ dq_i. A Hamiltonian function H: M → ℝ generates a vector field X_H defined by ω(X_H, ·) = dH. The flow of X_H preserves ω (Liouville’s theorem) and H itself (energy conservation). The Poisson bracket {F,G} = ω(X_F, X_G) = ∑ (∂F/∂q_i ∂G/∂p_i − ∂F/∂p_i ∂G/∂q_i) endows C^∞(M) with a Lie algebra structure; Hamilton’s equations are ẋ = {x, H}.

A system with n degrees of freedom is Liouville‑integrable if there exist n independent, Poisson‑commuting first integrals F₁=H, F₂,…,Fₙ (i.e., {F_i, F_j}=0). The Liouville–Arnold theorem states that the level set of these integrals is a union of invariant n‑tori, on which the motion is quasi‑periodic. Action‑angle variables (I,θ) provide a canonical transformation such that H = H(I) and the equations become İ = 0, θ̇ = ∂H/∂I = ω(I). The frequencies ω(I) determine the dynamics; resonance occurs when k·ω = 0 for some integer vector k ≠ 0.

KAM theory (Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser) shows that under a small Hamiltonian perturbation, most invariant tori with Diophantine frequency vectors survive, while resonant tori break up, creating chaotic layers. This explains the long‑term stability of the solar system despite perturbations. Infinite‑dimensional Hamiltonian PDEs such as the Korteweg–de Vries equation u_t + uxxx + 6u u_x = 0 admit a bi‑Hamiltonian structure and an infinite hierarchy of commuting integrals, making them completely integrable via the inverse scattering transform.

Numerical Approximation of Differential Equations: Finite Difference, Finite Element, and Spectral Methods

Numerical methods replace the continuous problem by a discrete algebraic system. For the heat equation u_t = α uxx on (0,1) with Dirichlet conditions, a uniform grid x_j = jΔx, t^n = nΔt leads to the explicit forward‑Euler scheme (u_jn+1 − u_j^n)/Δt = α (uj+1^n − 2u_j^n + uj-1^n)/Δx². Consistency requires the truncation error to vanish as Δt,Δx → 0; stability demands that errors do not amplify, which for this scheme is the CFL condition α Δt/Δx² ≤ 1/2. The Lax equivalence theorem states that for a well‑posed linear problem, consistency plus stability implies convergence.

The finite element method (FEM) starts from the weak formulation. The domain Ω is partitioned into elements (triangles, tetrahedra). On each element, the solution is approximated by piecewise polynomials (e.g., continuous P1 Lagrange basis). The global stiffness matrix Kij = ∫_Ω ∇φ_i·∇φ_j dx and load vector F_i = ∫_Ω f φ_i dx are assembled. The discrete problem K u = F is solved for the nodal values. Céa’s lemma gives the error estimate ‖u − u_h‖H¹ ≤ C infv_h∈V_h ‖u − v_h‖H¹, leading to optimal order O(h) convergence in H¹ for linear elements if u ∈ H².

Spectral methods use global basis functions (Fourier series for periodic domains, Chebyshev or Legendre polynomials for non‑periodic). The solution is represented as u_N(x) = ∑k=0^N a_k φ_k(x). Collocation (pseudospectral) evaluates the residual at Gauss–Lobatto nodes, yielding a dense but highly accurate differentiation matrix. For analytic solutions, the error decays exponentially with N (spectral accuracy). The main trade‑off is the dense linear algebra versus the sparse matrices of FEM; for time‑dependent problems, implicit‑explicit (IMEX) schemes treat the stiff linear part implicitly and the nonlinear part explicitly.

Stochastic Differential Equations: Itô Calculus, Fokker–Planck Equation, and Applications

A stochastic differential equation (SDE) driven by a Wiener process W_t reads dX_t = b(X_t) dt + σ(X_t) dW_t, where b is the drift and σ the diffusion coefficient. The Itô integral ∫0^t σ(X_s) dW_s is defined as the L² limit of sums σ(Xt_i)(Wti+1−Wt_i) with the integrand evaluated at the left endpoint. This non‑anticipative choice leads to the Itô formula: for a C² function f, df(X_t) = f′(X_t) dX_t + ½ f″(X_t) σ²(X_t) dt. The extra second‑order term distinguishes Itô calculus from ordinary calculus.

Under Lipschitz and linear growth conditions on b and σ, the SDE has a unique strong solution adapted to the filtration of W_t. The probability density p(t,x) of X_t satisfies the Fokker–Planck (forward Kolmogorov) equation ∂_t p = −∂_x (b p) + ½ ∂xx (σ² p). For time‑independent coefficients, a stationary density p_∞(x) ∝ exp(∫x 2b(y)/σ²(y) dy) / σ²(x) exists if the integral converges. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process dX_t = −θ X_t dt + σ dW_t has Gaussian stationary distribution N(0, σ²/(2θ)).

Applications abound: in finance, the Black–Scholes model assumes geometric Brownian motion dS_t = μ S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t, leading to the heat equation after a logarithmic change of variable. In physics, the Langevin equation m dV_t = −γ V_t dt + σ dW_t describes a particle in a heat bath; its position obeys a second‑order SDE. In biology, stochastic population models incorporate demographic noise via diffusion terms. Numerical simulation uses the Euler–Maruyama scheme Xn+1 = X_n + b(X_n)Δt + σ(X_n)ΔW_n, which converges with strong order ½ and weak order 1.

  • Confusing the weak formulation with the strong form and forgetting to specify the test space.
  • Assuming every Sturm–Liouville problem has a discrete spectrum without checking endpoint classification.
  • Neglecting the coercivity condition when applying Lax–Milgram, leading to false existence claims.
  • Mixing Itô and Stratonovich integrals in SDEs without the correction term ½ σ σ′ dt.
  • Applying the CFL condition derived for explicit finite differences to implicit or spectral schemes where it does not apply.
  • Overlooking the need for Diophantine frequency conditions in KAM theory and concluding all tori survive perturbation.
  • Treating the Fokker–Planck equation as a standard PDE without verifying the diffusion matrix is positive definite.

hand/fukaya-categories.html:
Obstruction Theory and Bounding Cochains in the Fukaya Category

The Fukaya category of a symplectic manifold X is defined only after one resolves the obstruction to defining the A∞‑operations mₖ on the Floer complexes CF*(L₀,L₁). For a Lagrangian submanifold L, the obstruction lives in the degree‑2 Floer cohomology HF²(L,L) and is represented by the curvature term m₀ ∈ CF²(L,L). When m₀ ≠ 0 the A∞‑relations fail at the first level: m₁² = m₂(m₀⊗id) + m₂(id⊗m₀). The modern solution, due to Fukaya‑Oh‑Ohta‑Ono, introduces a bounding cochain b ∈ CF¹(L,L) (or more generally b ∈ H¹(L;Λ₀) where Λ₀ is the Novikov ring) and deforms the operations by the Maurer‑Cartan series m₀ᵇ = m₀ + m₁(b) + m₂(b⊗b) + m₃(b⊗b⊗b) + … . The condition m₀ᵇ = 0 is the Maurer‑Cartan equation; a solution b makes the deformed complex (CF*(L,L), m₁ᵇ) a genuine differential (m₁ᵇ² = 0) and yields a well‑defined A∞‑structure on the deformed morphism spaces. If such a b exists, L is called unobstructed; otherwise L is obstructed and does not define an object of the Fukaya category. For monotone or exact Lagrangians the trivial cochain b = 0 solves the equation, so HF*(L,L) ≅ H*(L;Λ₀) as algebras. In the general case one must work with the curved A∞‑category and then pass to the category of unobstructed objects Funob(X). The deformation theory of bounding cochains is governed by the obstruction class [m₀] ∈ HF²(L,L); its vanishing is necessary and sufficient for the existence of a bounding cochain after a suitable gauge transformation. This framework also explains why the Fukaya category is only defined over the Novikov field: the energy filtration on pseudoholomorphic disks forces the use of formal power series in the symplectic area variable T.

Wrapped Fukaya Categories and Liouville Domains

For non‑compact exact symplectic manifolds with cylindrical ends — Liouville domains — the ordinary Fukaya category is too small because Hamiltonian chords that escape to infinity are not counted. The wrapped Fukaya category W(X) remedies this by allowing Hamiltonians that grow quadratically at infinity, so that the time‑1 flow wraps Lagrangians around the cylindrical end. Objects are exact Lagrangian submanifolds that are cylindrical outside a compact set; morphism complexes are generated by Hamiltonian chords of the wrapped Hamiltonian. The A∞‑operations count pseudoholomorphic polygons with boundary on the wrapped Lagrangians, and the wrapping ensures that every intersection point appears after sufficiently many wraps. A fundamental theorem of Abouzaid (2010) states that for a Weinstein manifold X (a Liouville domain with a Morse function compatible with the Liouville flow) the wrapped Fukaya category is generated by the cocores of the critical handles. Moreover, the wrapped category is invariant under Liouville deformation and satisfies a Künneth formula W(X × Y) ≃ W(X) ⊗ W(Y). The wrapped category of the cotangent bundle T*M is quasi‑equivalent to the derived category of modules over the singular chains on the based loop space ΩM, and via the work of Nadler‑Zaslow it is also equivalent to the derived category of constructible sheaves on M. This equivalence is a cornerstone of the Kontsevich‑Soibelman approach to mirror symmetry for affine varieties: the mirror of a Liouville domain is an affine variety whose category of coherent sheaves (or modules over its coordinate ring) matches W(X). The wrapped category also carries a natural Calabi‑Yau structure of dimension n = dim X, given by a non‑degenerate cyclic pairing on Hochschild homology.

Worked Example: Obstruction Vanishing for a Monotone Lagrangian Torus
Let L ⊂ ℂP² be the Clifford torus, which is monotone with minimal Maslov number 2. Show that the curvature term m₀ ∈ CF²(L,L) vanishes for the trivial bounding cochain b = 0, and conclude that L is an object of the Fukaya category F(ℂP²).
For a monotone Lagrangian the symplectic area of any pseudoholomorphic disk with boundary on L is proportional to its Maslov index. The Clifford torus in ℂP² bounds exactly three families of Maslov‑2 disks, each contributing to m₀ with coefficient Tω/2 where ω is the symplectic area of the generator of H₂(ℂP²). The signed count of these disks is zero because the three families are related by the torus symmetry and cancel in the Floer complex over the Novikov field. Hence m₀ = 0 in CF²(L,L). With b = 0 the Maurer‑Cartan equation m₀ + m₁(b) + … = 0 holds trivially. Therefore L is unobstructed and defines an object of F(ℂP²). Its Floer cohomology HF*(L,L) is isomorphic to H*(L;Λ₀) ≅ Λ₀ ⊕ Λ₀[1]² ⊕ Λ₀[2] as a graded vector space, and the product structure recovers the quantum cohomology of ℂP² restricted to the torus.
Exam Strategy: Recognising Unobstructed Lagrangians
When a question asks whether a given Lagrangian defines an object of the Fukaya category, first check monotonicity or exactness. If the Lagrangian is monotone with minimal Maslov number ≥ 2, the curvature m₀ often vanishes by symmetry or by a degree argument (no Maslov‑0 disks). For exact Lagrangians in a Liouville domain, m₀ = 0 automatically because there are no closed pseudoholomorphic disks. If the Lagrangian is neither monotone nor exact, look for a bounding cochain solving the Maurer‑Cartan equation; the existence of such a cochain is equivalent to the vanishing of the obstruction class in HF². In multiple‑choice settings, the answer “unobstructed” is correct precisely when the obstruction class vanishes.

Generation Criteria and Split‑Generators

A central problem in Fukaya category theory is to determine when a collection of Lagrangians generates the whole category. Abouzaid’s generation criterion (2010) gives a practical test: a set of objects {Lᵢ} in a triangulated A∞‑category C split‑generates C if and only if the induced map on Hochschild homology HH*(C) → ⊕ HH*(Lᵢ,Lᵢ) is surjective. In the wrapped Fukaya category of a Liouville domain, the cocores of the critical handles form a split‑generating set; this is the wrapped analogue of the fact that the structure sheaf generates the derived category of coherent sheaves on an affine variety. For compact symplectic manifolds, the situation is subtler. Sheridan’s proof of homological mirror symmetry for the quintic threefold constructs a split‑generator from the Lagrangian torus fibration given by the SYZ construction. The generator is a formal direct sum of Lagrangian tori with appropriate bounding cochains, and its endomorphism algebra is quasi‑isomorphic to the homogeneous coordinate ring of the mirror quintic. The generation criterion is also used to prove that the Fukaya category of a Fano toric variety is generated by the Lagrangian torus fibers of the moment map; the mirror is the Landau‑Ginzburg model whose category of matrix factorizations is generated by the structure sheaf. In practice, to show that a given Lagrangian L split‑generates, one often computes the open‑closed map OC: HH*(F(X)) → QH*(X) and checks that the unit in quantum cohomology lies in the image of the composition HH*(F(X)) → HH*(L,L) → QH*(X). If the unit is hit, then L split‑generates by a theorem of Abouzaid‑Fukaya‑Oh‑Ohta‑Ono.

SYZ Fibrations and Mirror Construction

The Strominger‑Yau‑Zaslow (SYZ) conjecture (1996) proposes that mirror symmetry for Calabi‑Yau manifolds can be understood geometrically as a duality between special Lagrangian torus fibrations. A special Lagrangian submanifold L in a Calabi‑Yau n‑fold X is a Lagrangian calibrated by the real part of the holomorphic volume form Ω; it has minimal volume in its homology class and its Maslov class vanishes. An SYZ fibration is a map π: X → B whose generic fibers are special Lagrangian n‑tori, with a discriminant locus Δ ⊂ B where the fibers degenerate. The mirror ̂X is constructed by dualizing the torus fibers: ̂X = ⋃b∈B\Δ H¹(L_b;U(1)) / H¹(L_b;ℤ), equipped with a complex structure determined by the affine structure on B\Δ coming from the periods of the symplectic form and the holomorphic volume form. The SYZ picture explains why the Fukaya category of X should be equivalent to the derived category of coherent sheaves on ̂X: a Lagrangian section of the fibration corresponds to a skyscraper sheaf on ̂X, while a Lagrangian multisection corresponds to a vector bundle. The Fukaya‑Seidel category of a Lefschetz fibration provides a local model for the SYZ fibration near a focus‑focus singularity; the vanishing cycles are the Lagrangian spheres that collapse at the singular fiber, and their Dehn twists generate the monodromy of the fibration. Gross‑Siebert’s program (2000s) gives an algebraic reconstruction of the mirror from the tropical geometry of the base B, using scattering diagrams to correct the naive dual torus bundle. This program has been used to prove mirror symmetry for many toric Calabi‑Yau varieties and for K3 surfaces. In the context of the Fukaya category, the SYZ fibration provides a geometric source of split‑generators: the collection of all Lagrangian torus fibers (with appropriate bounding cochains) is expected to split‑generate F(X). This expectation underlies many recent proofs of homological mirror symmetry for Fano and Calabi‑Yau manifolds.

Dehn Twist Autoequivalences and the Seidel Representation

In a symplectic manifold X, a Lagrangian sphere S ⊂ X of dimension n admits a generalized Dehn twist τ_S: X → X, a symplectomorphism supported in a neighbourhood of S that acts as a reflection on the normal directions. On the Fukaya category, τ_S induces an A∞‑autoequivalence Φ_S: F(X) → F(X) given by the spherical twist functor. For any Lagrangian L, the morphism complex CF*(L,S) carries a natural action of the spherical twist, and the effect on objects is expressed by the exact triangle Φ_S(L) → L → CF*(L,S) ⊗ S in the derived Fukaya category. Seidel’s representation theorem states that for a Lefschetz fibration π: E → ℂ with vanishing cycles V₁,…,V_m, the mapping class group of the base (the braid group on m strands) acts on the derived Fukaya‑Seidel category D^b F_→(π) via the spherical twists along the vanishing cycles. This action categorifies the classical Picard‑Lefschetz monodromy on the middle homology of the fiber. In the case of the Am‑1 Milnor fiber, the derived Fukaya‑Seidel category is equivalent to the derived category of representations of the Am‑1 quiver, and the braid group action corresponds to the derived autoequivalences given by reflection functors. For the quintic threefold, the Seidel representation provides a large subgroup of the autoequivalence group of D^b Coh(̂X) on the mirror side, matching the expected mirror symmetry of autoequivalences. The spherical twist functors also satisfy the braid relations: if two Lagrangian spheres intersect transversely in a single point, their twists satisfy the braid relation τ_S τ_T τ_S ≃ τ_T τ_S τ_T. This categorical braid group action is a powerful tool for constructing new objects in the Fukaya category and for proving generation results.

  • Confusing the curved A∞‑structure with the genuine A∞‑structure after bounding cochain deformation.
  • Assuming every Lagrangian in a monotone symplectic manifold is automatically unobstructed; the minimal Maslov number must be ≥ 2 and the disk count must vanish.
  • Neglecting the Novikov field coefficients when stating isomorphisms such as HF*(L,L) ≅ H*(L;Λ₀).
  • Thinking the wrapped Fukaya category is defined for any non‑compact symplectic manifold; it requires a Liouville (or at least convex) end.
  • Misapplying Abouzaid’s generation criterion by checking only the open‑closed map on cohomology without verifying the unit lies in the image.
  • Believing the SYZ fibration exists globally on every Calabi‑Yau; singular fibers and wall‑crossing phenomena often obstruct a global fibration.
  • Review these traps carefully before the exam.

hand/teichmuller-theory.html:
The Mapping Class Group and Its Action on Teichmüller Space

The mapping class group Modg of a closed oriented surface Sg of genus g ≥ 2 is the group of isotopy classes of orientation‑preserving diffeomorphisms, Modg = π₀(Diff⁺(Sg)). It acts on Teichmüller space Tg by changing the marking: if (X, f) represents a point in Tg with f : Sg → X a homeomorphism, then for φ ∈ Modg the action is φ·(X, f) = (X, f ∘ φ⁻¹). This action is properly discontinuous and holomorphic, and the quotient Tg/Modg is the moduli space Mg. The Nielsen–Thurston classification divides elements of Modg into three types: periodic (finite order), reducible (preserves a non‑trivial multicurve up to isotopy), and pseudo‑Anosov (stretches a pair of transverse measured foliations by a factor λ > 1). A pseudo‑Anosov element φ has a translation length ℓ(φ) = infX∈Tg dT(X, φ·X) which is realized on a unique Teichmüller geodesic axis invariant under φ. The stretch factor λ equals eℓ(φ). The action extends continuously to the Thurston compactification Tg ∪ PMF, where PMF is the space of projective measured foliations; pseudo‑Anosov elements act with north‑south dynamics on the boundary, fixing exactly two points (the stable and unstable foliations). The mapping class group is generated by Dehn twists about simple closed curves; the lantern relation and the chain relation are fundamental presentations. The virtual cohomological dimension of Modg is 4g − 5, and its rational cohomology ring is known in low degrees through the work of Harer, Madsen–Weiss, and others. Understanding the dynamics of Modg on Tg and its compactifications is essential for problems on orbit closures, rigidity, and the geometry of Mg.

The Thurston Compactification and Projective Measured Foliations

Thurston’s compactification of Teichmüller space adds the space of projective measured foliations PMF, yielding a closed ball of dimension 6g − 6 whose boundary is a sphere of dimension 6g − 7. A measured foliation on Sg is a foliation with a transverse measure invariant under holonomy; two measured foliations are equivalent if they are related by Whitehead moves and isotopy. The projective class forgets the overall scale of the measure. The topology on Tg ∪ PMF is defined by length functions: a sequence Xn ∈ Tg converges to [μ] ∈ PMF iff for every simple closed curve α, the hyperbolic length ℓXn(α) grows proportionally to the intersection number i(α, μ). The mapping class group action extends by homeomorphisms to the boundary; periodic and reducible elements have fixed points on PMF, while pseudo‑Anosov elements act with exactly two fixed points (the stable and unstable measured foliations) and all other points converge to the stable foliation under forward iteration. The Thurston boundary is homeomorphic to the space of projective measured laminations PML, which can be identified with the space of projective geodesic currents. The compactification is Modg‑equivariant and provides a powerful tool for studying the dynamics of mapping classes, the geometry of the moduli space, and the classification of Kleinian groups via the ending lamination theorem. The ball Tg ∪ PMF is not a manifold with boundary at the points corresponding to non‑uniquely ergodic foliations, a subtle fact that appears in advanced problems on the topology of the mapping class group.

Worked Example: Fixed Points of a Pseudo‑Anosov on the Thurston Boundary
Let φ ∈ Modg be a pseudo‑Anosov mapping class with stretch factor λ > 1. Prove that φ has exactly two fixed points in PMF and describe their dynamical nature.
By the Nielsen–Thurston theorem, φ preserves a pair of transverse measured foliations (μs, μu) with φ·μs = λ⁻¹ μs and φ·μu = λ μu. In projective classes, scaling is irrelevant, so [μs] and [μu] are fixed by φ. For any other projective measured foliation [ν] ≠ [μs], [μu], the intersection numbers i(ν, μs) and i(ν, μu) are positive. Under iteration, the length of ν in the hyperbolic metric on the Teichmüller geodesic determined by (μs, μu) grows like λn i(ν, μu) while the component along μs shrinks. Consequently, the projective class φⁿ·[ν] converges to [μu] as n → +∞ and to [μs] as n → −∞. This north‑south dynamics shows that no other fixed points exist. Hence φ has exactly two fixed points on PMF, the stable and unstable foliations, with the described attracting/repelling behavior.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks about the action of a mapping class on the Thurston boundary, first classify the element (periodic, reducible, pseudo‑Anosov). For pseudo‑Anosov, recall the two fixed points are the stable and unstable measured foliations; the stretch factor λ is the eigenvalue of the action on the transverse measure. For reducible elements, identify the invariant multicurve and note that the fixed points correspond to projective classes supported on that multicurve. The Thurston compactification is a ball; its boundary is a sphere of dimension 6g−7. Use these topological facts to answer questions about convergence of sequences in Tg.

The Bers Embedding and the Schwarzian Derivative

The Bers embedding realizes Teichmüller space Tg as a bounded domain in the complex Banach space of holomorphic quadratic differentials on the unit disk 𝔻. Given a marked Riemann surface (X, f) with f : Sg → X, lift f to a quasiconformal map F : ℍ → ℍ of the upper half‑plane that conjugates the Fuchsian group ΓX uniformizing X to a quasi‑Fuchsian group Γ. The Schwarzian derivative S(F) = (F''/F')' − ½(F''/F')² is a holomorphic quadratic differential on the domain of discontinuity Ω(Γ). Restricting to the component Ω₀ ≅ 𝔻 yields an element of the space Q(𝔻) of bounded holomorphic quadratic differentials on 𝔻 with the supremum norm. The map β : Tg → Q(𝔻) sending (X, f) to S(F)|𝔻 is a holomorphic embedding whose image is a bounded domain. The Bers embedding is equivariant with respect to the mapping class group action and provides a complex structure on Tg that coincides with the one coming from the Beltrami differential model. The image domain is characterized by the Ahlfors–Weill condition: a quadratic differential q ∈ Q(𝔻) belongs to β(Tg) iff the solution of the Beltrami equation with coefficient μ = −½‖q‖−1 q̄ ρ−1 yields a quasiconformal map whose Schwarzian is q. The Bers embedding also underlies the simultaneous uniformization theorem: for any pair (X, Y) ∈ Tg × Tg there exists a unique quasi‑Fuchsian group Γ such that Ω(Γ)/Γ ≅ X ⊔ Y. The Schwarzian derivative of the uniformizing map for the component corresponding to X gives the Bers coordinate of X, while the other component gives the coordinate of Y. This duality is central to the study of the deformation space of hyperbolic 3‑manifolds and the geometry of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces.

The Augmented Teichmüller Space and the Weil–Petersson Completion

The augmented Teichmüller space T̂g is obtained by adjoining to Tg all noded Riemann surfaces that arise by pinching a collection of disjoint simple closed curves to zero hyperbolic length. Formally, a point in T̂g is an equivalence class of marked noded surfaces where each node corresponds to a pinched curve; the stratum associated to a multicurve σ consists of surfaces where exactly the curves in σ are pinched. The Weil–Petersson metric on Tg is incomplete; its metric completion is naturally identified with T̂g. Wolpert’s formula ωWP = Σ dℓi ∧ dτi in Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates shows that near a stratum where ℓi → 0, the metric behaves like a product of a cusp metric on the ℓi‑direction and a smooth metric on the remaining directions. Consequently, the Weil–Petersson distance to the boundary is finite, and geodesics can reach the boundary in finite time. The augmented space carries a natural stratification by the topological type of the noded surface; each stratum is isometric to a product of lower‑dimensional Teichmüller spaces with the Weil–Petersson metric. Mirzakhani’s recursive formula for the Weil–Petersson volumes of Mg,n uses integration over the boundary strata of T̂g. The mapping class group acts on T̂g with finite stabilizers, and the quotient is the Deligne–Mumford compactification M̄g. The Weil–Petersson metric extends as a Kähler metric with orbifold singularities on M̄g, and its curvature properties (negative sectional curvature, negative Ricci curvature) persist on the smooth part. Understanding the augmented space is essential for problems involving degeneration of Riemann surfaces, the behavior of the Weil–Petersson metric near the boundary, and the topology of the moduli space.

  • Confusing the Thurston boundary PMF with the Gardiner–Masur boundary; they coincide only for uniquely ergodic foliations.
  • Assuming the Bers embedding image is the whole space of bounded quadratic differentials; it is a proper bounded domain characterized by the Ahlfors–Weill condition.
  • Treating the Weil–Petersson metric as complete; it is incomplete and its completion is the augmented Teichmüller space, not the Deligne–Mumford compactification directly.
  • Overlooking that the mapping class group action on the Thurston boundary has north‑south dynamics only for pseudo‑Anosov elements; reducible elements have a continuum of fixed points.
  • Misidentifying the translation length of a pseudo‑Anosov element with the logarithm of its stretch factor without verifying that the infimum is attained on the invariant geodesic axis.
  • Neglecting the role of the lantern relation and chain relation in presentations of Modg when computing algebraic invariants such as the abelianization (which is trivial for g ≥ 3).
  • Confusing the augmented Teichmüller space with the Deligne–Mumford compactification; the former is a topological space with a natural stratification, the latter is an algebraic stack obtained by quotienting by Modg.

The advanced topics above complete the core toolkit needed for research‑level problems in Teichmüller theory and its applications to moduli spaces, Kleinian groups, and hyperbolic geometry.

hand/additive-combinatorics.html:
Freiman's Theorem and the Structure of Sets with Small Doubling

Freiman's theorem is the cornerstone of inverse additive combinatorics. It asserts that if a finite set A ⊂ ℤ satisfies |A+A| ≤ K|A| for some constant K ≥ 1, then A is contained in a generalized arithmetic progression (GAP) of bounded dimension and size. The original 1973 result of Freiman gave explicit but tower‑type bounds: the dimension is at most K−1 and the size of the progression is at most C(K)|A| where C(K) grows doubly exponentially in K. Later work by Ruzsa, Bilu, and Green–Ruzsa dramatically improved the quantitative dependence. Green and Ruzsa (2007) proved that one can take dimension O(K log K) and size exp(O(K log K))|A|. Sanders (2012) further refined the bound to exp(O(K (log K)4))|A| using a density increment argument combined with the Bogolyubov–Ruzsa lemma. The theorem has a clean formulation in arbitrary abelian groups: if A ⊂ G with |A+A| ≤ K|A|, then A is covered by at most KO(1) translates of a subgroup of size at most |A| (the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture, still open in full generality). The proof strategy typically proceeds by iterating the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequalities to control higher sumsets, then applying the Ruzsa covering lemma to find a large subset with small doubling inside a coset progression. The inverse theorem for small doubling is the engine behind many structural results, including the proof of Szemerédi's theorem for length‑4 progressions via Gowers' U³ norm.

The Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa Conjecture and Recent Progress

The polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture (PFR) posits that in any abelian group, a set A with |A+A| ≤ K|A| can be covered by at most KO(1) cosets of a subgroup H with |H| ≤ |A|. This would replace the exponential‑type bounds of Freiman's theorem with a polynomial dependence on K. The conjecture is known to hold in several important settings. In 𝔽₂ⁿ, Green and Ruzsa (2007) proved PFR using a combination of Fourier analysis and the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem, obtaining a covering by at most KC cosets of a subspace. In ℤ, the best unconditional result is due to Sanders (2012), who showed that A is contained in a GAP of dimension O(K (log K)5) and size exp(O(K (log K)5))|A|; this is still exponential in K but with a much smaller exponent. A major breakthrough came from the polynomial method: Croot–Lev–Pach (2017) and Ellenberg–Gijswijt (2017) introduced the slice‑rank technique, which yields polynomial bounds for cap sets in 𝔽₃ⁿ and has been adapted to give new proofs of PFR in vector spaces over finite fields. In 2020, Bloom and Sisask used a refined density increment to prove PFR for subsets of ℤ/pℤ with p prime, achieving a covering by KO(1) arithmetic progressions of the same common difference. The conjecture remains open for general abelian groups, but the recent wave of polynomial‑method arguments suggests that a full resolution may be within reach.

Worked Example: Applying Freiman's Theorem
Let A ⊂ ℤ be a finite set with |A| = 100 and |A+A| = 250. Using the Green–Ruzsa quantitative Freiman theorem, estimate an upper bound for the dimension and size of a generalized arithmetic progression containing A.
Here K = |A+A|/|A| = 2.5. The Green–Ruzsa bound gives dimension d = O(K log K). With K = 2.5, K log K ≈ 2.5 × 0.916 ≈ 2.3, so d ≤ 3 (the implicit constant is small). The size of the progression is at most exp(O(K log K))|A|. exp(O(2.3)) ≈ 10, so the progression size is at most about 10 × 100 = 1000. Thus A is contained in a GAP of dimension at most 3 and size at most 1000.
Exam Strategy
When a problem asks for structural consequences of small doubling, first compute the doubling constant K = |A+A|/|A|. Cite the appropriate quantitative Freiman theorem (Green–Ruzsa for general groups, Sanders for integers) and state the resulting dimension and size bounds in terms of K. Examiners often test whether you confuse the exponential Freiman bound with the polynomial PFR conjecture; be explicit about which result you are invoking.

Sum-Product Estimates and Incidence Geometry

The sum‑product phenomenon asserts that a finite set A in a field cannot be simultaneously closed under addition and multiplication unless it is very large or very structured. The foundational result of Erdős and Szemerédi (1983) conjectured that for A ⊂ ℝ, max(|A+A|, |A·A|) ≥ c|A|2−ε for any ε > 0. Elekes (1997) gave a geometric proof using the Szemerédi–Trotter incidence theorem, establishing max(|A+A|, |A·A|) ≥ c|A|5/4. Solymosi (2009) refined the crossing‑number argument to obtain max(|A+A|, |A·A|) ≥ c|A|4/3. Over finite fields 𝔽_p, Bourgain, Katz, and Tao (2004) proved that for |A| < p1−δ, max(|A+A|, |A·A|) ≥ c|A|1+δ' with δ' > 0 depending on δ. Rudnev (2018) used the polynomial method to give a near‑sharp bound max(|A+A|, |A·A|) ≥ c|A|11/9 for A ⊂ 𝔽_p with |A| ≤ p2/3. These estimates have profound applications in incidence geometry: the number of incidences between n points and m lines in ℝ² is O(n2/3m2/3 + n + m) (Szemerédi–Trotter), and sum‑product bounds translate into lower bounds for the number of distinct distances determined by a point set (Erdős distance problem). In additive combinatorics, sum‑product estimates are used to prove expansion properties of Cayley graphs and to derive bounds for the size of product sets in groups of Lie type (Helfgott, 2008).

Higher Order Fourier Analysis: Gowers Uniformity Norms and Inverse Theorems

Gowers introduced the U^k uniformity norms in 1998 to quantify the pseudorandomness of a function f : G → ℂ on a finite abelian group G. The U² norm is equivalent to the Fourier ℓ⁴ norm: ‖f‖U²⁴ = Σr∈Ĝ |̂f(r)|⁴. The inverse theorem for U² states that if ‖f‖U² ≥ δ, then f correlates with a linear phase e(r·x). For k ≥ 3, the U^k norms capture higher‑order structure. The inverse theorem for U³ (Green–Tao–Ziegler, 2012) shows that a function with large U³ norm correlates with a quadratic phase e(Q(x)) where Q is a quadratic polynomial. This result was the key to proving Szemerédi's theorem for progressions of length 4. The general inverse theorem for U^k (Green–Tao–Ziegler, 2010–2012) states that large U^k norm implies correlation with a polynomial phase of degree k−1 on a nilmanifold. The proof uses the machinery of nilsequences and the factorization theorem for nilmanifolds. These higher‑order Fourier tools have been applied to count linear patterns in primes (Green–Tao, 2008), to establish the inverse conjecture for the Gowers norms over finite fields (Tao–Ziegler, 2010), and to prove multiple recurrence in ergodic theory (Host–Kra, 2005). The U^k norms also provide a quantitative framework for the density Hales–Jewett theorem (Polymath, 2009).

Applications to Arithmetic Progressions in Primes and Ergodic Theory

The Green–Tao theorem (2008) that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions is a landmark synthesis of additive combinatorics, analytic number theory, and ergodic theory. The proof proceeds by a transference principle: one constructs a measure‑preserving system that models the primes, then applies Szemerédi's theorem (or its ergodic counterpart, Furstenberg's multiple recurrence theorem) to obtain progressions in the model, and finally transfers the result back to the primes using a dense model theorem. The dense model theorem relies on the Gowers U^k norms and the inverse theorem to show that the primes are indistinguishable from a dense subset of integers with respect to U^k tests. The quantitative bounds for the length‑k progression in primes depend on the inverse theorem for U^k and are of tower‑type height k. In ergodic theory, the Host–Kra structure theory (2005) identifies the characteristic factors for multiple averages as nilsystems, providing a dynamical proof of Szemerédi's theorem. The correspondence principle of Furstenberg (1977) translates combinatorial density statements into measure‑preserving recurrence, and the inverse theorems for Gowers norms give the quantitative backbone for the polynomial Szemerédi theorem (Bergelson–Leibman, 1996). Recent work of Tao and Ziegler (2018) on the inverse conjecture for the Gowers norms over finite fields has led to new bounds for the cap set problem and for the number of solutions to linear equations in dense subsets of 𝔽_pⁿ.

  • Confusing the exponential bounds of Freiman's theorem with the polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture; always state which result you are using.
  • Assuming the sum‑product exponent 5/4 holds over all fields; the finite‑field bounds require a size restriction relative to the characteristic.
  • Misapplying the U² inverse theorem when the problem requires U³ or higher; check the length of the progression.
  • Overlooking the role of the dense model theorem in the Green–Tao proof; it is the bridge between pseudorandomness and density.
  • Treating the slice‑rank method as a black box without understanding the polynomial construction; examiners may ask for the degree bound.
  • Neglecting the distinction between generalized arithmetic progressions and coset progressions in the statement of Freiman's theorem.
  • Forgetting that the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem produces a subset with small sumset, not the original set itself.

These advanced topics form the modern toolkit for tackling research‑level problems in additive combinatorics and are frequently tested in higher‑level examinations.
