hand/stochastic-proc.html:
Filtrations, Adapted Processes, and the Usual Conditions

A filtration (ℱₜ)ₜ≥0 on a probability space (Ω, ℱ, ℙ) is an increasing family of σ‑algebras ℱₛ ⊆ ℱₜ for s ≤ t. A stochastic process X = (Xₜ) is adapted if Xₜ is ℱₜ‑measurable for every t. The usual conditions require (i) ℱ₀ contains all ℙ‑null sets and (ii) the filtration is right‑continuous: ℱₜ = ⋂s>t ℱₛ. These conditions guarantee the existence of càdlàg modifications for martingales and allow the definition of stopping times τ with the property {τ ≤ t} ∈ ℱₜ. The augmented filtration ℱₜ⁺ = σ(ℱₜ ∪ 𝒩) where 𝒩 are the ℙ‑null sets, together with right‑continuity, yields the completed, right‑continuous filtration that is standard in stochastic calculus. Without the usual conditions, optional stopping and the martingale representation theorem can fail; for instance, a martingale may lack a càdlàg version and the stochastic integral ∫₀ᵗ Hₛ dMₛ may be ill‑defined for predictable integrands H. In practice, one always works with the usual augmentation of the natural filtration of a Brownian motion or a Lévy process.

Stochastic Integration Beyond Itô: Stratonovich, Rough Paths, and Applications

The Itô integral ∫₀ᵗ Hₛ dBₛ is defined for predictable integrands and satisfies the Itô isometry E[(∫₀ᵗ Hₛ dBₛ)²] = E[∫₀ᵗ Hₛ² ds]. The Stratonovich integral ⨍₀ᵗ Hₛ ∘ dBₛ is defined as the limit in probability of Riemann sums with the integrand evaluated at the midpoint of each subinterval. For a C² function f, the Stratonovich chain rule reads df(Xₜ) = f'(Xₜ) ∘ dXₜ, i.e. no second‑order correction term appears. The conversion formula between the two integrals is ⨍₀ᵗ Hₛ ∘ dBₛ = ∫₀ᵗ Hₛ dBₛ + ½[H, B]ₜ, where [H, B] is the quadratic covariation. In physical modelling, Stratonovich calculus preserves the classical chain rule and is natural for systems with coloured noise approximated by white noise (Wong–Zakai theorem). Rough path theory (Lyons, 1998) lifts a path X to a rough path 𝐗 = (X, 𝑿) where 𝑿 encodes iterated integrals ∫ X ⊗ dX. The solution map of a differential equation driven by a rough path is continuous in the p‑variation topology, allowing pathwise solutions for signals with Hölder regularity > 1/3, including fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index H > 1/4. This framework underpins modern numerical schemes such as the log‑ODE method for SDEs on manifolds and provides a deterministic interpretation of stochastic integrals without probability.

Conversion Between Itô and Stratonovich Integrals
Let B be a standard Brownian motion and consider the Stratonovich integral ⨍₀ᵗ Bₛ ∘ dBₛ. Compute its Itô representation and evaluate its expectation.
Using the conversion formula ⨍₀ᵗ Hₛ ∘ dBₛ = ∫₀ᵗ Hₛ dBₛ + ½[H, B]ₜ with Hₛ = Bₛ. The quadratic covariation [B, B]ₜ = t, so ½[H, B]ₜ = ½ t. Hence ⨍₀ᵗ Bₛ ∘ dBₛ = ∫₀ᵗ Bₛ dBₛ + ½ t. By Itô's lemma, ∫₀ᵗ Bₛ dBₛ = ½ Bₜ² − ½ t. Substituting gives ⨍₀ᵗ Bₛ ∘ dBₛ = ½ Bₜ². The expectation E[½ Bₜ²] = ½ t, which matches the known mean of the Stratonovich integral.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Stratonovich integral of a polynomial in Brownian motion, first write the Itô integral using Itô's lemma, then add the ½ quadratic covariation correction. Remember that the Stratonovich integral of a martingale is not a martingale unless the integrand is deterministic; this distinction is a frequent trap in multiple‑choice items.

Girsanov Theorem and Change of Measure in Finance and Filtering

The Girsanov theorem provides a rigorous method to change the probability measure so that a Brownian motion with drift becomes a standard Brownian motion under the new measure. Let (Ω, ℱ, (ℱₜ), ℙ) satisfy the usual conditions and let B be a ℙ‑Brownian motion. For an adapted process θ satisfying Novikov's condition E[exp(½∫₀ᵀ θₛ² ds)] < ∞, define the exponential martingale Zₜ = exp(∫₀ᵗ θₛ dBₛ − ½∫₀ᵗ θₛ² ds). Then the measure ℚ defined by dℚ/dℙ|ℱₜ = Zₜ is a probability measure and the process B̃ₜ = Bₜ − ∫₀ᵗ θₛ ds is a ℚ‑Brownian motion. In mathematical finance, θ = (μ − r)/σ transforms the physical dynamics dS = μ S dt + σ S dB into the risk‑neutral dynamics dS = r S dt + σ S dB̃, enabling arbitrage‑free pricing via expectation under ℚ. In nonlinear filtering, the Kallianpur–Striebel formula expresses the conditional law of a signal given observations as a ratio of expectations under a reference measure where the observation noise is a standard Brownian motion; Girsanov's theorem supplies the Radon–Nikodym derivative linking the physical and reference measures. The theorem extends to Lévy processes: if X is a Lévy process with characteristic triplet (b, c, ν) under ℙ, a change of measure with a suitable density modifies the drift, the Gaussian coefficient, and the Lévy measure according to the Esscher transform.

Spectral Theory of Markov Operators and Mixing Times

For a reversible Markov chain with transition matrix P and stationary distribution π, the operator P acts on L²(π) as a self‑adjoint contraction. Its spectrum lies in [−1, 1]; the eigenvalue 1 is simple and corresponds to the constant eigenfunction. The spectral gap γ = 1 − λ₂, where λ₂ is the second largest eigenvalue in absolute value, controls the exponential convergence rate: ‖Pⁿ(x,·) − π‖TV ≤ ½ √(π(x)⁻¹) (1−γ)ⁿ. For non‑reversible chains, one studies the singular values of P or the additive reversiblization (P + P*)/2. Mixing time tmix(ε) = min{n : max_x ‖Pⁿ(x,·) − π‖TV ≤ ε} satisfies tmix(ε) ≤ (1/γ) log(1/(ε πmin)). The cutoff phenomenon occurs when the total variation distance drops from near 1 to near 0 in a window of order smaller than the mixing time; classic examples include the random transpositions shuffle (Diaconis–Shahshahani, 1981) and the Ehrenfest urn. Coupling provides a probabilistic bound: if a coupling (Xₙ, Yₙ) meets with probability 1, then ‖Pⁿ(x,·) − π‖TV ≤ ℙ(Xₙ ≠ Yₙ). The path coupling technique (Bubley–Dyer, 1997) reduces the analysis to neighbouring states, yielding polynomial mixing bounds for Glauber dynamics on colourings and the Ising model at high temperature.

Stochastic Partial Differential Equations: Existence, Uniqueness, and Numerical Approximation

A stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) typically takes the form ∂ₜ u = A u + F(u) + G(u) ξ, where A is a differential operator (e.g. the Laplacian Δ), ξ is space‑time white noise, and the solution u(t,x) is a random field. The Walsh integral defines ∫₀ᵗ ∫_D φ(s,x) W(ds,dx) for predictable integrands φ against a martingale measure W. For the stochastic heat equation ∂ₜ u = Δ u + ξ on a bounded domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions, the mild solution is u(t) = ∫₀ᵗ S(t−s) dW(s) where S(t) = etΔ is the analytic semigroup generated by Δ. Existence and uniqueness hold in the space of predictable processes with values in L²(Ω; H-α) for α > d/2 − 1 (d spatial dimension). In one dimension, the solution is function‑valued and Hölder continuous in space with exponent < ½. Numerical approximation uses finite element discretisation in space and Euler–Maruyama in time; the strong error satisfies E[‖u(t_n) − u_h^n‖L²] ≤ C (h1−ε + Δt½−ε) for any ε > 0. For semilinear SPDEs with globally Lipschitz nonlinearities, the same rates persist. The Malliavin calculus on Wiener space yields smoothness of the law of u(t,x) and enables density estimates for the solution at a fixed point.

  • Confusing the usual conditions with mere right‑continuity; the inclusion of null sets is essential for stopping time theorems.
  • Applying the Itô chain rule where the Stratonovich rule is required, or vice‑versa, without adding the ½ quadratic covariation correction.
  • Assuming Girsanov's theorem holds without verifying Novikov's or Kazamaki's condition; the exponential martingale may fail to be a true martingale.
  • Equating spectral gap with mixing time for non‑reversible chains; the singular value gap or the additive reversiblization must be used.
  • Ignoring the regularity restriction on space‑time white noise: in dimensions d ≥ 2 the solution is a distribution, not a function, so pointwise evaluation is meaningless.
  • Using Euler–Maruyama time stepping for SPDEs without accounting for the CFL condition linking Δt and spatial mesh h; instability appears when Δt ≫ h².
  • Treating the Stratonovich integral of a martingale as a martingale; it generally acquires a drift term unless the integrand is deterministic.
The advanced sections above complete the stochastic processes module with measure‑theoretic foundations, alternative integration theories, measure change techniques, spectral mixing analysis, and SPDE fundamentals.

hand/solutions.html:
Non‑Ideal Solution Models and Activity Coefficients

Real solutions deviate from Raoult’s law because intermolecular forces between unlike molecules differ from those in the pure components. The thermodynamic framework replaces mole fraction xi with activity ai = γi xi, where γi is the activity coefficient. For a binary mixture the excess Gibbs energy GE = RT Σ xi ln γi quantifies the deviation. Common models include the Margules two‑parameter equation, the Wilson equation, and the NRTL (Non‑Random Two‑Liquid) model. The Margules expression for a symmetric system is ln γ1 = A x2² and ln γ2 = A x1², where A is an empirical constant obtained from vapour‑pressure data. The Wilson model introduces local‑composition concepts and is particularly effective for highly non‑ideal systems such as ethanol–water. NRTL adds a non‑randomness parameter α (typically 0.2–0.47) and can represent both positive and negative deviations. Activity coefficients are temperature dependent; they are usually correlated with the van’t Hoff equation ln γ = –ΔHE/RT + ΔSE/R. In practice, γ values are used to calculate equilibrium constants for reactions in solution, to design distillation columns, and to predict azeotrope composition. For example, the ethanol–water azeotrope at 1 atm contains 95.6 % ethanol by mass; the corresponding γethanol ≈ 1.0 and γwater ≈ 2.5 at that composition. Understanding these models enables the examiner to test whether a student can convert experimental vapour‑pressure data into activity coefficients and then predict phase behaviour.

Temperature Dependence of Henry’s Constant and Gas Solubility

Henry’s law constant KH (in units of pressure · mole‑fraction⁻¹) varies with temperature according to the van’t Hoff relation d ln KH/d(1/T) = –ΔHsol/R, where ΔHsol is the enthalpy of solution of the gas. For most gases ΔHsol is negative (exothermic dissolution), so KH increases as temperature rises, meaning solubility decreases. The temperature coefficient is often expressed as the Ostwald coefficient L = Cgas/Cliquid at equilibrium, which is inversely proportional to KH. Experimental data for O₂ in water show KH ≈ 1.3 × 10³ atm at 298 K and ≈ 2.5 × 10³ atm at 313 K, corresponding to a drop in dissolved O₂ from 1.3 mmol L⁻¹ to 0.7 mmol L⁻¹ at 1 atm. This temperature effect underlies the seasonal stratification of lakes and the design of aeration systems in wastewater treatment. In carbonated beverages, the pressure of CO₂ in the headspace is set at 2–3 atm at 277 K; warming to 298 K raises KH by roughly 40 %, causing rapid loss of fizz. The examiner may ask to calculate the new equilibrium concentration after a temperature jump, requiring the student to integrate the van’t Hoff equation assuming ΔHsol constant over the range. A typical trap is to confuse the Henry constant expressed in pressure‑over‑concentration units (kH = p/C) with the dimensionless form; the temperature dependence is identical but the numerical values differ by a factor of RT.

Worked Example: Henry’s Constant Temperature Shift
At 298 K the Henry constant for N₂ in water is 6.1 × 10⁴ atm·M⁻¹. The enthalpy of solution is –12 kJ mol⁻¹. Estimate the Henry constant at 313 K and the dissolved N₂ concentration at 1 atm.
Use the integrated van’t Hoff equation: ln(K₂/K₁) = –ΔHsol/R (1/T₂ – 1/T₁). Insert ΔHsol = –12 000 J mol⁻¹, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T₁ = 298 K, T₂ = 313 K. 1/T₂ – 1/T₁ = (1/313 – 1/298) = –1.61 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Then ln(K₂/K₁) = –(–12 000)/8.314 × (–1.61 × 10⁻⁴) = –0.232. Hence K₂ = K₁ e⁻⁰·²³² = 6.1 × 10⁴ × 0.793 ≈ 4.8 × 10⁴ atm·M⁻¹. The concentration at 1 atm is C = p/K₂ = 1/4.8 × 10⁴ = 2.1 × 10⁻⁵ M. At 298 K the concentration would have been 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ M, confirming the decrease in solubility with temperature.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question gives ΔHsol and asks for the new Henry constant, write the van’t Hoff equation in logarithmic form first; this avoids sign errors. Remember that a negative ΔHsol makes KH increase with temperature, so solubility falls. Keep units consistent: if KH is given in atm·M⁻¹, the concentration will be in mol L⁻¹ directly.

Colligative Properties in Mixed Solvent Systems

Colligative property equations are derived for a single solvent. In a mixed‑solvent system the effective cryoscopic and ebullioscopic constants become composition‑dependent. For a binary solvent mixture of components A and B, the freezing‑point depression is ΔTf = Kf,mix msolute, where Kf,mix = Σ xi Kf,i (γi/γsolvent) under the assumption of ideal mixing of the solvents. In practice, the solvent activity asolvent = γsolvent xsolvent replaces the pure‑solvent mole fraction in the thermodynamic derivation: ΔTf = (R Tf²/ΔHfus) ln asolvent. For dilute solutes, ln asolvent ≈ –xsolute (γsolute/γsolvent), leading to an apparent van’t Hoff factor that includes solvent‑solvent interactions. A classic example is the determination of molar mass of a polymer in a water‑ethanol mixture; the measured ΔTf is smaller than predicted using pure‑water Kf because ethanol lowers the solvent’s freezing point and changes its activity coefficient. Examiners often test this by giving a binary solvent composition and asking for the corrected Kf or the apparent molar mass. The key step is to calculate the solvent activity from known vapour‑pressure data or from a model such as UNIFAC, then apply the modified freezing‑point equation.

Application of van’t Hoff Factor to Degree of Dissociation and Association

The van’t Hoff factor i links the observed colligative effect to the number of particles in solution. For a weak electrolyte AB ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻ with degree of dissociation α, i = 1 + α (for a 1:1 electrolyte) or i = 1 + (ν – 1)α in general, where ν is the total number of ions produced per formula unit. For association, e.g. 2 HA ⇌ (HA)₂ in benzene, the equilibrium constant Kassoc = [(HA)₂]/[HA]². If the total analytical concentration is c, the monomer concentration is c (1 – α) and dimer concentration is c α/2, giving i = 1 – α/2. Measuring ΔTf or π at several concentrations allows a plot of i versus c; extrapolation to infinite dilution yields the limiting i (ν for complete dissociation, 1 for non‑electrolyte). The Ostwald dilution law Kd = c α²/(1 – α) can be combined with i = 1 + α to determine Kd from colligative data. A typical problem provides freezing‑point depressions for acetic acid in benzene at two concentrations; the student calculates i at each concentration, obtains α, and then evaluates Kassoc. Care must be taken to use molality (temperature‑independent) and to apply the correct Kf for benzene (5.12 K kg mol⁻¹). The examiner may also ask to distinguish between ion‑pair formation (which reduces i) and true association (which also reduces i but follows a different equilibrium expression).

Solubility Product Calculations with Complex Ion Formation and pH Effects

When a sparingly soluble salt shares an ion with a complex‑forming ligand, the apparent solubility increases because the free metal ion concentration is lowered. For AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) and Ag⁺ + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ (Kf = 1.6 × 10⁷), the overall dissolution in ammonia is AgCl(s) + 2 NH₃ ⇌ [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + Cl⁻ with K = Ksp Kf = 2.9 × 10⁻³. If the ammonia concentration is 0.1 M, the solubility s ≈ √(K [NH₃]²) = √(2.9 × 10⁻³ × 0.01) ≈ 5.4 × 10⁻³ M, far larger than the 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M in pure water. pH influences solubility when the anion is basic. For CaCO₃ (Ksp = 3.3 × 10⁻⁹), carbonate reacts with H⁺: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ (Ka2 = 4.7 × 10⁻¹¹). At pH 5, [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M, the fraction of carbonate present as CO₃²⁻ is α₂ = Ka1Ka2/([H⁺]² + Ka1[H⁺] + Ka1Ka2) ≈ 0.02. The effective solubility product becomes Ksp/α₂, raising the molar solubility by roughly √(1/α₂) ≈ 7‑fold. Examiners often combine both effects: a metal hydroxide dissolving in a buffer containing a complexing agent. The systematic approach is to write all equilibria, express the total dissolved metal as the sum of free ion and complex, substitute the ligand concentration (often fixed by a buffer), and solve the resulting polynomial for s. Approximations (e.g., ligand in large excess, pH fixed) simplify the algebra and are expected in timed tests.

  • Assuming activity coefficients are unity for concentrated solutions when calculating colligative properties.
  • Using molarity instead of molality in ΔT = i K m, ignoring temperature‑induced volume changes.
  • Confusing the Henry constant expressed as pressure‑over‑concentration with the dimensionless form, leading to wrong temperature‑dependence signs.
  • Neglecting the common‑ion effect when a complexing ligand also supplies the common ion (e.g., NH₄Cl in AgCl/NH₃ system).
  • Treating the van’t Hoff factor as constant for weak electrolytes across all concentrations.
  • Forgetting to convert Ksp to the appropriate units when the solubility expression involves mixed molarity and molality.
  • Applying the simple ΔT = K m formula to mixed‑solvent systems without correcting the cryoscopic constant for solvent activity.

hand/birational-geometry.html:
Log Minimal Model Program and Pairs

The Minimal Model Program extends naturally to pairs (X, Δ) where X is a normal projective variety and Δ is an effective ℚ-divisor such that KX + Δ is ℚ-Cartier. The singularities of the pair are measured by discrepancies: for a log resolution f : Y → X write KY + ΔY = f*(KX + Δ) + Σ aiEi. The pair is terminal if all ai > 0, canonical if ai ≥ 0, kawamata log terminal (klt) if ai > −1, and log canonical (lc) if ai ≥ −1. Intermediate classes such as divisorially log terminal (dlt) and purely log terminal (plt) are defined by requiring the discrepancies to satisfy the inequalities on a suitable resolution with simple normal crossings support.

The Cone Theorem and Contraction Theorem hold for klt pairs: the Mori cone NE(X) is generated by the KX + Δ-nonnegative part and countably many extremal rays spanned by rational curves C with −(KX + Δ)·C ≤ dim X + 1. Each extremal ray admits a contraction morphism φ : X → Z which is either a Fano contraction, a divisorial contraction, or a small contraction. When the contraction is small, a log flip replaces it by a small KX + Δ-positive contraction φ+ : X+ → Z. The existence of log flips for klt pairs in all dimensions was proved by Hacon and McKernan (2010) using the technique of minimal model program with scaling and the finite generation of the log canonical ring.

The outcome of the log MMP for a klt pair is either a log minimal model — a birational model Xmin where KXmin + Δmin is nef — or a Mori fiber space — a contraction X → S with −(KX + Δ) relatively ample and dim S < dim X. The Basepoint-Free Theorem (Kawamata–Shokurov) asserts that if KX + Δ is nef and big, then some multiple m(KX + Δ) is basepoint-free, yielding the log canonical model. The Abundance Conjecture predicts that nef implies semiample for log canonical pairs; it is known for surfaces, threefolds, and for pairs with κ = 0 (the log Calabi–Yau case).

Key Technical Tools

  • Dlt modifications: any lc pair admits a dlt model where the boundary has simple normal crossings and discrepancies are controlled.
  • Adjunction and inversion of adjunction: for a divisor D on X, the pair (X, Δ + D) is lc near D iff (D, ΔD) is lc, where ΔD is the different.
  • ACC for log canonical thresholds: the set of lc thresholds in a fixed dimension satisfies the ascending chain condition (Hacon–McKernan–Xu, 2014), a crucial ingredient for termination of flips.

Termination of Flips and the ACC Conjecture

Termination of flips means that any sequence of KX + Δ-flips cannot be infinite. In dimension three, Mori (1988) proved termination by a detailed analysis of the possible flipping curves and the behavior of the Hilbert polynomial. In higher dimensions, the problem was open until the work of Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) who established termination for varieties of general type (i.e., when KX + Δ is big). Their proof relies on two pillars: the finite generation of the log canonical ring and the Ascending Chain Condition (ACC) for log canonical thresholds.

The ACC conjecture, formulated by Alexeev, Birkar, Hacon, and McKernan, states that for a fixed dimension d, the set of all log canonical thresholds lct(X, Δ; D) where (X, Δ) is a log canonical pair of dimension d and D is an effective ℚ-Cartier divisor, satisfies the ascending chain condition — there is no infinite strictly increasing sequence. Hacon, McKernan, and Xu (2014) proved this conjecture using the minimal model program for pairs and the theory of complements. The ACC implies that the set of possible discrepancies in a bounded family of pairs is finite, which in turn forces any sequence of flips to terminate because each flip strictly increases the log canonical threshold of the flipped curve.

For pairs that are not of general type (e.g., Calabi–Yau or Fano type), termination of flips remains a major open problem. The existence of flips for all lc pairs in all dimensions (Hacon–McKernan, 2010) does not automatically give termination. Recent progress includes the proof of termination for log flips in dimension four (Birkar, 2016) and for certain special classes such as toric varieties (where flips correspond to stellar subdivisions of fans and termination follows from the finiteness of the fan). The general termination conjecture is equivalent to the existence of minimal models for all lc pairs, a central goal of birational geometry.

Worked Example: Computing a Log Flip
Let X ⊂ ℙ4 be the cone over a smooth quadric surface Q ⊂ ℙ3, with vertex P. The divisor Δ = 0. The variety X has an isolated singularity at P which is canonical but not terminal. Consider the blow-up f : Y → X at P. The exceptional divisor E ≅ Q is a ℙ1 × ℙ1. Compute the discrepancy a(E, X) and determine whether the contraction of a ruling of E gives a flip.
The canonical divisor of X satisfies KX = f*KX + a(E, X)E. Since X is a hypersurface of degree 2 in ℙ4, KX = (Kℙ4 + X)|X = (−5H + 2H)|X = −3H where H is the hyperplane class. On Y, f*H = HY (the proper transform of a hyperplane section) and E is the exceptional divisor. The normal bundle of E in Y is OE(−1, −1). By adjunction, KE = (KY + E)|E. Since E ≅ ℙ1 × ℙ1, KE = −2H1 − 2H2. One finds a(E, X) = 0, so the singularity is canonical. The ruling curves C ≅ ℙ1 on E satisfy KY·C = −1. Contracting one ruling gives a small contraction φ : Y → Z with KY-negative. The flip Y ⇢ Y+ replaces the ruling by the other ruling; the flipped variety Y+ is isomorphic to Y (the Atiyah flop). This is a log flip for the pair (X, 0).
Exam Strategy: Recognizing Flip Configurations
When a problem asks whether a given birational map is a flip, check three conditions: (1) the map is an isomorphism in codimension one (small), (2) the canonical divisor (or log canonical divisor) is negative on the contracted curves on the source, and (3) it becomes positive on the corresponding curves on the target. If the exceptional locus is a divisor, it is a divisorial contraction, not a flip. In practice, compute intersection numbers with the extremal ray; a sign change of K·C across the map is the hallmark of a flip.

Boundedness of Varieties of General Type and Canonical Ring Finite Generation

A projective variety X is of general type if its Kodaira dimension κ(X) = dim X, equivalently the canonical divisor KX is big. The finite generation of the canonical ring R(X, KX) = ⊕m≥0 H0(X, mKX) was conjectured by Zariski and proved in full generality by Birkar–Cascini–Hacon–McKernan (2010) using the minimal model program. Finite generation implies that the pluricanonical maps φmKX : X ⇢ ℙh0(mKX)−1 stabilize for large m and define a birational model Xcan, the canonical model, which has canonical singularities and ample KXcan.

Boundedness of varieties of general type means that for fixed dimension n and volume V = KXn, the set of isomorphism classes of smooth (or canonical) models with KXn = V is contained in a finite number of algebraic families. This was established by Kollár–Matsusaka (1983) for surfaces and by Hacon–McKernan–Xu (2014) in all dimensions using the ACC for log canonical thresholds and the theory of complements. The boundedness result is equivalent to the existence of a coarse moduli space for canonically polarized varieties (the moduli stack of stable varieties) which is proper and of finite type (Kollár–Shepherd-Barron, Alexeev).

The proof strategy combines the minimal model program with the following steps: (1) run the MMP to reach a minimal model Xmin with KXmin nef and big; (2) apply the Basepoint-Free Theorem to obtain the canonical model Xcan with ample KXcan; (3) use the ACC to show that the set of possible singularities and volumes is discrete; (4) invoke the boundedness of Fano varieties (Birkar, 2018) to control the fibers of the pluricanonical fibrations. The finite generation of the log canonical ring for klt pairs (X, Δ) with KX + Δ big is a parallel result, essential for the log MMP.

Consequences for Moduli

  • The moduli stack 𝔐n,V of stable varieties of dimension n and volume V is a proper Deligne–Mumford stack with a projective coarse moduli space.
  • Degenerations of canonically polarized varieties are controlled by the minimal model program: any family over a punctured curve extends uniquely to a family of stable varieties after a finite base change (the stable reduction theorem).
  • The boundedness of the canonical ring implies that the Hilbert polynomial of the canonical model depends only on n and V, giving a uniform embedding into a fixed projective space.

Moduli of Fano Varieties and K-Stability

Fano varieties, defined by the ampleness of −KX, are the building blocks of the MMP with negative curvature. The boundedness theorem of Birkar (2018) shows that for each dimension n and volume V = (−KX)n, the set of ℚ-factorial klt Fano varieties is bounded. This finiteness result allows the construction of a moduli stack 𝔛n,V of Fano varieties, which is an Artin stack of finite type. However, not all Fano varieties in a bounded family are geometrically stable; the appropriate stability notion is K-stability, introduced by Tian and Donaldson in the context of Kähler–Einstein metrics.

A Fano variety X is K-semistable if for every test configuration (𝒳, ℒ) (a flat family over 𝔸1 with a relatively ample line bundle extending −KX), the Donaldson–Futaki invariant DF(𝒳, ℒ) ≥ 0. It is K-polystable if equality holds only for product test configurations. The Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture, proved by Chen–Donaldson–Sun (2015) and Tian (2015), states that a smooth Fano variety admits a Kähler–Einstein metric iff it is K-polystable. For singular Fano varieties, the equivalence between K-polystability and the existence of a Kähler–Einstein metric (in the sense of singular metrics) was established by Berman–Boucksom–Jonsson (2021) and Xu–Zhuang (2021).

The moduli space of K-polystable Fano varieties, often called the K-moduli, is a proper Artin stack with a good moduli space which is a projective scheme (Xu, 2020; Blum–Xu, 2022). The boundedness of Fano varieties ensures that the K-moduli stack is of finite type. The wall-crossing between different stability conditions (e.g., K-stability vs. GIT stability for embedded Fano varieties) is governed by the minimal model program: a K-polystable degeneration corresponds to a sequence of log flips and divisorial contractions leading to a log canonical model. This deep link between birational geometry and moduli theory is a central theme of current research.

Key Results

  • Birkar (2018): Boundedness of ℚ-factorial klt Fano varieties of fixed dimension and volume.
  • Chen–Donaldson–Sun, Tian (2015): Smooth Fano admits Kähler–Einstein metric ⇔ K-polystable.
  • Xu (2020), Blum–Xu (2022): Existence of projective coarse moduli space for K-polystable Fano varieties.
  • Liu–Xu–Zhuang (2022): The K-moduli stack is a proper Artin stack with a good moduli space.

Applications to Mirror Symmetry and String Theory

Birational geometry provides the mathematical framework for several phenomena in mirror symmetry. The minimal model program predicts that any two birational Calabi–Yau varieties are connected by a sequence of flops (flips with KX ≡ 0). Bondal and Orlov (2001) proved that the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves Db(Coh X) is invariant under flops, establishing a categorical equivalence between the derived categories of birational Calabi–Yau varieties. This invariance is the geometric counterpart of the physical statement that the topological string theory is unchanged under flop transitions.

In the gauged linear sigma model (GLSM) description of Calabi–Yau sigma models, the phases of the GLSM correspond to different birational models of the same Calabi–Yau variety. The walls in the Kähler moduli space where the phase changes are precisely the flopping contractions. The derived category of the Calabi–Yau is expected to be equivalent to the Fukaya category of its mirror (Homological Mirror Symmetry, Kontsevich). The MMP organizes the birational models into a chamber structure that matches the wall-crossing of stability conditions on the derived category (Bridgeland stability).

For Fano varieties, the MMP produces Mori fiber space structures that correspond to different GLSM phases in the context of the Fano/Landau–Ginzburg correspondence. The boundedness of Fano varieties implies that the number of such phases is finite. The K-stability condition selects the phase that admits a Kähler–Einstein metric, which is the geometric realization of the vacuum in the associated superconformal field theory. Recent work by Halverson–Long–Tian (2023) uses the MMP to classify all possible phases of GLSMs for toric Fano varieties, linking the combinatorics of the fan to the birational geometry of the variety.

Open Directions

  • Prove derived equivalence for all crepant birational maps between log Calabi–Yau pairs (the Kawamata conjecture).
  • Extend the wall-crossing picture to non-commutative crepant resolutions and categories of matrix factorizations.
  • Understand the role of the ACC for log canonical thresholds in the finiteness of GLSM phases.
  • Confusing log terminal with log canonical singularities: klt requires discrepancies > −1, lc allows = −1; this distinction determines whether the pair admits a minimal model or only a log canonical model.
  • Assuming termination of flips holds in all dimensions for all pairs; it is only known for varieties of general type and in low dimensions.
  • Misapplying the Basepoint-Free Theorem without verifying that KX + Δ is nef and big; the theorem fails if only nef is assumed (Abundance Conjecture).
  • Overlooking the need for a dlt modification before running the log MMP; the cone theorem for lc pairs requires a dlt model to control the extremal rays.
  • Treating K-stability as equivalent to GIT stability for all Fano varieties; they coincide only for certain polarizations and require the variety to be K-polystable.
  • Neglecting the role of the ACC in boundedness proofs; the ACC for log canonical thresholds is the engine that makes the set of possible volumes discrete.
  • These traps cover the most frequent errors in advanced birational geometry.

hand/chromatic-homotopy.html:
The Thick Subcategory Theorem and Its Classification

The thick subcategory theorem, proved by Hopkins and Smith in 1998, gives a complete classification of the thick subcategories of the category of finite spectra. A thick subcategory is a full triangulated subcategory closed under retracts. The theorem states that for each integer n ≥ 0 the collection C_n of finite spectra of type ≥ n forms a thick subcategory, and every non‑zero thick subcategory of finite spectra equals C_n for a unique n. Here a finite spectrum X has type n if K(m)_*(X) = 0 for m < n and K(n)_*(X) ≠ 0, where K(m) denotes the Morava K‑theory at height m. The type of a finite spectrum is therefore detected by the Morava K‑theories, and the filtration by type coincides with the chromatic filtration on the finite subcategory.

The proof uses the nilpotence theorem to show that any map between finite spectra which is zero on all Morava K‑theories is nilpotent. From this one deduces that the Bousfield class of a finite spectrum is determined by its type, and that the thick subcategory generated by a finite spectrum of type n is exactly C_n. Consequently the lattice of thick subcategories is a chain C0 ⊃ C1 ⊃ C2 ⊃ … . This result has far‑reaching consequences: it implies the periodicity theorem (every finite spectrum of type n admits a v_n self‑map), it underlies the classification of localizing subcategories in the K(n)‑local category, and it provides the algebraic input for the telescope conjecture (which predicts that the smashing localization at C_n coincides with the telescope of a v_n self‑map). The theorem also extends to the derived category of coherent sheaves on classifying spaces of finite groups, where thick subcategories are classified by support varieties.

In practice, the thick subcategory theorem allows one to reduce many questions about finite spectra to questions about a single type n. For example, the computation of the homotopy groups of spheres in a given chromatic layer can be approached by studying the K(n)‑local category, because the inclusion C_n → Cn-1 induces an equivalence after K(n)‑localization. The theorem is also the starting point for the chromatic approach to the stable homotopy category: one builds the category from the monochromatic layers M_n = C_n / Cn+1, each of which is equivalent to the K(n)‑local category of finite spectra.

The Chromatic Convergence Theorem and Its Proof Sketch

The chromatic convergence theorem, established by Hopkins and Ravenel in 1992, asserts that for any finite spectrum X the canonical map X → holim_n L_n X is an equivalence, where L_n denotes Bousfield localization with respect to the wedge K(0) ∨ … ∨ K(n). In other words, a finite spectrum can be recovered from its chromatic localizations. The theorem is a global statement that the chromatic tower converges on finite objects, and it is the homotopical analogue of the fact that a formal group over a complete local ring is determined by its reductions modulo powers of the maximal ideal.

The proof proceeds in several stages. First one shows that the fiber of the map L_n X → Ln-1 X is the monochromatic layer M_n X, which is K(n)‑local and K(n-1)‑acyclic. The collection of these fibers forms a tower whose homotopy limit is the homotopy limit of the L_n X. Using the nilpotence theorem one proves that the map X → holim_n L_n X induces an isomorphism on all Morava K‑theories K(m) for every m. Since the Morava K‑theories form a conservative family on the category of finite spectra (a map of finite spectra is an equivalence iff it is an equivalence on all K(m)), the map must be an equivalence. The conservativity of the Morava K‑theories on finite spectra is itself a consequence of the thick subcategory theorem: if a map is zero on all K(m), its cofiber lies in every C_n, hence is zero.

A key technical ingredient is the construction of the chromatic fracture square, which expresses LK(n) X as a homotopy pullback of LE(n) X and LE(n-1) X. This square allows one to relate the K(n)‑localization to the more computable E(n)‑localization. The convergence theorem also implies that the chromatic spectral sequence, which computes the homotopy groups of the monochromatic layers, converges to the homotopy groups of X after completion at the prime p. In practice, the theorem justifies the strategy of computing stable homotopy groups by first computing them in each K(n)‑local category and then assembling the results via the chromatic spectral sequence.

Worked Example: Verifying Chromatic Convergence for a Type‑2 Complex
Let V(2) be a Smith–Toda complex of type 2 at a prime p ≥ 5. Show that the natural map V(2) → holim_n L_n V(2) is an equivalence.
The spectrum V(2) is finite of type 2, so K(m)_*(V(2)) = 0 for m < 2 and K(2)_*(V(2)) ≠ 0. For n ≥ 2 the localization L_n V(2) is equivalent to LK(2) V(2) because higher Morava K‑theories vanish on V(2). For n = 1 the localization L1 V(2) is contractible since V(2) is K(1)‑acyclic. Thus the tower L_n V(2) stabilizes at n = 2: L2 V(2) ≃ L3 V(2) ≃ … . The homotopy limit of a constant tower is the constant value, so holim_n L_n V(2) ≃ L2 V(2). The map V(2) → L2 V(2) is the K(2)‑localization map. By the nilpotence theorem, a map of finite spectra that induces an isomorphism on all Morava K‑theories is an equivalence. The localization map induces an isomorphism on K(2) (by definition of K(2)‑localization) and on K(m) for m ≠ 2 both sides are zero. Hence the map is an equivalence, establishing chromatic convergence for V(2).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to apply the chromatic convergence theorem, first identify the type of the finite spectrum involved. Then determine the smallest n for which L_n X is non‑trivial; the tower stabilizes there. Use the conservativity of the Morava K‑theories on finite spectra to conclude that the map to the homotopy limit is an equivalence. Remember that the theorem only holds for finite spectra; for infinite spectra the map need not be an equivalence.

The Goerss–Hopkins–Miller Theorem and E∞ Structures

The Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem, proved in the early 2000s, endows each Morava E‑theory E_n with a canonical E_∞‑ring structure and an action of the extended Morava stabilizer group G_n = O_n^× ⋊ Gal(𝔽p^n/𝔽_p) by E_∞‑maps. Here O_n is the endomorphism ring of the Honda formal group of height n over 𝔽p^n. The theorem is a deep result in obstruction theory: it shows that the Lubin–Tate deformation space of the Honda formal group carries a universal deformation that is not only a formal group law but a commutative S‑algebra. The construction uses the Goerss–Hopkins obstruction theory for E_∞‑structures on a given homology theory, together with the fact that the Lubin–Tate ring W(𝔽p^n)[[u1,…,un-1]] is a complete regular local ring of dimension n.

The E_∞‑structure has several crucial consequences. First, it allows one to form homotopy fixed point spectra E_nhH for any closed subgroup H ≤ G_n; these are again E_∞‑ring spectra. In particular, the homotopy fixed points under the full group G_n recover topological modular forms at the prime p: E_nhG_n ≃ TMF(p). Second, the action of G_n on E_n makes the K(n)‑local category equivalent to the category of continuous G_n‑modules over the Morava module K(n)_*(X) = E_n^*(X) ⊗E_n^* K(n)_*. This equivalence is the foundation of the algebraic approach to K(n)‑local homotopy theory, where computations are reduced to continuous group cohomology of G_n. Third, the E_∞‑structure provides power operations on E_n and on K(n), which are essential for the construction of the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence and for the analysis of the chromatic spectral sequence.

The theorem also implies that the Morava E‑theories are the initial objects in the category of E_∞‑ring spectra with a formal group of height n. This universal property is used to construct maps from E_n to other E_∞‑ring spectra, for instance the map E_n → TMF arising from the universal elliptic curve. The Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem is therefore a bridge between the geometric world of formal groups and the algebraic world of structured ring spectra, and it underlies much of the modern computation of the homotopy groups of spheres via the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence.

The Smith–Toda Complexes and Their Role in Detecting v_n‑Periodicity

The Smith–Toda complexes V(n) are finite p‑local spectra of type n, constructed by Smith and Toda in the 1970s and 1980s. For each n ≥ 0 there exists a finite spectrum V(n) with BP_*(V(n)) = BP_*/(p, v1, …, vn-1) (with the convention V(0) = S0). The construction proceeds inductively: given V(n-1), one chooses a v_n self‑map on a suitable suspension of V(n-1) and takes its cofiber to obtain V(n). The existence of such v_n self‑maps is guaranteed by the periodicity theorem, which itself follows from the nilpotence theorem and the thick subcategory theorem.

The spectra V(n) play a central role as test objects for v_n‑periodic phenomena. A map f: X → Y of finite spectra is a K(n)‑equivalence if and only if it induces an isomorphism on [V(n), -]_* (the graded homotopy classes of maps from V(n)). Equivalently, the Bousfield class of V(n) is the same as that of K(n) on the finite subcategory. This makes V(n) a finite model for the K(n)‑local sphere: the K(n)‑localization of V(n) is equivalent to the K(n)‑local sphere LK(n) S0. Consequently, the homotopy groups of the K(n)‑local sphere can be computed as the homotopy groups of the function spectrum F(V(n), LK(n) S0), which is a finite spectrum in the K(n)‑local category.

The Smith–Toda complexes also appear in the construction of the telescope T(n) of a v_n self‑map on a type‑n spectrum. The telescope conjecture (now known to be false in general) predicted that the smashing localization at V(n) coincides with smashing with T(n). Counterexamples by Mahowald–Ravenel–Shick and later by Barthel–David–Salch show that the localization L_n^f on finite spectra is strictly larger than the telescope localization. Nevertheless, V(n) remains the canonical finite representative of chromatic height n, and its Adams–Novikov spectral sequence is the primary computational tool for the K(n)‑local homotopy groups of spheres.

The Gross–Hopkins Duality and Its Consequences for Local Duality

Gross–Hopkins duality, discovered by Gross and Hopkins in the 1990s, provides a canonical dualizing object in the K(n)‑local category. Let I_n denote the Brown–Comenetz dual of the K(n)‑local sphere LK(n) S0. Gross and Hopkins proved that I_n is equivalent to a suspension of the Spanier–Whitehead dual of the Morava E‑theory E_n: I_n ≃ Σn2-n E_n^∨. Moreover, the Brown–Comenetz dual of the Morava K‑theory K(n) itself is a suspension of K(n): IK(n) ≃ Σ2(p^n-1)n K(n). This self‑duality of K(n) reflects the fact that the Morava stabilizer group G_n is a Poincaré duality group of dimension n2.

The duality has several powerful applications. First, it identifies the K(n)‑local dual of a finite spectrum X with a suspension of the K(n)‑localization of the Spanier–Whitehead dual of X: DK(n) X ≃ Σ-n2+n LK(n) DX. This formula allows one to transfer finiteness properties across the duality. Second, it implies that the category of K(n)‑local spectra is a rigidly‑compactly generated tensor triangulated category, with the compact objects precisely the K(n)‑localizations of finite spectra. Third, Gross–Hopkins duality is the key input for the construction of the Gross–Hopkins spectral sequence, which computes the homotopy groups of the K(n)‑local sphere from the continuous cohomology of G_n with coefficients in the Morava module.

In the context of the chromatic spectral sequence, Gross–Hopkins duality provides a symmetry between the E1‑page and the E_∞‑page: the monochromatic layer M_n is self‑dual up to a shift. This symmetry is used to deduce vanishing lines and to relate the homotopy groups of spheres in complementary stems. The duality also plays a role in the proof of the chromatic convergence theorem, where the identification of the fiber of L_n → Ln-1 with M_n relies on the fact that M_n is K(n)‑local and K(n-1)‑acyclic, properties that are preserved under the duality.

  • Confusing the thick subcategory theorem (classification of thick subcategories of finite spectra) with the classification of localizing subcategories in the K(n)‑local category; the latter is a different theorem (Hovey–Strickland).
  • Assuming the chromatic convergence theorem holds for all spectra; it is false for infinite spectra such as the sphere spectrum completed at p.
  • Thinking the Goerss–Hopkins–Miller theorem gives a unique E_∞‑structure on E_n; it gives a canonical one, but other E_∞‑structures may exist.
  • Believing the Smith–Toda complexes V(n) are unique up to equivalence; they are unique up to a non‑canonical equivalence, and different choices affect the explicit v_n self‑maps.
  • Misapplying Gross–Hopkins duality by forgetting the suspension shift Σn2-n; the shift is essential for the duality to hold on the level of homotopy groups.
  • Overlooking that the telescope conjecture is false in general; many exam questions test the distinction between L_n^f and the telescope localization.
  • Neglecting the role of the Morava stabilizer group G_n as a Poincaré duality group; its cohomological dimension n2 underlies the shift in Gross–Hopkins duality.

These advanced topics form the backbone of modern chromatic homotopy theory and are essential for any serious examination of the stable homotopy category.

hand/scattering-theory.html:
Multichannel Scattering and Coupled-Channel Equations

In many physical systems the asymptotic Hilbert space splits into several orthogonal channels, each labelled by a set of quantum numbers such as total angular momentum, spin, or internal excitation. The free Hamiltonian H₀ then acts as a direct sum H₀ = ⊕ₙ H₀⁽ⁿ⁾ on the channel subspaces ℋₙ. The interacting Hamiltonian H = H₀ + V contains off‑diagonal couplings Vₘₙ that transfer probability between channels. The multichannel Møller operators are defined by the strong limits Ω_± = s‑limt→±∞ eiHt e-iH₀t Pac(H₀), where Pac(H₀) projects onto the absolutely continuous subspace of H₀. Existence and completeness of these operators require that the interchannel couplings satisfy suitable short‑range conditions, typically ∫₁^∞ ‖Vₘₙ(r)‖ dr < ∞ for all channel pairs.

The stationary formulation leads to a system of coupled Lippmann–Schwinger equations for the channel components ψ⁺ₙ(k) of an outgoing scattering state:

ψ⁺ₙ(k) = φₙ(k) + Σₘ ∫ G₀ₙ⁺(E) Vₙₘ ψ⁺ₘ(k) dE,

where φₙ(k) is the incoming plane wave in channel n and G₀ₙ⁺(E) = (E - H₀ₙ + i0)-1 is the free resolvent in that channel. The multichannel S‑matrix S(E) is a unitary matrix on the direct sum of channel spaces; its elements Sₘₙ(E) give the transition amplitudes from incoming channel n to outgoing channel m. Unitarity S†S = I encodes flux conservation across all open channels. When a channel is closed at a given energy (its threshold lies above E), the corresponding column of S(E) vanishes, but analytic continuation in the complex energy plane reveals virtual transitions that manifest as resonance poles.

Coupled‑channel equations are the workhorse of nuclear, atomic, and molecular scattering. In the close‑coupling approximation one truncates the infinite channel set to a finite basis, solves the resulting finite system of radial equations, and checks convergence by enlarging the basis. The R‑matrix method provides a numerically stable way to match interior solutions (where the potential is strong) to exterior asymptotic forms, yielding the S‑matrix at each energy. The eigenphase sum Σⱼ δⱼ(E), obtained from the diagonalisation of S(E), obeys a multichannel Levinson theorem: the total phase shift at zero energy equals π times the total number of bound states across all channels, provided no half‑bound states occur at thresholds.

Long-Range Potentials and the Dollard Modification

Standard time‑dependent scattering theory assumes that the interaction potential V(x) decays faster than |x|-1 (short‑range condition). For Coulomb‑type potentials V(x) ∼ γ/|x| the free evolution e-iH₀t no longer provides a correct asymptotic reference because the phase accumulated along a classical trajectory diverges logarithmically with time. Dollard (1964) introduced a modified free dynamics U_D(t) = e-iH₀t e-iγ log|t| (in one dimension; in three dimensions the phase factor becomes e-iγ log(t) with an angular‑dependent coefficient). The Dollard wave operators are then defined as Ω_±^D = s‑limt→±∞ eiHt U_D(t) Pac(H₀). Existence of these modified operators restores asymptotic completeness for a large class of long‑range potentials, including the pure Coulomb potential and potentials with a Coulomb tail plus a short‑range remainder.

In the stationary picture the Dollard modification corresponds to replacing the free Green’s function G₀⁺(x,y;k) by the Coulomb Green’s function G_C⁺(x,y;k), which incorporates the exact Coulomb phase shifts. The Lippmann–Schwinger equation becomes ψ⁺_C(k,x) = φ_C(k,x) - ∫ G_C⁺(x,y;k) Vsr(y) ψ⁺_C(k,y) dy, where Vsr is the short‑range part of the potential. The scattering amplitude then splits into a known Coulomb amplitude f_C(θ) (the Rutherford formula) plus a correction fsr(θ) that is analytic in the momentum transfer. This separation is essential for extracting nuclear phase shifts from proton‑proton scattering data, where the Coulomb interaction dominates at small angles.

For potentials decaying as |x|-α with 0 < α ≤ 1 the Dollard phase must be generalised to e-i c t1-α (or logarithmic for α = 1). The Enss method provides a geometric proof of asymptotic completeness for such potentials by constructing propagation observables that separate particles into clusters moving apart with distinct velocities. The key estimate is a minimal escape velocity bound: if a state has energy E, its position operator satisfies ‖x ψ(t)‖ ≥ vmin |t| for large |t|, where vmin depends on the long‑range tail. This geometric approach avoids explicit phase modifications and underlies modern proofs of asymptotic completeness for N‑body systems with Coulomb interactions.

Worked Example: Dollard Phase for a 1/r Potential
Consider the one‑dimensional Hamiltonian H = -½ d²/dx² + γ/|x| with γ > 0. Show that the standard Møller operator Ω_+ = s‑limt→∞ eiHt e-iH₀t does not exist, but the Dollard‑modified operator Ω_+^D = s‑limt→∞ eiHt e-iH₀t e-iγ log t does exist on the absolutely continuous subspace.
The free propagator in momentum representation is (e-iH₀t φ)(p) = e-i p² t/2 φ(p). For a wave packet concentrated near momentum p₀ > 0, the classical trajectory is x(t) ≈ p₀ t. The phase accumulated from the potential along this trajectory is ∫₀^t γ/(p₀ s) ds = (γ/p₀) log t. In the interacting evolution the state acquires an extra factor e-i (γ/p₀) log t. Since p₀ varies across the packet, the phase is not a simple multiple of the identity, and the strong limit of eiHt e-iH₀t fails to converge. Multiplying the free evolution by e-iγ log t (which corresponds to the average phase for p₀ = 1 in suitable units) removes the leading logarithmic divergence. A rigorous proof uses the Cook method: one shows that ‖(V - γ/|x|) e-iH₀t e-iγ log t ψ‖ is integrable in t for ψ ∈ ℋac(H₀), which implies existence of the modified wave operator by the Cook–Kuroda theorem.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions a Coulomb or 1/r tail, immediately recall the Dollard modification. Write the modified free propagator U_D(t) = e-iH₀t e-iγ log t and state that standard wave operators fail because the phase diverges logarithmically. For multichannel problems, note that each open channel may require its own Dollard phase if the long‑range part is channel‑dependent. This distinction often separates a passing answer from a top‑mark answer.

Trace Class Conditions and the Existence of Wave Operators

The abstract existence theory for Møller operators relies on operator‑ideal criteria for the perturbation V. Kato’s smooth perturbation theory shows that if V is H₀-smooth on an interval I, i.e. ∫_ℝ ‖V e-iH₀t ψ‖² dt ≤ C ‖ψ‖² for all ψ, then the wave operators exist and are complete on the spectral subspace EH₀(I)ℋ. A sufficient condition for H₀-smoothness is that V factorises as V = G* J G with G bounded from the domain of H₀ to a Hilbert space 𝒦 and J a bounded self‑adjoint operator on 𝒦. In the concrete setting H₀ = -Δ on L²(ℝ³), the Rollnik condition ∫∫ |V(x) V(y)| / |x-y|² dx dy < ∞ guarantees that V is H₀-smooth on (0,∞).

A more refined criterion uses trace‑class and Hilbert‑Schmidt ideals. If V is relatively trace class with respect to H₀, i.e. V (H₀ + i)-1 ∈ 𝔖₁ (the trace class), then the wave operators exist and the scattering operator S = Ω_+* Ω_- differs from the identity by a trace‑class operator. The Birman–Krein formula det S(λ) = e-2π i ξ(λ) then holds with a well‑defined spectral shift function ξ(λ). If V (H₀ + i)-1 ∈ 𝔖₂ (Hilbert‑Schmidt) but not trace class, the wave operators still exist, but S - I is only Hilbert‑Schmidt; the determinant must be interpreted as a regularised (Fredholm) determinant. The Kato–Rosenblum theorem states that if V is trace class, the absolutely continuous parts of H and H₀ are unitarily equivalent, so singular continuous spectrum cannot be created by a trace‑class perturbation.

For potentials decaying as |x|-α with α > 3 in three dimensions, V (H₀ + i)-1 is trace class. For 2 < α ≤ 3 it is Hilbert‑Schmidt but not trace class. The borderline α = 2 corresponds to the critical Rollnik class. These thresholds are sharp: there exist potentials with α = 2 for which the wave operators fail to exist on a set of energies of positive measure. In the N‑body setting, the HVZ theorem describes the essential spectrum, and the Mourre estimate provides a positive commutator method to prove absence of singular continuous spectrum and asymptotic completeness for a wide class of long‑range pair potentials.

Analytic Continuation of the S‑Matrix and Regge Poles

The scattering matrix S(k) for a short‑range, spherically symmetric potential is a meromorphic function of the complex momentum k in the cut plane ℂ i[0,∞). Its poles in the upper half‑plane correspond to bound states (purely imaginary k = iκ, κ > 0), while poles in the lower half‑plane correspond to resonances. For non‑central or multichannel problems, S becomes a matrix‑valued function of the energy E = k². Analytic continuation in the complex angular momentum ℓ plane, introduced by Regge (1959), reveals Regge poles ℓ_n(E) — complex values of ℓ at which the partial‑wave S‑matrix element S_ℓ(E) has a pole. The Regge trajectory ℓ(E) describes how the pole moves with energy; its real part gives the effective angular momentum of a resonance, while its imaginary part is related to the resonance width.

The Sommerfeld–Watson transform rewrites the partial‑wave expansion of the scattering amplitude as a contour integral in the complex ℓ plane: f(θ) = (1/2ik) Σℓ=0^∞ (2ℓ+1) (S_ℓ - 1) P_ℓ(cos θ) = (1/2ik) ∫_C (ℓ+½) (S_ℓ - 1) P_ℓ(cos θ) dℓ / sin πℓ. Deforming the contour picks up contributions from Regge poles, yielding a representation of the amplitude as a sum over Regge poles plus a background integral. At high energies, the leading Regge pole (the Pomeron in hadronic physics) dominates the forward scattering amplitude, giving a power‑law behaviour f(θ) ∼ sα(0) where α(0) is the intercept of the leading trajectory. This Regge theory underpins the analytic structure of scattering amplitudes in quantum field theory and string theory.

In potential scattering, the Jost function F_ℓ(k) is an entire function of ℓ for fixed k, and its zeros give the Regge poles. The Mandelstam representation expresses the scattering amplitude as a double spectral integral over the Mandelstam variables s and t, assuming analyticity and crossing symmetry. The Froissart bound σtot(s) ≤ C log² s follows from the assumption that the amplitude is analytic in a Lehmann ellipse in the cos θ plane. These analytic properties are not merely mathematical curiosities; they constrain dispersion relations that connect the real and imaginary parts of the forward amplitude, enabling precise predictions for low‑energy parameters from high‑energy data.

  • Assuming standard Møller operators exist for Coulomb‑type potentials — they do not; the Dollard modification is mandatory.
  • Confusing the Rollnik condition with the Kato smoothness condition — Rollnik is a sufficient condition for smoothness, not equivalent.
  • Treating the multichannel S‑matrix as a scalar — it is a unitary matrix; unitarity must be checked channel by channel.
  • Neglecting threshold effects in Levinson’s theorem — half‑bound states at zero energy contribute an extra π/2 to the phase shift.
  • Using the Breit‑Wigner formula far from the resonance peak — it is a local approximation valid only when |E - E_r| ≪ Γ.
  • Assuming all Regge poles lie on linear trajectories — only in specific models (e.g., string theory) are trajectories exactly linear; in potential scattering they are curved.
  • Forgetting that the spectral shift function is defined only up to an additive integer — the Birman–Krein formula fixes it modulo integers.

These advanced topics complete the rigorous toolkit needed for research‑level scattering problems and for the most demanding examination questions.

hand/d-modules.html:
Microlocal Analysis and the Characteristic Cycle of Holonomic D-modules

Microlocal analysis refines the study of singularities of solutions to differential equations by working in the cotangent bundle T*X. For a coherent D_X-module M, the characteristic variety Ch(M) is a conical Lagrangian subvariety of T*X. The characteristic cycle CC(M) is a Lagrangian cycle — a finite linear combination of irreducible components of Ch(M) with integer multiplicities — that encodes finer invariants than the variety alone. Kashiwara's index theorem identifies the Euler characteristic of the solution complex of M with the intersection number of CC(M) with the zero section. The multiplicities in CC(M) are given by the lengths of the graded pieces of a good filtration on M, and they satisfy the additivity property CC(M) = CC(M') + CC(M'') for any short exact sequence 0 → M' → M → M'' → 0. This makes CC a homomorphism from the Grothendieck group of holonomic D-modules to the group of Lagrangian cycles. The characteristic cycle is preserved under the de Rham functor: CC(M) equals the singular support cycle SS(DR(M)) of the associated perverse sheaf, providing a bridge between microlocal geometry and constructible sheaf theory. In practice, computing CC(M) for a given D-module often reduces to analyzing the associated graded module with respect to a good filtration and applying the Kashiwara–Schapira microlocal Morse lemma. The theory also underpins the proof of the Kashiwara constructibility theorem and the functoriality of the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence with respect to proper and smooth morphisms.

Irregular Holonomic D-modules and Stokes Phenomena

Regular holonomic D-modules are those whose solutions have moderate growth at infinity; they correspond under the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence to perverse sheaves. Irregular holonomic D-modules allow exponential growth and are classified by Stokes data — a collection of local systems on sectors around singular points together with Stokes matrices describing the transition between sectors. The irregular Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, developed by Deligne, Malgrange, and later by Sabbah and Mochizuki, establishes an equivalence between irregular holonomic D-modules on a complex curve and Stokes-filtered local systems. On higher-dimensional varieties, the theory uses the notion of good formal structure after a sequence of blow-ups (Hironaka resolution) and the construction of the Stokes sheaf on the real blow-up of the divisor of singularities. The Stokes filtration refines the usual filtration by growth order and captures the asymptotic behavior of solutions. The Stokes matrices are constant on each stratum of a stratification adapted to the irregularity, and they satisfy the cocycle condition. The irregularity complex Irr(M) measures the failure of regularity and is a constructible complex whose cohomology sheaves are the Stokes sheaves. This framework has been essential for the geometric Langlands program with wild ramification and for the study of quantum differential equations arising from mirror symmetry.

Worked Example: Characteristic Cycle of a Rank‑One Connection
Let X = ℂ with coordinate x, and let M = D_X / D_X·(x∂_x − λ) for λ ∈ ℂ. Compute the characteristic variety Ch(M) and the characteristic cycle CC(M).
The operator x∂_x − λ has symbol xξ in the associated graded ring gr D_X ≅ ℂ[x, ξ]. The characteristic variety is defined by xξ = 0 in T*X ≅ ℂ², which is the union of the zero section {ξ = 0} and the fiber {x = 0}. Both components have dimension 1, so M is holonomic. The module M is a rank‑one connection with regular singularity at x = 0. The multiplicity of the zero section in CC(M) equals the generic rank, which is 1. The multiplicity of the fiber {x = 0} equals the residue of the connection, which is λ. Hence CC(M) = 1·[T*_X X] + λ·[T*0 X]. If λ ∉ ℤ, the module is irreducible and the cycle is as stated; if λ ∈ ℤ, the module has a nontrivial Jordan–Hölder series and the multiplicities adjust accordingly, but the cycle remains the same in the Grothendieck group.
Exam Strategy
When asked to compute a characteristic cycle, first find a good filtration (e.g., the order filtration) and the associated graded module. The support of the graded module gives Ch(M). Then determine multiplicities by comparing the length of the graded pieces at generic points of each component. Remember that additivity in the Grothendieck group allows you to break a module into simpler pieces whose cycles are known.

The Six Functors Formalism for D-modules and the Kashiwara Equivalence

The six operations (f⁻¹, f_*, f_!, f^!, ⊗, ℋom) for constructible sheaves have analogues for D-modules, developed by Kashiwara and Schapira. For a morphism f: X → Y of smooth varieties, the direct image f_+ and inverse image f+ are defined using the transfer bimodules DX→Y and DY←X. The functor f_+ is right exact and preserves holonomicity; its derived functor Rf_+ maps the bounded derived category of holonomic D-modules to itself. The exceptional inverse image f^! is defined as f+ ⊗ ωX/Y[dim X − dim Y] where ωX/Y is the relative canonical bundle. The Kashiwara equivalence states that for a closed immersion i: Z X, the functor i_+ gives an equivalence between the category of D_Z-modules and the category of D_X-modules supported on Z. This equivalence respects the six functors: for instance, i_+ commutes with ⊗ and ℋom, and the adjunctions (i+, i_+) and (i_+, i^!) correspond to the usual adjunctions for sheaves. The compatibility of the six functors with the de Rham functor DR is a cornerstone of the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence: DR(Rf_+ M) ≅ Rf_* DR(M) for proper f, and DR(f+ N) ≅ f-1 DR(N) for smooth f. These compatibilities allow one to transfer topological constructions (e.g., nearby cycles, vanishing cycles) to the differential setting, leading to the theory of mixed Hodge modules and the proof of the decomposition theorem for algebraic maps.

Bernstein–Sato Polynomials, b-Functions, and the Theory of Nearby Cycles

For a regular function f on a smooth variety X, the Bernstein–Sato polynomial b_f(s) ∈ ℂ[s] is the monic polynomial of minimal degree satisfying a functional equation P(s)·fs+1 = b_f(s)·f^s in the D_X-module generated by f^s, where s is a formal parameter. The roots of b_f(s) are negative rational numbers, and the largest root is −1. The b-function controls the poles of the meromorphic family f^s and the structure of the nearby cycles ψ_f and vanishing cycles φ_f functors on D-modules. Kashiwara and Malgrange proved that the roots of b_f(s) are eigenvalues of the monodromy on the nearby cycles. The V-filtration of Kashiwara and Malgrange along the divisor {f = 0} provides a filtration on the D_X-module M indexed by rational numbers, whose graded pieces compute the nearby and vanishing cycles. The theory extends to the case of a morphism f: X → Y, giving the relative b-function and the microlocal V-filtration. These tools are essential for the proof of the rationality of the roots of b_f(s), for the construction of the mixed Hodge structure on the cohomology of the Milnor fiber, and for the study of the monodromy weight filtration in the context of the decomposition theorem.

Geometric Langlands Correspondence and D-modules on the Moduli Stack of Bundles

The geometric Langlands program seeks a categorical equivalence between D-modules on the moduli stack Bun_G of G-bundles on a smooth projective curve X and quasi-coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSys^L G of local systems for the Langlands dual group ^L G. The Hecke eigensheaf property translates into the condition that a D-module on Bun_G is an eigenobject for the Hecke functors, which are integral transforms given by correspondences involving modifications of bundles. The Beilinson–Drinfeld construction of the affine Grassmannian and the Satake equivalence provides the geometric Satake correspondence, identifying the category of representations of ^L G with the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian. This yields a commutative algebra structure on the spherical Hecke category, which acts on D-modules on Bun_G. The spectral side is built from the Hitchin fibration on the moduli of Higgs bundles, and the non-abelian Hodge theorem relates Higgs bundles to local systems. The recent proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture for GL_n by Gaitsgory and Lurie uses the theory of ind-coherent sheaves and the six functors for D-modules on stacks, together with a deep analysis of the Whittaker category. The correspondence also predicts a compatibility with the classical Langlands correspondence via the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence for irregular connections, linking wild ramification to the geometry of the affine Grassmannian at higher level.

  • Confusing the characteristic variety with the characteristic cycle — the former is a set, the latter a cycle with multiplicities.
  • Assuming all holonomic D-modules are regular; irregular ones require Stokes data and a different Riemann–Hilbert correspondence.
  • Neglecting the shift by the relative canonical bundle in the definition of f^! for D-modules.
  • Misapplying the Kashiwara equivalence to non-closed immersions; it holds only for closed embeddings.
  • Overlooking that the Bernstein–Sato polynomial depends on the choice of the function f, not just on the divisor.
  • Treating the geometric Langlands correspondence as a bijection of sets rather than an equivalence of derived categories.
  • Forgetting that the de Rham functor intertwines the six functors only up to canonical isomorphism, not strict equality.

These advanced topics form the backbone of modern research in D-module theory and its applications to representation theory and algebraic geometry.

hand/quantum-information.html:
Quantum State Tomography and Process Tomography

Quantum state tomography reconstructs the density matrix ρ of an unknown quantum state by performing measurements in a tomographically complete set of bases. For a single qubit, measuring the three Pauli observables σₓ, σ_y, σ_z yields the Bloch vector components ⟨σᵢ⟩ = Tr(ρ σᵢ), from which ρ = (I + Σᵢ ⟨σᵢ⟩ σᵢ)/2. For n qubits the number of required measurement settings grows as 3ⁿ, because each qubit must be measured in three independent bases. Linear inversion gives a raw estimate but can produce non‑physical matrices with negative eigenvalues; maximum‑likelihood estimation (MLE) enforces positivity and trace‑one constraints by maximizing the likelihood of the observed counts under a parameterized ρ. Process tomography extends this idea to quantum channels ℰ: one prepares a set of linearly independent input states {ρⱼ}, applies the unknown process, and performs state tomography on each output ℰ(ρⱼ). The Choi–Jamiołkowski isomorphism maps ℰ to a bipartite state (I ⊗ ℰ)(|Φ⁺⟩⟨Φ⁺|), allowing process reconstruction via state tomography on the Choi state. In practice, compressed sensing and adaptive tomography reduce the measurement burden for low‑rank states, while randomized benchmarking provides a scalable estimate of average gate fidelity without full tomography.

Key Formulas

  • Single‑qubit Bloch reconstruction: ρ = ½ (I + x σₓ + y σ_y + z σ_z) with x = ⟨σₓ⟩, y = ⟨σ_y⟩, z = ⟨σ_z⟩.
  • Choi state: χ = (I ⊗ ℰ)(|Φ⁺⟩⟨Φ⁺|), where |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
  • Average gate fidelity: F_avg = (d F_e + 1)/(d + 1) with d = 2ⁿ and F_e = ⟨Φ⁺| χ |Φ⁺⟩.

Entanglement Measures and Monogamy Relations

Quantifying entanglement requires measures that are monotonic under local operations and classical communication (LOCC). The von Neumann entropy of the reduced density matrix, E(ψ) = S(Tr_B|ψ⟩⟨ψ|), is the unique measure for pure bipartite states. For mixed states, the entanglement of formation E_f(ρ) = min Σ pᵢ S(Tr_B|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ|) (minimized over all pure‑state decompositions) and the distillable entanglement E_d(ρ) (maximal rate of Bell pairs extractable by LOCC) are central but generally hard to compute. The concurrence C(ρ) = max{0, λ₁−λ₂−λ₃−λ₄} (with λᵢ the square roots of eigenvalues of ρ(σ_y⊗σ_y)ρ*(σ_y⊗σ_y) in decreasing order) gives a closed form for two‑qubit entanglement of formation via E_f = h((1+√(1−C²))/2), where h is the binary entropy. Monogamy of entanglement is captured by the Coffman‑Kundu‑Wootters (CKW) inequality for three qubits: C²A|BC ≥ C²A|B + C²A|C. This implies a qubit cannot be maximally entangled with two partners simultaneously. For n‑qubit systems, the generalized monogamy relation uses the tangle τ = C² and holds for all qubit states. Squashed entanglement E_sq(ρ) = ½ inf I(A;B|E) (conditional mutual information minimized over extensions) is additive and monogamous for arbitrary dimensions, making it a powerful tool in quantum cryptography.

Worked Example: Concurrence of a Two‑Qubit Mixed State
Compute the concurrence of ρ = p |Φ⁺⟩⟨Φ⁺| + (1−p) |00⟩⟨00| with 0 ≤ p ≤ 1.
The state is diagonal in the Bell basis only for the |Φ⁺⟩ component. Write ρ in the computational basis: ρ = p/2 (|00⟩⟨00| + |00⟩⟨11| + |11⟩⟨00| + |11⟩⟨11|) + (1−p) |00⟩⟨00|. The matrix representation in the ordered basis {|00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩} is [[ (1+p)/2 , 0 , 0 , p/2 ], [ 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ], [ 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ], [ p/2 , 0 , 0 , p/2 ]]. Compute R = ρ (σ_y⊗σ_y) ρ* (σ_y⊗σ_y). Since σ_y⊗σ_y maps |00⟩ → -|11⟩, |11⟩ → -|00⟩, the only non‑zero block is the 2×2 subspace spanned by |00⟩,|11⟩. The eigenvalues of R are {p², 0, 0, 0}. Thus λ₁ = p, λ₂=λ₃=λ₄=0, giving C = max{0, p−0−0−0} = p. The concurrence equals the weight p of the Bell component.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for an entanglement measure of a two‑qubit state, first check if the state is rank‑two or diagonal in the Bell basis; concurrence often yields a simple analytic answer. For higher‑rank states, recall that the CKW inequality provides a quick bound without full optimization.

Fault‑Tolerant Quantum Computation with Magic State Distillation

Clifford gates (Hadamard, Phase, CNOT) can be implemented transversally in many stabilizer codes, but they are not universal for quantum computation. The π/8 gate T = diag(1, eiπ/4) completes a universal set. Fault‑tolerant T gates are realized by preparing noisy magic states |A⟩ = (|0⟩ + eiπ/4|1⟩)/√2 and distilling high‑fidelity copies using only Clifford operations. The Bravyi‑Kitaev 15‑to‑1 protocol takes 15 noisy |A⟩ states, encodes them into a [[15,1,3]] Reed‑Muller code, measures the stabilizers, and post‑selects on the +1 syndrome to output a single |A⟩ with error probability reduced from ε to O(ε³). The protocol succeeds with probability ≈ 1−15ε for small ε. More efficient schemes such as the 10‑to‑1 and 8‑to‑3 protocols reduce overhead. Magic state distillation is the dominant resource cost in surface‑code architectures; the space‑time volume scales as O(log(1/ε_target)) for a target logical error ε_target. Recent advances include flag‑based distillation that detects correlated errors during syndrome extraction, and the use of low‑density parity‑check (LDPC) codes to achieve constant overhead distillation.

Distillation Thresholds

  • 15‑to‑1 protocol: input error ε < 0.141 (≈ 14.1%) for asymptotic convergence.
  • 10‑to‑1 protocol: threshold ε < 0.097.
  • Flag‑based 8‑to‑3: threshold ε < 0.03 with reduced qubit count.

Quantum Communication Complexity and Nonlocal Games

Communication complexity studies the minimum amount of classical or quantum communication required for distributed parties to compute a function f(x,y). Quantum protocols can exponentially reduce communication for certain problems. The Razborov‑Raz‑Tal result shows a quantum protocol with O(log n) qubits solves the Hidden Matching problem, while any classical protocol needs Ω(√n) bits. Nonlocal games formalize Bell inequalities as cooperative tasks: a referee sends inputs x,y to Alice and Bob, who return outputs a,b; they win if V(a,b|x,y)=1. The CHSH game has quantum value ω_q = cos²(π/8) ≈ 0.854 and classical value ω_c = 0.75. The Magic Square game and the Mermin‑Peres game achieve perfect quantum winning probability (ω_q = 1) while any classical strategy wins with probability ≤ 8/9. These games demonstrate quantum pseudo‑telepathy: entanglement enables coordination impossible classically without communication. The parallel repetition theorem for nonlocal games states that the optimal winning probability for n independent repetitions decays exponentially with n for classical strategies, but the quantum value may remain constant for certain games, highlighting fundamental differences between classical and quantum correlations.

Key Results

  • Hidden Matching: quantum O(log n) vs classical Ω(√n).
  • CHSH: ω_q = cos²(π/8), ω_c = 3/4.
  • Magic Square: ω_q = 1, ω_c = 8/9.
  • Parallel repetition: classical value decays exponentially; quantum value can stay constant.

Topological Quantum Codes Beyond the Surface Code

The surface code is a two‑dimensional topological stabilizer code with planar geometry and weight‑four plaquette and star operators. Its high threshold (≈ 1%) and local syndrome extraction make it the leading candidate for near‑term fault tolerance. However, its encoding rate k/n → 0 as the lattice grows, and logical operators have weight O(√n). Generalizations include color codes on trivalent lattices, which admit transversal implementation of the full Clifford group and a transversal T gate in three dimensions. The 3D gauge color code supports a transversal T gate, enabling universal fault‑tolerant computation without magic state distillation. Subsystem codes such as Bacon‑Shor codes reduce syndrome measurement weight to two‑body interactions at the cost of gauge fixing. Quantum low‑density parity‑check (qLDPC) codes achieve constant rate k/n = Θ(1) and linear distance d = Θ(n) while maintaining constant‑weight stabilizers; recent constructions (e.g., the lifted product codes) approach the Gilbert‑Varshamov bound. Fracton models like the X‑cube code exhibit subdimensional excitations and may provide new routes to self‑correcting quantum memories in three dimensions. Each family trades off threshold, overhead, gate set, and hardware connectivity, guiding architectural choices for large‑scale quantum processors.

Comparative Table

Topological Code Families

Surface code2D4→ 0Clifford
Color code (2D)2D4–6→ 0Clifford
3D gauge color code3D4–6→ 0Clifford + T
qLDPC (lifted product)2D/3DO(1)Θ(1)Clifford (typically)
X‑cube fracton3D4→ 0Limited
  • Common Trap: Assuming the surface code threshold applies unchanged to all topological codes; thresholds vary with decoder and noise model.
  • Common Trap: Confusing entanglement of formation with distillable entanglement; they coincide only for pure states and certain symmetric mixed states.
  • Common Trap: Treating magic state distillation as a single‑step process; multiple rounds are required to reach target logical error rates.
  • Common Trap: Overlooking that nonlocal game values are defined under the no‑signalling principle; quantum strategies respect no‑signalling but can exceed classical bounds.
  • Common Trap: Believing qLDPC codes automatically have high thresholds; many constructions have low thresholds despite good asymptotic parameters.
  • Common Trap: Ignoring the monogamy constraint when designing multipartite entanglement distribution protocols; it limits simultaneous high‑fidelity links.
  • Common Trap: Assuming linear inversion tomography always yields a physical state; maximum‑likelihood or Bayesian methods are needed for positivity.
