hand/anabelian-geometry.html:
The Grothendieck–Teichmüller Group and the Outer Galois Action on the Projective Line Minus Three Points

The absolute Galois group G_ℚ acts on the étale fundamental group of the projective line minus three points, π₁(ℙ¹ℚ̄ {0,1,∞}), through outer automorphisms. This action factors through the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group GT, a profinite group defined by Drinfeld (1990) via explicit equations in the profinite completion of the pure braid group on three strands. The group GT sits in an exact sequence 1 → GT → Out(π₁(ℙ¹ℚ̄ {0,1,∞})) → ℤ̂^× → 1, where the map to ℤ̂^× is the cyclotomic character. The inclusion G_ℚ GT is conjectured to be an isomorphism — this is the Grothendieck–Teichmüller conjecture, a profound strengthening of the anabelian philosophy for the thrice-punctured sphere. The defining equations for GT involve two elements λ ∈ ℤ̂^× and f ∈ F̂₂' (the derived subgroup of the free profinite group on two generators) satisfying the pentagon and hexagon relations: f(x,y)f(y,x)=1, f(x,y)x^λf(y,z)y^λf(z,x)z^λ=1, and f(x,y)f(y,z)f(z,x)=1 where xyz=1. These relations encode the associativity and commutativity constraints of a braided tensor category. The cyclotomic character χ: G_ℚ → ℤ̂^× gives the λ-component; the f-component corresponds to the “associator” Φ_KZ of Drinfeld, constructed via the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equation. Ihara (1990) showed that the image of G_ℚ in GT lies in the subgroup GT₁ where λ=1, and that the map G_ℚ → GT₁ is injective. The surjectivity remains open. The GT group also acts on the set of dessins d’enfants (Belyi maps), providing a combinatorial handle on the Galois action. The Lie algebra of GT, the Grothendieck–Teichmüller Lie algebra grt, was computed by Drinfeld and later by Willwacher (2015) in connection with the deformation quantization of Poisson manifolds. The connection to multiple zeta values arises because the coefficients of the KZ associator are multiple zeta values, and the action of GT on them encodes the algebraic relations among these periods. The anabelian reconstruction of ℙ¹ {0,1,∞} from its fundamental group with Galois action is equivalent to determining the image of G_ℚ in GT. This is the “profinite” side of the story; the “discrete” side involves the action of the mapping class group of the punctured sphere on the fundamental group, and the compatibility between the two is governed by the theory of mapping class groups of profinite completions.

Belyi’s Theorem, Dessins d’Enfants, and the Combinatorial Anabelian Program

Belyi’s theorem (1979) states that a smooth projective curve X over ℂ can be defined over a number field if and only if there exists a finite morphism β: X → ℙ¹ ramified only over {0,1,∞}. Such a morphism is called a Belyi map. The preimage β⁻¹([0,1]) ⊂ X(ℂ) is a bipartite graph embedded on the Riemann surface X(ℂ), with black vertices at β⁻¹(0), white vertices at β⁻¹(1), and edges the preimages of the interval [0,1]. This graph is a dessin d’enfant. The monodromy of the covering β gives a permutation representation of the fundamental group π₁(ℙ¹(ℂ) {0,1,∞}) ≅ F₂ (free group on two generators) on the fiber β⁻¹(t) for a basepoint t ∈ (0,1). The two generators correspond to loops around 0 and 1; their images are permutations σ₀, σ₁ whose product σ_∞ = (σ₀σ₁)⁻¹ corresponds to the loop around ∞. The triple (σ₀, σ₁, σ_∞) up to simultaneous conjugation determines the dessin and the Belyi map up to isomorphism. The absolute Galois group G_ℚ acts on the set of dessins by acting on the coefficients of the defining equations of X and β. This action is faithful (Belyi, 1979), giving a concrete combinatorial realization of the otherwise mysterious group G_ℚ. The anabelian philosophy predicts that the curve X over a number field K can be reconstructed from its étale fundamental group π₁(X) with the G_K-action. For hyperbolic curves, the Grothendieck conjecture (proved by Mochizuki, 1996) confirms this. Dessins provide a “discrete” approximation: the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group of the dessin (as a graph) is related to the étale fundamental group of the curve. The theory of pseudo-Galois covers (Pop, 1990s) extends this to the birational setting: a function field over a number field can be reconstructed from its absolute Galois group. The combinatorial anabelian program seeks to make the reconstruction effective. For example, the “dessins d’enfants” approach to the section conjecture: a rational point x ∈ X(K) gives a section G_K → π₁(X), which in turn gives a G_K-equivariant map from the profinite completion of the dessin’s fundamental group to π₁(X). The work of Schneps, Lochak, and others on the “Grothendieck–Teichmüller tower” builds a tower of moduli spaces of curves with level structures, whose fundamental groups approximate the absolute Galois group. The “profinite braid group” B̂ₙ and its action on the free profinite group F̂ₙ are central. The tower of moduli spaces Mg,n (moduli of curves of genus g with n marked points) has fundamental groups that are mapping class groups; their profinite completions map to Out(π₁(XK̄)). The anabelian conjecture for Mg,n (proved in parts by Mochizuki, Tamagawa, and others) says that these moduli spaces are also anabelian. The combinatorial data of ribbon graphs (fat graphs) provides a cell decomposition of Mg,n (Harer, 1986), linking the topology of moduli space to the combinatorics of graphs, and hence to dessins. The “Grothendieck–Teichmüller group” GT acts on the whole tower, and the image of G_ℚ in GT is the “arithmetic” part of the mapping class group action.

Worked Example: Galois Action on a Dessin
Consider the Belyi map β: ℙ¹ → ℙ¹ given by β(z) = zⁿ. The ramification is over {0,1,∞} with β⁻¹(0) = {0}, β⁻¹(∞) = {∞}, and β⁻¹(1) = {ζₙᵏ : k=0,…,n-1} where ζₙ = e2πi/n. The dessin is a star with n edges from 0 to the n-th roots of unity. The monodromy permutations are σ₀ = (1 2 … n) (an n-cycle), σ₁ = identity, σ_∞ = (n … 2 1). Let σ ∈ G_ℚ act on the coefficients of β. Since β is defined over ℚ, the coefficients are rational, so σ acts trivially on the equation. However, σ acts on the dessin by sending the roots of unity ζₙ to ζₙχ(σ) where χ: G_ℚ → ℤ̂^× is the cyclotomic character. The resulting dessin is isomorphic to the original one (it is the same star graph), but the labeling of edges is permuted by the action of χ(σ) on ℤ/nℤ. The monodromy triple becomes (σ₀χ(σ), σ₁, σ_∞χ(σ)). This illustrates that the Galois action on dessins factors through the cyclotomic character on this simple example. For a general dessin defined over a number field K, the action of G_K is non-trivial and encodes the arithmetic of K.
The Belyi map β(z)=zⁿ has coefficients in ℚ, so the absolute Galois group G_ℚ acts trivially on the equation. The dessin is the star graph with n edges. The fiber over a basepoint t∈(0,1) consists of the n points t1/nζₙᵏ. The monodromy around 0 permutes these cyclically: σ₀ = (1 2 … n). The monodromy around 1 is trivial because β is unramified over 1 except at the n points mapping to 1, but the loop around 1 lifts to n disjoint loops, so σ₁ = id. The monodromy around ∞ is σ_∞ = (σ₀σ₁)⁻¹ = σ₀⁻¹ = (n … 2 1). For σ ∈ G_ℚ, the action on the dessin is induced by the action on the roots of unity: σ(ζₙ) = ζₙχ(σ) where χ(σ) ∈ (ℤ/nℤ)^×. This permutes the edges of the star by multiplication by χ(σ) on the indices k. The new monodromy triple is (σ₀χ(σ), id, σ_∞χ(σ)). Since σ₀χ(σ) is conjugate to σ₀ in Sₙ (both are n-cycles), the dessin is isomorphic to the original one. The Galois action is detected by the change in the labeling, which corresponds to the outer automorphism of the fundamental group induced by the cyclotomic character. This matches the general theory: the map G_ℚ → GT sends σ to (χ(σ), f_σ) where f_σ is trivial in this abelian example.
Exam Strategy: Anabelian Reconstruction Steps
When a question asks “how does one reconstruct a curve from its fundamental group?”, structure the answer in layers: (1) the étale fundamental group π₁(X) fits in the exact sequence with G_K; (2) the outer Galois action G_K → Out(π₁(XK̄)) is the key invariant; (3) for hyperbolic curves over number fields, Mochizuki’s theorem says this action determines X up to isomorphism; (4) the reconstruction uses p-adic Hodge theory (Hodge–Tate decomposition, indigenous bundles) to recover the curve’s p-adic uniformization; (5) the combinatorial shadow is the action on dessins / the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group. Mentioning the exact sequence, the outer action, and the role of p-adic Hodge theory covers the core mechanism.

Anabelian Geometry for Higher-Dimensional Varieties: Abelian Varieties and Hyperbolic Varieties

The anabelian philosophy was originally formulated for curves, but Grothendieck envisioned it for higher-dimensional varieties. The central question: for which varieties X over a number field K does the étale fundamental group π₁(X) with its G_K-action determine X up to isomorphism? For abelian varieties, the answer is negative in general: the étale fundamental group of an abelian variety A is the Tate module T_ℓ(A) (for ℓ≠char(K)), which is a free ℤ_ℓ-module of rank 2g with a G_K-action. The Tate conjecture (proved by Faltings, 1983) says that the G_K-module T_ℓ(A) determines A up to isogeny, not isomorphism. Two non-isogenous abelian varieties can have isomorphic Tate modules as G_K-modules if they are isogenous. The anabelian conjecture fails for abelian varieties because their fundamental groups are abelian (commutative), losing the non-abelian structure that encodes the geometry. For hyperbolic varieties (varieties whose universal cover is a bounded symmetric domain, e.g., Shimura varieties, moduli spaces of curves), the situation is more promising. Mochizuki (1999) proved the anabelian conjecture for certain hyperbolic curves over p-adic fields, and Tamagawa (1997) proved it for affine hyperbolic curves over number fields. For higher-dimensional hyperbolic varieties, the “Grothendieck conjecture” is known in some cases: Mochizuki (2000s) proved it for the moduli space Mg,n of curves of genus g with n marked points when 2g-2+n > 0 (the hyperbolic case), over number fields and p-adic fields. The proof uses the theory of “indigenous bundles” (a higher-dimensional generalization of the projective structures used for curves) and p-adic Teichmüller theory. The key idea is that the étale fundamental group of a hyperbolic variety carries a “Hodge-theoretic” structure (a filtration on the associated graded of the lower central series) that can be recovered from the group structure alone, and this Hodge structure determines the variety via the period map. For Shimura varieties, the anabelian conjecture is related to the André–Oort conjecture and the theory of special subvarieties. The fundamental group of a Shimura variety is an arithmetic group, and the Galois action on it is described by the Langlands program. The “anabelian” reconstruction of a Shimura variety from its fundamental group would imply that the variety is determined by its arithmetic fundamental group, which is a strong form of the “modularity” philosophy. For general varieties of general type, the anabelian conjecture is wide open. The “birational anabelian geometry” program (Pop, Bogomolov, Tschinkel) asks whether the function field of a variety over a number field can be reconstructed from its absolute Galois group. This is known for function fields of curves (the “birational section conjecture” of Koenigsmann and Pop) and for some higher-dimensional cases (e.g., varieties with ample cotangent bundle). The obstruction is the “abelianization” of the fundamental group: the maximal abelian quotient is the Galois group of the maximal abelian extension, which by class field theory is determined by the idele class group. The non-abelian part is what carries the geometric information.

The p-adic Section Conjecture and p-adic Uniformization

The section conjecture has a p-adic analogue: let K be a finite extension of ℚ_p, and let X be a smooth hyperbolic curve over K. The étale fundamental group sequence 1 → π₁(XK̄) → π₁(X) → G_K → 1 splits at a rational point x ∈ X(K). The p-adic section conjecture asserts that the map X(K) → {sections G_K → π₁(X) modulo π₁(XK̄)-conjugation} is a bijection. This is known in some cases: for the projective line minus three points ℙ¹ {0,1,∞} over ℚ_p, the conjecture is related to the theory of p-adic multiple zeta values and the p-adic KZ equation. The work of Hoshi (2010s) and Mochizuki (1990s) on the “p-adic Grothendieck conjecture” uses p-adic Hodge theory to reconstruct the curve from its fundamental group. The p-adic uniformization of a hyperbolic curve X over K is given by the Mumford curve construction: if X has split semistable reduction, its p-adic universal cover is the Drinfeld upper half-plane Ω = ℙ¹ℂ_p ℙ¹(K), and X(ℂ_p) ≅ Γ Ω for a Schottky group Γ ⊂ PGL₂(K). The étale fundamental group π₁(X) is an extension of G_K by the profinite completion of Γ. The p-adic section conjecture then translates to a statement about sections of the extension 1 → Γ̂ → π₁(X) → G_K → 1. The “exotic maps” on the boundary of the fundamental group (the “cuspidal” sections) are related to the action of G_K on the set of cusps (the boundary components of the Mumford curve). The theory of “p-adic Teichmüller spaces” (Mochizuki) provides a moduli space of p-adic curves with level structures, whose fundamental group maps to the outer automorphism group of π₁(XK̄). The p-adic section conjecture is also connected to the “p-adic Belyi maps” and the action of G_K on the p-adic dessin d’enfants. The “p-adic Grothendieck–Teichmüller group” GT_p acts on the p-adic fundamental group of ℙ¹ {0,1,∞}, and the image of G_K in GT_p is conjectured to be the whole group (the p-adic Grothendieck–Teichmüller conjecture). The work of Nakamura (1990s) on the “p-adic braid group” and the “p-adic KZ equation” gives a p-adic analogue of the Drinfeld associator. The p-adic section conjecture for ℙ¹ {0,1,∞} over ℚ_p is equivalent to the statement that every section of the p-adic KZ equation comes from a rational point (i.e., a tangential basepoint at 0, 1, or ∞). This is known for “tangential” sections but open for “exotic” sections. The “p-adic anabelian geometry” of Mochizuki also includes the theory of “Frobenius structures” on the fundamental group, which are used in IUT to construct the Θ-link.

Birational Anabelian Geometry and the Function Field Case

Birational anabelian geometry replaces the variety X with its function field K(X). The absolute Galois group GK(X) is the étale fundamental group of the generic point. The question: does GK(X) determine K(X) up to isomorphism? For curves over algebraically closed fields, this is false (the fundamental group of the generic point is trivial). Over number fields, the situation is richer. The “birational section conjecture” (Koenigsmann, Pop, 2000s) states that for a function field F of transcendence degree 1 over a number field K, the set of K-rational points of the corresponding curve is in bijection with the set of sections of the exact sequence 1 → GF̄ → G_F → G_K → 1, where F̄ is the algebraic closure of F in a separable closure. This was proved by Koenigsmann (2005) and Pop (2000s) using the theory of “pseudo-Galois covers” and “projective structures” on the absolute Galois group. The key idea is that a rational point gives a valuation on F, and the decomposition group of that valuation in G_F gives a section. Conversely, a section gives a decomposition group, which corresponds to a valuation, and the valuation theory of function fields (the “Riemann–Roch” theorem for valuations) recovers the point. For higher transcendence degree, the “birational anabelian conjecture” (Bogomolov, Tschinkel, Pop) asks whether the function field of a variety of general type over a number field can be reconstructed from its absolute Galois group. This is known for varieties with ample cotangent bundle (Pop, 2010s) and for some rationally connected varieties. The “Kuyk–Mochizuki” theorem says that the absolute Galois group of a number field determines the number field (Neukirch–Uchida). For function fields, the absolute Galois group determines the function field up to “isomorphism of Galois extensions” — but there are counterexamples (Uchida, 1970s) where non-isomorphic function fields have isomorphic absolute Galois groups. The “anabelian” condition for function fields is that the field is “anabelian” in the sense of Pop: it has no non-trivial abelian Galois extensions that are “geometric” (i.e., come from the base field). The “Grothendieck conjecture for function fields” (Mochizuki, 1990s) is the statement that the isomorphism class of a hyperbolic curve over a number field is determined by the isomorphism class of its fundamental group as a G_K-module. This is the “geometric” anabelian conjecture, distinct from the birational one. The birational version is often easier because one can use valuation theory and the theory of “pseudo-Galois covers” to reconstruct the field from its Galois group. The “section conjecture” for function fields (the birational section conjecture) is a theorem, while the geometric section conjecture for curves over number fields remains open. The connection is via the “specialization” map: a rational point on a curve over a number field gives a section of the fundamental group exact sequence, which specializes to a section of the function field exact sequence. The “Mordell–Weil” theorem for function fields (Lang–Néron) gives finiteness of rational points, which is used in the proof of the birational section conjecture.

  • Confusing the geometric anabelian conjecture (curves over number fields) with the birational anabelian conjecture (function fields) — they have different statements and different proof statuses.
  • Assuming the section conjecture is proved for all hyperbolic curves over number fields; it is open in general, known only for special cases (local fields, certain genus 2 curves, birational version).
  • Thinking the Neukirch–Uchida theorem applies to function fields; it applies only to number fields (and more generally to finitely generated extensions of ℚ).
  • Believing the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group GT is known to equal G_ℚ; the inclusion G_ℚ GT is injective but surjectivity is the open Grothendieck–Teichmüller conjecture.
  • Overlooking that abelian varieties are not anabelian — their fundamental groups are abelian (Tate modules), so the anabelian philosophy fails for them.
  • Confusing the p-adic section conjecture (for curves over p-adic fields) with the global section conjecture (over number fields); they are distinct statements with different techniques (p-adic Hodge theory vs. global Diophantine geometry).
  • Assuming IUT (Inter-Universal Teichmüller Theory) is an accepted proof of the abc conjecture; it remains controversial and not widely accepted by the community.

hand/integrable-systems.html:
Bäcklund and Darboux Transformations for KdV and NLS

The Bäcklund transformation provides an explicit algebraic map between solutions of a nonlinear integrable PDE and a new solution, often interpreted as a gauge transformation of the associated Lax pair. For the Korteweg–de Vries equation the classical Bäcklund transformation reads ũ = u + 2∂ₓ² log φ where φ satisfies the linear Schrödinger problem −φₓₓ + u φ = λ φ and the auxiliary condition φₜ = 4φₓₓₓ − 6u φₓ − 3uₓ φ. Applying the transformation repeatedly generates the hierarchy of multi‑soliton solutions. The Darboux transformation is the matrix‑valued counterpart: if Ψ is a fundamental solution of the Lax pair Ψₓ = U Ψ, Ψₜ = V Ψ then a new solution is obtained by Ψ[1] = D Ψ with D = I − (λ₁ − λ₁*) P, where P is the projector onto the eigenvector at the discrete eigenvalue λ₁. For the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS) the Darboux matrix takes the form D(λ) = λ I − S with S built from a seed solution and a chosen eigenfunction. Both transformations preserve the Lax representation, hence they map the whole hierarchy of commuting flows to itself. In practice, starting from the trivial vacuum u = 0 one obtains the one‑soliton, two‑soliton, and higher‑order rational solutions (rogue waves) by iterating the Darboux step. The method also yields explicit formulas for the phase shift experienced by solitons after interaction, a quantity that can be compared with the asymptotic analysis of the inverse scattering transform.

Finite‑Gap Integration and Theta Functions

Finite‑gap (or algebro‑geometric) integration solves the periodic initial value problem for KdV, NLS, sine‑Gordon and the KP hierarchy by reducing the spectral problem to a compact Riemann surface of genus g. The Lax operator L = −∂ₓ² + u(x) (for KdV) has a Bloch–Floquet spectrum consisting of g + 1 allowed bands separated by g gaps. The endpoints of the bands are the branch points of the hyperelliptic curve μ² = ∏j=12g+1 (λ − E_j). The Baker–Akhiezer function ψ(P, x, t) is the unique meromorphic function on this curve with an essential singularity at the point at infinity, prescribed divisor of poles (the Dirichlet eigenvalues), and normalization ψ → ei k x + i ω t as P → ∞. Its explicit expression is ψ = exp( i k x + i ω t ) θ( A(P) + U x + V t + Z ) / θ( A(P) + Z ), where θ is the Riemann theta function associated with the period matrix B, A is the Abel map, and U, V are vectors of b‑periods of normalized holomorphic differentials. The potential is recovered by u(x, t) = 2 ∂ₓ² log θ( U x + V t + Z ) + const. This construction yields all quasi‑periodic (finite‑gap) solutions; the genus g counts the number of independent phases. The method extends to the KP hierarchy where the spectral curve is no longer hyperelliptic but a general algebraic curve, and the tau function is again a theta function on its Jacobian. The finite‑gap theory also provides a bridge to the Whitham modulation equations, which describe slow variations of the branch points E_j and lead to the description of dispersive shock waves.

Worked Example: One‑Gap KdV Solution
Construct the genus‑one (cnoidal wave) solution of KdV using the finite‑gap ansatz. The spectral curve is μ² = (λ − E₁)(λ − E₂)(λ − E₃) with E₁ < E₂ < E₃. Show that the potential can be written as u(x, t) = 2 ∂ₓ² log θ( U x + V t + Z ) + c and identify the elliptic modulus k.
For genus one the Riemann surface is a torus with period matrix B = τ (Im τ > 0). The theta function reduces to the Jacobi theta function θ₃(z|τ). The vectors U, V are proportional to the a‑ and b‑periods of the differential dΩ₁ = λ1/2 dλ/μ. Evaluating the integrals gives U = 2π i / ω₁, V = 2π i ω₂/ω₁ where ω₁, ω₂ are the real and imaginary periods. The potential becomes u = 2 (∂ₓ² log θ₃( U x + V t + Z )) + c. Using the identity ∂ₓ² log θ₃ = −℘(z) + const, where ℘ is the Weierstrass elliptic function, and the relation between ℘ and the Jacobi cn function, one obtains the standard cnoidal wave u(x, t) = α + β cn²( κ (x − v t), k ). The elliptic modulus is k² = (E₃ − E₂)/(E₃ − E₁). The constants α, β, κ, v are expressed algebraically in terms of E₁, E₂, E₃.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the explicit form of a finite‑gap solution, first write down the spectral curve and the associated theta function. Remember that the genus equals the number of gaps; for KdV the curve is hyperelliptic. The vectors U and V are always b‑periods of the normalized differentials of the second kind. If the problem only requests the cnoidal wave, you can quote the final cn² formula and state the modulus in terms of the band edges. This avoids lengthy theta‑function manipulations and still earns full marks.

Hirota Bilinear Method and Multi‑Soliton Solutions

The Hirota bilinear formalism rewrites a nonlinear PDE as a quadratic equation in a new dependent variable τ (the tau function) using the Hirota D‑operator defined by Dₓⁿ Dₜᵐ f·g = (∂ₓ − ∂ₓ')ⁿ (∂ₜ − ∂ₜ')ᵐ f(x, t) g(x', t')|x'=x, t'=t. For KdV the substitution u = 2 ∂ₓ² log τ yields the bilinear equation (Dₓ Dₜ + Dₓ⁴) τ·τ = 0. The NLS equation becomes (i Dₜ + Dₓ²) g·f = 0, Dₓ² f·f = 2 |g|² with u = g/f. The power of the method lies in the perturbation expansion τ = 1 + ε τ₁ + ε² τ₂ + …; each τₙ is a sum of exponentials exp( η_i ) with η_i = k_i x + ω_i t + δ_i. The dispersion relation ω_i = −k_i³ for KdV follows from the linearized bilinear equation. The two‑soliton tau function is τ = 1 + eη₁ + eη₂ + A12 eη₁+η₂ where the phase‑shift factor A12 = ((k₁ − k₂)/(k₁ + k₂))². For N solitons the tau function is a Gram determinant or a Pfaffian, and the general N‑soliton solution is obtained by the Wronskian representation τ = Wr( f₁, …, f_N ) with f_i = eη_i + e−η_i. The bilinear form also accommodates rational solutions (lump solutions) by taking long‑wave limits k_i → 0, leading to rogue‑wave expressions such as the Peregrine soliton for NLS. Hirota’s method extends to difference equations, providing the discrete KdV and discrete KP equations on a lattice.

Classical r‑Matrix and Poisson‑Lie Structures

The classical r‑matrix formalism encodes the Poisson brackets of the Lax matrix L(λ) in the compact form { L(λ) ⊗, L(μ) } = [ r(λ, μ), L(λ) ⊗ I + I ⊗ L(μ) ]. Here r(λ, μ) is a matrix‑valued function satisfying the classical Yang–Baxter equation [ r12(λ, μ), r13(λ, ν) ] + [ r12(λ, μ), r23(μ, ν) ] + [ r13(λ, ν), r23(μ, ν) ] = 0. For the KdV hierarchy the Lax operator is a differential operator, but after a suitable discretization or restriction to a finite‑dimensional phase space (e.g., the periodic Toda lattice) the Lax matrix becomes a finite‑size matrix depending on the spectral parameter. The standard rational r‑matrix is r(λ, μ) = P/(λ − μ) where P is the permutation operator on V ⊗ V. The trigonometric and elliptic r‑matrices correspond to the XXZ and XYZ spin chains respectively. The existence of an r‑matrix guarantees that the spectral invariants Tr L(λ)^k are in involution, providing the Liouville integrals. Moreover, the r‑matrix defines a Poisson‑Lie group structure on the loop group; the Sklyanin bracket on the space of monodromy matrices is the classical limit of the quantum Yang–Baxter algebra. The classical r‑matrix also appears in the Hamiltonian formulation of the KP hierarchy via the Adler–Kostant–Symes scheme, where the phase space is a coadjoint orbit of the loop algebra and the Lax equation is the Hamiltonian flow generated by the Casimir functions. Understanding the r‑matrix is essential for constructing action‑angle variables on the finite‑gap tori and for the separation of variables method pioneered by Sklyanin.

Integrable Discretizations: Lattice KdV and Hirota Difference Equations

Integrable discretizations preserve the Lax pair, the infinite hierarchy of conservation laws, and the soliton solutions in a fully discrete setting. The Hirota–Miwa equation (also called the discrete KP equation) is the fundamental bilinear difference equation τl+1,m,n τl,m+1,n+1 − τl,m+1,n τl+1,m,n+1 + τl,m,n+1 τl+1,m+1,n = 0 on a three‑dimensional integer lattice. By imposing periodic reductions one recovers the discrete KdV, discrete NLS, and discrete Toda equations. The lattice KdV equation in potential form reads (vn+1m+1 − v_n^m)(vn+1^m − v_nm+1) = α − β where α, β are lattice parameters. Its Lax pair consists of 2×2 matrices L_n^m(λ) and M_n^m(λ) satisfying the zero‑curvature condition Ln+1^m M_n^m = M_nm+1 L_n^m. The discrete soliton solutions are obtained by the same Hirota ansatz τ = Σ exp( Σ η_i ) with the discrete dispersion relation eω_i = (1 + α ek_i)/(1 + β ek_i). The continuum limit α, β → 0 with appropriate scaling reproduces the continuous KdV solitons. The discrete inverse scattering transform has been developed for the Ablowitz–Ladik lattice (the integrable discretization of NLS), where the scattering data evolve linearly and the reconstruction uses a discrete Gel'fand–Levitan–Marchenko equation. These lattice models are not only mathematically elegant; they appear in numerical analysis as structure‑preserving integrators that avoid the numerical instability of standard finite‑difference schemes for soliton dynamics.

  • Confusing the Bäcklund transformation with the Darboux transformation; they are equivalent only after a specific gauge choice.
  • Assuming the finite‑gap theta function is always the Riemann theta function of a hyperelliptic curve; for KP the spectral curve can be non‑hyperelliptic.
  • Forgetting that the Hirota D‑operator acts on a product of two functions, not on a single function.
  • Misidentifying the classical r‑matrix for a given model; the rational, trigonometric, and elliptic cases correspond to distinct Poisson‑Lie groups.
  • Treating the discrete KdV equation as a mere approximation of the continuous KdV; it is an independent integrable system with its own Lax pair and conservation laws.
  • Neglecting the role of the spectral parameter in the discrete Lax matrices; the zero‑curvature condition holds for all λ, which is the source of the infinite hierarchy.
  • Overlooking the long‑wave limit that converts exponential solitons into rational (rogue‑wave) solutions in the Hirota formalism.

The advanced topics above complete the core toolkit needed for research‑level problems in integrable systems.

hand/chemical-thermodynamics.html:
Temperature Dependence of Reaction Enthalpy and Kirchhoff’s Law

The standard enthalpy change of a reaction ΔH° is tabulated at 298 K, yet most practical processes occur at other temperatures. Kirchhoff’s law provides the rigorous link: the temperature derivative of ΔH at constant pressure equals the difference in heat capacities between products and reactants.

Mathematical statement: (∂ΔH/∂T)P = ΔCp = Σν Cp(products) − Σν Cp(reactants). Integrating from a reference temperature T₁ (usually 298 K) to a target temperature T₂ gives ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ∫T₁T₂ ΔCp dT.

Heat‑capacity models. For gases, Cp is often expressed as a polynomial in temperature: Cp = a + bT + cT² + dT⁻² (Shomate equation) or the simpler NASA 7‑coefficient form. For condensed phases, Cp is frequently treated as constant over modest ranges, but high‑precision work uses the same polynomial approach.

Practical integration. When ΔCp is approximated as constant, ΔH(T₂) ≈ ΔH(T₁) + ΔCp(T₂ − T₁). If polynomial coefficients are available, the integral is evaluated term‑by‑term: ∫(a + bT + cT² + dT⁻²)dT = aΔT + ½b(T₂²−T₁²) + ⅓c(T₂³−T₁³) − d(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

Example. For the synthesis of ammonia, N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), standard enthalpies of formation at 298 K give ΔH°₍₂₉₈₎ = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹. Using Shomate coefficients for each species, ΔCp at 500 K evaluates to about −45 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The integrated correction from 298 K to 500 K is roughly −9 kJ mol⁻¹, yielding ΔH°₍₅₀₀₎ ≈ −101 kJ mol⁻¹. This temperature correction is essential for accurate equilibrium‑constant predictions via the van’t Hoff equation.

Limitations. Kirchhoff’s law assumes no phase change occurs between T₁ and T₂. If a reactant or product melts, boils, or undergoes a solid‑solid transition, the enthalpy of that transition must be added explicitly, and the heat‑capacity integration must be split at the transition temperature.

Maxwell Relations and Thermodynamic Potentials

Four fundamental thermodynamic potentials — internal energy U, enthalpy H, Helmholtz free energy A, and Gibbs free energy G — are linked by Legendre transforms. Each potential is a natural function of a specific pair of variables, and the exactness of its total differential yields the Maxwell relations, which connect measurable derivatives.

Definitions and natural variables

  • U(S, V): dU = T dS − P dV
  • H(S, P): dH = T dS + V dP
  • A(T, V): dA = −S dT − P dV
  • G(T, P): dG = −S dT + V dP

Because each differential is exact, the mixed second derivatives are equal. Equating ∂²U/∂V∂S = ∂²U/∂S∂V gives (∂T/∂V)S = −(∂P/∂S)V. Repeating for the other potentials produces the four classic Maxwell relations:

Maxwell Relations
PotentialRelation
U(S,V)(∂T/∂V)S = −(∂P/∂S)V
H(S,P)(∂T/∂P)S = (∂V/∂S)P
A(T,V)(∂S/∂V)T = (∂P/∂T)V
G(T,P)(∂S/∂P)T = −(∂V/∂T)P

Utility. These relations replace difficult entropy derivatives with readily measurable volume, pressure, and temperature derivatives. For instance, (∂S/∂P)T = −(∂V/∂T)P = −Vα, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion. This allows calculation of entropy changes during isothermal compression from PVT data alone.

Deriving thermodynamic identities

Combining Maxwell relations with definitions of heat capacities yields powerful identities. The difference between CP and CV is CP − CV = TVα²/κT, where κT = −(1/V)(∂V/∂P)T is the isothermal compressibility. The Joule‑Thomson coefficient μJT = (∂T/∂P)H = (Tα − 1)/CP V follows from the H‑based Maxwell relation and the definition of enthalpy.

Application to real gases

For a van der Waals gas, (∂P/∂T)V = R/(V−b). Using the A‑based Maxwell relation, (∂S/∂V)T = R/(V−b). Integration gives the entropy change on isothermal expansion: ΔS = R ln[(V₂−b)/(V₁−b)], which reduces to the ideal‑gas result when b → 0. Such derivations illustrate how Maxwell relations bridge microscopic equations of state and macroscopic thermodynamic quantities.

Worked Example: Using a Maxwell Relation
For one mole of a van der Waals gas (a = 1.39 Pa m⁶ mol⁻², b = 3.91×10⁻⁵ m³ mol⁻¹) at 300 K, calculate the entropy change when the volume increases from 0.02 m³ to 0.05 m³ isothermally.
From the Maxwell relation derived from Helmholtz free energy: (∂S/∂V)T = (∂P/∂T)V. For a van der Waals gas, P = RT/(V−b) − a/V², so (∂P/∂T)V = R/(V−b). Integrate: ΔS = ∫V₁V₂ R/(V−b) dV = R ln[(V₂−b)/(V₁−b)]. Insert values: R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, V₁ = 0.02 m³, V₂ = 0.05 m³, b = 3.91×10⁻⁵ m³. ΔS = 8.314 ln[(0.05−3.91×10⁻⁵)/(0.02−3.91×10⁻⁵)] ≈ 8.314 ln(2.499) ≈ 8.314 × 0.916 ≈ 7.62 J K⁻¹. The entropy increase is 7.6 J K⁻¹.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a derivative like (∂S/∂P)T or (∂V/∂T)P, immediately write the corresponding Maxwell relation from the G‑potential. Identify the measurable quantity (α, κT, or an equation‑of‑state derivative) and substitute. This avoids memorising dozens of individual formulas and works for any simple compressible system.

Chemical Potential, Activity, and Non‑Ideal Systems

The chemical potential μi = (∂G/∂ni)T,P,nj≠i is the partial molar Gibbs free energy. For a pure ideal gas, μ = μ° + RT ln(P/P°). In real systems the effective pressure or concentration is replaced by the activity ai, defined so that μi = μi° + RT ln ai retains the same formal structure.

Fugacity and gas‑phase activity

For a real gas, the activity is the fugacity f divided by the standard pressure P°: a = f/P°. Fugacity is defined by the requirement that the chemical potential expression remains valid: μ = μ° + RT ln(f/P°). The fugacity coefficient φ = f/P quantifies deviation from ideality; φ → 1 as P → 0. It can be obtained from the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT via ln φ = ∫₀P (Z−1)/P dP.

Solution‑phase activity

In liquid solutions the activity of solute i is ai = γi xi (mole‑fraction basis) or ai = γi mi/m° (molality basis), where γi is the activity coefficient. For the solvent, the Raoult’s‑law standard state gives asolvent = γsolvent xsolvent with γ → 1 as x → 1. For the solute, the Henry’s‑law standard state gives asolute = γsolute xsolute with γ → 1 as x → 0.

Debye–Hückel limiting law

For dilute electrolyte solutions, the mean ionic activity coefficient γ± follows log₁₀ γ± = −A |z₊z₋| √I, where I = ½ Σ mizi² is the ionic strength, A ≈ 0.509 mol⁻¹ᐟ² kg¹ᐟ² at 298 K in water, and z are ionic charges. The extended Debye–Hückel equation adds a linear term in I to improve accuracy up to I ≈ 0.1 mol kg⁻¹.

Reaction quotient in terms of activities

The thermodynamic equilibrium constant K is defined by the product of activities raised to stoichiometric powers: K = Π aiνi. The reaction quotient Q uses the same expression with instantaneous activities. The Gibbs energy of reaction at any composition is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0 gives ΔG° = −RT ln K. This formulation is exact; all non‑ideality is absorbed into the activity coefficients.

Phase Equilibria and the Clapeyron Equation

At equilibrium between two phases α and β of a pure substance, the chemical potentials are equal: μα(T,P) = μβ(T,P). Differentiating along the coexistence curve gives the Clapeyron equation: dP/dT = ΔS/ΔV = ΔH/(T ΔV), where ΔS, ΔV, ΔH are the molar entropy, volume, and enthalpy changes for the transition α → β.

Solid–liquid equilibrium

For melting, ΔV is usually positive (water is a notable exception). Since ΔHfus > 0, the slope dP/dT is positive for most substances. The melting curve is nearly linear over moderate ranges because ΔH and ΔV vary slowly. For water, ΔV < 0 gives a negative slope, explaining why ice melts under pressure.

Liquid–vapor and solid–vapor equilibrium

Here ΔV ≈ Vgas (since Vcondensed ≪ Vgas). Using the ideal‑gas approximation Vgas = RT/P, the Clapeyron equation becomes the Clausius–Clapeyron equation: d(ln P)/dT = ΔHvap/(RT²). Integration assuming constant ΔH yields ln(P₂/P₁) = −ΔHvap/R (1/T₂ − 1/T₁). This relation underpins the estimation of boiling points at different pressures and the determination of ΔHvap from vapor‑pressure data.

Triple point and critical point

The triple point is the unique (T,P) where solid, liquid, and vapor coexist; it satisfies the three Clapeyron equations simultaneously. The critical point terminates the liquid–vapor coexistence curve; there ΔV → 0 and ΔH → 0, so dP/dT remains finite. Near the critical point, the Clapeyron equation fails because the phases become indistinguishable and fluctuations dominate.

Application to polymorphism

For solid–solid transitions (e.g., graphite diamond), ΔV is small but non‑zero. The Clapeyron slope determines the pressure required for synthesis at a given temperature. For the graphite‑diamond transition, ΔV ≈ −1.9 cm³ mol⁻¹ and ΔH ≈ 1.9 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K, giving dP/dT ≈ 3.5 MPa K⁻¹. This steep positive slope explains why high pressure (≈ 1.5 GPa) and high temperature (≈ 1800 K) are needed for diamond formation.

Electrochemical Thermodynamics: ΔG, Cell Potential, and the Nernst Equation

Electrochemical cells convert chemical free energy into electrical work. The maximum non‑expansion work obtainable from a galvanic cell at constant T and P equals the decrease in Gibbs free energy: ΔG = −n F E, where n is the number of electrons transferred per reaction event, F = 96 485 C mol⁻¹ is Faraday’s constant, and E is the cell potential.

Standard potentials and the equilibrium constant

For a cell reaction written as a reduction, the standard cell potential E° relates to the standard Gibbs energy: ΔG° = −n F E°. Combining with ΔG° = −RT ln K gives the fundamental link E° = (RT/nF) ln K. At 298 K, (RT/F) ln 10 ≈ 0.05916 V, so log₁₀ K = n E°/0.05916. This allows calculation of equilibrium constants from tabulated standard reduction potentials.

The Nernst equation

For non‑standard conditions, the cell potential depends on the reaction quotient Q expressed in activities: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q. For a half‑reaction aA + ne⁻ ⇌ bB, the reduction potential is E = E° − (RT/nF) ln(aBb/aAa). In dilute aqueous solutions, activities are approximated by concentrations (or partial pressures for gases), yielding the familiar form E = E° − (0.05916/n) log₁₀ Q at 298 K.

Temperature dependence of cell potential

Differentiating ΔG = −nFE with respect to T at constant P gives (∂E/∂T)P = ΔS/(nF). The entropy change of the cell reaction can therefore be obtained from the temperature coefficient of the emf. Conversely, ΔH = ΔG + TΔS = −nF(E − T(∂E/∂T)P). These relations are the basis of thermodynamic analysis of batteries and fuel cells.

Concentration cells and liquid‑junction potentials

A concentration cell has identical electrodes but different electrolyte activities. Its emf arises solely from the activity difference: E = (RT/nF) ln(a₂/a₁). In practice, a liquid‑junction potential develops at the interface between solutions of different composition; the measured emf includes this contribution unless a salt bridge with a non‑selective electrolyte (e.g., KCl) minimizes it.

Applications

Standard potentials are used to construct the electrochemical series, predicting spontaneity of redox reactions. The Nernst equation underpins pH measurement (glass electrode), corrosion potential calculations, and the design of electrochemical sensors. In energy storage, the open‑circuit voltage of a lithium‑ion cell follows the Nernst equation with the activity of Li⁺ in the host materials.

  • Assuming ΔCp = 0 over large temperature intervals when Kirchhoff’s law requires integration of temperature‑dependent heat capacities.
  • Confusing the Maxwell relation derived from G (∂S/∂P)T = −(∂V/∂T)P with the one from A (∂S/∂V)T = (∂P/∂T)V.
  • Using concentrations instead of activities in the Nernst equation for solutions beyond the dilute limit, ignoring activity‑coefficient corrections.
  • Applying the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to solid–liquid transitions where ΔV is not negligible compared with the gas volume.
  • Neglecting the temperature dependence of ΔH in the van’t Hoff equation when the reaction enthalpy varies significantly with temperature.
  • Treating fugacity coefficient φ as unity for gases at moderate pressures (e.g., > 10 bar) where real‑gas deviations are appreciable.
  • Forgetting that the standard state for a solute in the Henry’s‑law convention is the hypothetical 1 mol kg⁻¹ solution with γ = 1, not the pure solute.

hand/toric-varieties.html:
Cox Ring, Homogeneous Coordinates, and GIT Quotients

The Cox ring (or total coordinate ring) of a toric variety X(Δ) is the polynomial ring ℂ[x_ρ : ρ ∈ Δ(1)] graded by the divisor class group Cl(X). Each variable x_ρ corresponds to the T‑invariant prime divisor D_ρ. The grading is given by deg(x_ρ) = [D_ρ] ∈ Cl(X). The irrelevant ideal B(Δ) is generated by monomials ∏ρ∉σ(1) x_ρ for each cone σ ∈ Δ. The toric variety is recovered as the GIT quotient (Spec Cox(X) V(B(Δ))) // Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*), where the torus Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*) acts with weights given by the grading. This construction generalizes the classical homogeneous coordinate ring of projective space and provides a uniform framework for studying line bundles, sections, and morphisms. For a smooth complete toric variety, the Cox ring is a polynomial ring, and the GIT quotient is a geometric quotient. In the singular or non‑projective case, one must choose a stability condition (a character of Hom(Cl(X), ℂ^*)) to obtain a well‑defined quotient; different choices correspond to different birational models related by toric flips. The Cox ring also encodes the Mori cone: the effective cone Eff(X) is the cone generated by the classes [D_ρ] in Cl(X)_ℝ, and the movable cone is the intersection of the nef cones of all small ℚ‑factorial modifications. This description makes the minimal model program for toric varieties completely combinatorial.

Toric Divisors, Intersection Theory, and the Polytope Formula

On a complete toric variety X(Δ) of dimension n, every T‑invariant Weil divisor is a ℤ‑linear combination D = Σ a_ρ D_ρ. The associated polytope P_D = {m ∈ M_ℝ : ⟨m, u_ρ⟩ ≥ −a_ρ for all ρ ∈ Δ(1)} is a lattice polytope whose normal fan refines Δ. The line bundle O(D) is globally generated iff P_D is a lattice polytope, and it is ample iff P_D is strictly convex with normal fan exactly Δ. The intersection number of n nef divisors D^(1), …, D^(n) equals n! times the mixed volume of the corresponding polytopes P1, …, P_n. In particular, the self‑intersection D^n = n! Vol(P_D). For a smooth projective toric variety, the Chow ring A^*(X) is generated by the divisor classes [D_ρ] subject to two types of relations: (i) linear relations Σ ⟨m, u_ρ⟩ [D_ρ] = 0 for all m ∈ M, and (ii) Stanley–Reisner relations ∏ρ∈S [D_ρ] = 0 whenever the rays in S do not span a cone in Δ. This presentation, due to Danilov and Jurkiewicz, allows explicit computation of intersection numbers by reducing monomials in the [D_ρ] to a linear combination of top‑degree classes corresponding to maximal cones. The Todd class of X is td(X) = ∏ρ ( [D_ρ] / (1 − e−[D_ρ]) ), and the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem reduces to a sum over lattice points of the polytope, recovering the Ehrhart polynomial.

Worked Example: Intersection Numbers on the Hirzebruch Surface F1
Let F1 be the toric surface with fan rays u1 = (1,0), u2 = (0,1), u3 = (−1,0), u4 = (0,−1) and maximal cones σ1 = ⟨u1,u2⟩, σ2 = ⟨u2,u3⟩, σ3 = ⟨u3,u4⟩, σ4 = ⟨u4,u1⟩. Compute the intersection matrix of the T‑invariant divisors D1, D2, D3, D4.
The linear relations come from M = ℤ2. For m = (1,0): ⟨m,u1⟩=1, ⟨m,u2⟩=0, ⟨m,u3⟩=−1, ⟨m,u4⟩=0 ⇒ D1 − D3 = 0. For m = (0,1): D2 − D4 = 0. Thus D1 = D3, D2 = D4. Stanley–Reisner relations: D1 D3 = 0 (rays 1 and 3 not in a cone), D2 D4 = 0. Using D1 = D3, we get D12 = 0. Similarly D22 = 0. The only non‑zero top products are D1 D2 (cone σ1) and D2 D3 (cone σ2) etc. Since D1 D2 corresponds to the maximal cone σ1, its class is the fundamental class [pt]. The intersection matrix in basis (D1, D2) is [[0,1],[1,0]]. Hence D1·D2 = 1, D12 = D22 = 0. This matches the known geometry: D1 is the fiber class, D2 is the section with self‑intersection −1, but in the Chow ring of F1 the section class is D2 − D1, giving (D2−D1)2 = −1.
Exam Strategy: Intersection Computations
When asked for intersection numbers on a toric variety, first write the linear relations from the lattice M, then impose Stanley–Reisner relations. Reduce any monomial of degree n to a sum of classes of maximal cones. Each maximal cone contributes 1 to the fundamental class. This algorithm works for any complete simplicial toric variety and avoids memorising case‑by‑case formulas.

Toric Vector Bundles and Klyachko's Classification

Equivariant vector bundles on a toric variety X(Δ) are classified by Klyachko's filtrations. For each ray ρ ∈ Δ(1), a T‑equivariant vector bundle E of rank r corresponds to a collection of decreasing filtrations E^ρ(i) (i ∈ ℤ) of the fiber E0 ≅ ℂ^r over the fixed point 0 ∈ T, indexed by integers, such that E^ρ(i) = E0 for i ≪ 0 and E^ρ(i) = 0 for i ≫ 0. These filtrations must satisfy a compatibility condition: for any cone σ ∈ Δ, the intersection of the subspaces E^ρ(i_ρ) over ρ ∈ σ(1) has dimension equal to the rank of the bundle restricted to the affine patch U_σ. Equivalently, the associated graded pieces define a representation of the fan. The Chern classes of E can be read off from the filtrations: c1(E) = Σ_ρ ( Σ_i i · dim Gr^ρ_i ) D_ρ. Klyachko's theorem also gives a combinatorial criterion for global generation, ampleness, and stability of toric vector bundles. For example, the tangent bundle T_X corresponds to the filtrations where E^ρ(i) = ℂ^n for i ≤ 0, E^ρ(i) = u_ρ^⊥ for i = 1, and 0 for i ≥ 2. This description makes the computation of equivariant cohomology and K‑theory of toric vector bundles completely algorithmic.

Tropical Geometry, Toric Degenerations, and the Secondary Fan

Tropical geometry provides a piecewise‑linear shadow of algebraic geometry over the valuation field. Given a projective toric variety X_P defined by a lattice polytope P ⊂ M_ℝ, a regular subdivision of P corresponds to a toric degeneration of X_P to a union of toric varieties glued along toric strata. The secondary fan of P is the fan in the space of height functions on P ∩ M whose cones parametrize regular subdivisions. Each maximal cone of the secondary fan corresponds to a unimodular triangulation of P, which yields a flat degeneration of X_P to a toric variety with at worst orbifold singularities. The tropical variety of a subvariety Y ⊂ X_P is the set of valuations of points of Y; it is a polyhedral complex of dimension dim Y balanced at each codimension‑1 face. For a hypersurface defined by a Laurent polynomial f with Newton polytope P, the tropical hypersurface is the corner locus of the piecewise‑linear function trop(f). The combinatorial structure of the tropical hypersurface encodes the Hodge numbers of Y via the tropical Hodge theory of Itenberg–Mikhalkin. Moreover, the secondary fan governs the birational geometry of X_P: its walls correspond to flips and flops in the toric minimal model program. This connection makes toric varieties a testing ground for mirror symmetry, where the tropical limit of a Calabi‑Yau hypersurface recovers the SYZ fibration.

Equivariant Cohomology and the Danilov–Jurkiewicz Theorem

The T‑equivariant cohomology ring H_T^*(X(Δ); ℤ) of a smooth complete toric variety is a free module over H_T^*(pt) ≅ Sym(M) ≅ ℤ[t1,…,t_n] with basis given by the equivariant classes of the orbit closures V(σ). The Danilov–Jurkiewicz theorem states that the ordinary cohomology ring H^*(X(Δ); ℤ) is the quotient of the polynomial ring ℤ[x_ρ : ρ ∈ Δ(1)] by the ideal generated by (i) linear forms Σ ⟨m, u_ρ⟩ x_ρ for all m ∈ M, and (ii) monomials ∏ρ∈S x_ρ where S does not span a cone in Δ. The equivariant version replaces the linear forms by Σ ⟨m, u_ρ⟩ x_ρ + Σ ⟨m, u_ρ⟩ t_ρ, where t_ρ are the equivariant parameters. This presentation allows the computation of equivariant Chern classes of tangent bundles, the localization formula for integrals, and the Gromov–Witten invariants of toric varieties via the virtual localization of Graber–Pandharipande. In particular, the equivariant cohomology of the Hilbert scheme of points on a toric surface can be expressed in terms of the Nakajima quiver variety construction, linking toric geometry to representation theory of affine Lie algebras.

  • Confusing the Cox ring grading by Cl(X) with the grading by Pic(X); they coincide only when X is ℚ‑factorial.
  • Forgetting that the Stanley–Reisner ideal uses sets of rays that do NOT span a cone, not the cones themselves.
  • Assuming every toric vector bundle splits as a sum of line bundles; Klyachko's classification shows many indecomposable bundles exist.
  • Misidentifying the secondary fan with the normal fan of the polytope; the secondary fan lives in the space of height functions, not in M_ℝ.
  • Neglecting the equivariant parameters in the Danilov–Jurkiewicz presentation when applying localization formulas.
  • Treating the tropical hypersurface as a mere graph without checking the balancing condition at each vertex.
  • Overlooking that the GIT quotient construction of X(Δ) from the Cox ring requires a choice of stability condition when X is not projective.

These traps highlight the subtle points that often separate a passing score from a top rank.

hand/quantum-groups.html:
Drinfeld's Quantum Double Construction and Universal R-Matrix

The quantum double D(H) of a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra H provides a canonical quasitriangular Hopf algebra. As a vector space D(H) = H ⊗ H*cop, where H*cop is the dual Hopf algebra with opposite comultiplication. The multiplication is defined by (a ⊗ f)(b ⊗ g) = a b₁ ⊗ f₂ g ⟨f₁, b₂⟩ ⟨f₃, S⁻¹(b₃)⟩ using Sweedler notation Δ(b) = b₁ ⊗ b₂ and Δ(f) = f₁ ⊗ f₂. The comultiplication on D(H) is ΔD(a ⊗ f) = (a₁ ⊗ f₂) ⊗ (a₂ ⊗ f₁). The antipode is SD(a ⊗ f) = (1 ⊗ S⁻¹(f₁))(S(a) ⊗ 1). The universal R-matrix is R = Σi ei ⊗ ei where {ei} is a basis of H and {ei} the dual basis of H*. This element satisfies (Δ ⊗ id)(R) = R13R23, (id ⊗ Δ)(R) = R13R12, and Δop(x) = R Δ(x) R⁻¹ for all x ∈ D(H). When H = Uq(𝔟+) the positive Borel subalgebra, D(H) is isomorphic to the full quantum group Uq(𝔤). The double construction also yields the Drinfeld element u = S(R₂)R₁, which implements the square of the antipode: S²(x) = u x u⁻¹. The ribbon element v = u⁻¹ K2ρ (with K2ρ the group-like element corresponding to twice the Weyl vector) satisfies v² = u S(u) and provides the pivotal structure needed for quantum traces.

Braided Monoidal Categories: Hexagon Axioms and Coherence

A braided monoidal category (C, ⊗, I, α, λ, ρ, c) consists of a monoidal category equipped with a natural isomorphism cX,Y: X ⊗ Y → Y ⊗ X called the braiding. The braiding must satisfy the two hexagon axioms: (idY ⊗ cX,Z) ∘ αY,X,Z ∘ (cX,Y ⊗ idZ) = αY,Z,X ∘ cX,Y⊗Z ∘ αX,Y,Z and (cX,Z ⊗ idY) ∘ αX,Z,Y⁻¹ ∘ (idX ⊗ cY,Z) = αZ,X,Y⁻¹ ∘ cX⊗Y,Z ∘ αX,Y,Z⁻¹. These diagrams encode the compatibility of braiding with associativity. In Rep(Uq(𝔤)) the braiding is given by cV,W = τ ∘ RV,W where τ(v ⊗ w) = w ⊗ v and RV,W is the action of the universal R-matrix. The hexagon axioms follow from the quasitriangular identities of R. Coherence theorems guarantee that any diagram built from α, λ, ρ, and c commutes, so the category is equivalent to a strict braided monoidal category. The Drinfeld center Z(C) of a monoidal category C is a canonical braided monoidal category; for C = Rep(H) with H a Hopf algebra, Z(C) ≅ Rep(D(H)). This explains why the quantum double yields the universal braiding.

Worked Example: Verifying the Hexagon Axiom for Uq(𝔰𝔩₂)
Let V, W, X be the fundamental two-dimensional representation of Uq(𝔰𝔩₂). Using the explicit R-matrix R = qH⊗H/2 Σn≥0 (1−q⁻²)n/[n]! qn(n−1)/2 En ⊗ Fn, compute both sides of the first hexagon axiom on a basis vector v ⊗ w ⊗ x and show they coincide.
The R-matrix acts as R(v ⊗ w) = q1/2 w ⊗ v + (q−q⁻¹) v ⊗ w for the standard basis. The associator α is trivial because we work in a strictified category. The left side of the hexagon is (id ⊗ cV,X) ∘ (cV,W ⊗ id) applied to v⊗w⊗x. First cV,W swaps v and w with the R-factor, then id ⊗ cV,X swaps the resulting first factor with x. The right side is cV,W⊗X which uses the coproduct Δ on the second tensor factor. Because R satisfies (Δ ⊗ id)(R) = R13R23, the two compositions give identical linear combinations of basis tensors. Explicit calculation on the four basis vectors confirms equality term by term, verifying the hexagon axiom for this case.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks to prove a braided category property, first identify whether the category is presented via a universal R-matrix or via explicit braiding formulas. Use the quasitriangular identities (Δ⊗id)(R)=R₁₃R₂₃ and (id⊗Δ)(R)=R₁₃R₁₂ to translate hexagon diagrams into algebraic equalities. Remember that the Drinfeld center construction is a universal method to produce a braided category from any monoidal category; citing this can earn full marks for conceptual questions.

Quantum Groups at Roots of Unity and Modular Tensor Categories

When the deformation parameter q is a primitive ℓ-th root of unity (ℓ odd, ℓ > Coxeter number), the representation theory of Uq(𝔤) changes dramatically. The restricted quantum group uq(𝔤) (Lusztig's finite-dimensional quotient) has finitely many simple modules, all of which are highest weight modules with dominant weights λ satisfying ⟨λ+ρ, α∨⟩ < ℓ for all positive roots α. The category of finite-dimensional uq(𝔤)-modules is a modular tensor category (MTC): it is a braided ribbon fusion category with a non-degenerate S-matrix. The simple objects are labelled by the alcove of dominant weights. The quantum dimensions dimq Vλ are given by the Weyl character formula evaluated at q, and they satisfy the Verlinde formula Nλμν = Σσ Sλσ Sμσ Sνσ* / S0σ. The modular S and T matrices are derived from the ribbon element and the braiding: Sλμ = (1/𝒟) Σw∈W ε(w) q⟨w(λ+ρ), μ+ρ⟩ and Tλμ = δλμ q⟨λ, λ+2ρ⟩/2. The total quantum dimension 𝒟 = √(Σλ (dimq Vλ)²). These data define the Reshetikhin-Turaev topological quantum field theory and the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariants of 3-manifolds. The non-degeneracy of S ensures that the MTC is modular, i.e., the braiding is maximally non-symmetric.

Topological Quantum Computation: Anyons, Braiding, and Universality

Modular tensor categories provide the algebraic framework for topological quantum computation. Anyons correspond to simple objects of an MTC; their fusion rules are the tensor product multiplicities Nabc. Braiding of anyons implements unitary operators on the space of conformal blocks (the Hilbert space of anyonic states). For the Fibonacci anyon model (the (G₂,1) or (SU(2),3) theory), there are two simple objects: the vacuum 1 and the Fibonacci anyon τ with fusion τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ. The braiding matrix for τ exchange is a 2×2 unitary matrix with eigenvalues e±4πi/5. The group generated by these braids is dense in SU(2), so any single-qubit gate can be approximated arbitrarily well by braiding τ anyons. For universal quantum computation one also needs a non-topological phase gate (e.g., π/8 rotation) which can be supplied by magic state distillation or by supplementing with a non-abelian anyon of higher quantum dimension such as the (SU(2),5) theory. The quantum double of a finite group D(G) yields abelian anyons for G abelian and non-abelian anyons for non-abelian G; the toric code corresponds to D(ℤ₂). Error correction in topological quantum computers relies on the energy gap separating the ground state degeneracy (the topological qubit) from excited states, which is a physical realization of the MTC's modularity.

Lusztig's Canonical Basis and Quantum Group Representations

Lusztig introduced the canonical basis (also called global crystal basis) of the negative part Uq(𝔫−) of a quantum group. This basis has remarkable positivity properties: structure constants for multiplication and comultiplication are polynomials in q with non-negative integer coefficients. The canonical basis is constructed via the geometry of quiver varieties or via the algebraic approach of Kashiwara's crystal bases. For each dominant weight λ, the highest weight module V(λ) inherits a canonical basis from the canonical basis of Uq(𝔫−) by acting on the highest weight vector. The transition matrix between the canonical basis and the PBW basis is unitriangular with polynomial entries. At q=0 the canonical basis specializes to Kashiwara's crystal basis, which encodes the combinatorics of the representation via the crystal graph. The canonical basis also provides a basis for the quantum coordinate ring ℂq[G] and for the dual Hopf algebra Uq(𝔤)*. Its existence proves the positivity conjectures for quantum cluster algebras and underlies the categorification of quantum groups via Khovanov-Lauda-Rouquier algebras. In the context of the geometric Langlands program, the canonical basis corresponds to the intersection cohomology complexes on the affine Grassmannian.

  • Common Trap: Confusing the unrestricted quantum group Uq(𝔤) at generic q with the restricted quantum group uq(𝔤) at roots of unity; the former has infinite-dimensional representation categories while the latter yields modular tensor categories.
  • Common Trap: Assuming the braiding in a braided monoidal category is symmetric (cY,X∘cX,Y = id); in quantum group categories it is generally not involutive.
  • Common Trap: Forgetting that the universal R-matrix lives in a completion of Uq(𝔤) ⊗ Uq(𝔤) and does not act on all tensor products without convergence considerations.
  • Common Trap: Misapplying the Verlinde formula by using the S-matrix of the unrestricted category instead of the modular S-matrix of the restricted category at roots of unity.
  • Common Trap: Overlooking the role of the ribbon element v in defining quantum traces; the quantum trace is Trq(f) = Tr(K2ρ f) not the ordinary trace.
  • Common Trap: Treating the canonical basis as a basis of the whole quantum group Uq(𝔤) rather than of its negative part Uq(𝔫−) and its highest weight modules.
  • Common Trap: Believing that any braided fusion category is modular; modularity requires non-degeneracy of the S-matrix, which fails for symmetric fusion categories such as Rep(G) for a finite group G.

hand/symplectic-geometry.html:
Symplectic Capacities and Embedding Problems

Symplectic capacities are numerical invariants that measure the “size” of a symplectic manifold in a way that respects symplectic embeddings. The first capacity, introduced by Gromov in 1985, is the Gromov width: for a symplectic manifold (M, ω) it is the supremum of πr² such that a standard ball B²ⁿ(r) embeds symplectically into M. Gromov’s non‑squeezing theorem states that a ball B²ⁿ(R) cannot be symplectically embedded into a cylinder B²(r) × ℝ²ⁿ⁻² unless R ≤ r. This result shows that symplectic geometry has rigid “size” constraints absent in volume‑preserving diffeomorphisms.

Subsequent capacities include the Ekeland–Hofer capacities, defined via the Conley–Zehnder index of periodic orbits on the boundary of a domain, and the Hofer–Zehnder capacity, which uses the existence of fast periodic Hamiltonian orbits. All these capacities satisfy monotonicity (if U V symplectically then c(U) ≤ c(V)), conformality (c(λU) = λ² c(U)), and normalization on the standard ball and cylinder. They have become the primary tool for solving embedding problems: for example, the exact embedding classification of four‑dimensional ellipsoids E(a,b) into balls was completed by McDuff and Schlenk (2012) using the sequence of ECH capacities derived from embedded contact homology.

Capacities also detect subtle phenomena such as symplectic packing. The packing numbers p_k(M) — the supremum of total volume fraction filled by k disjoint equal balls — are governed by the Gromov width and higher capacities. In dimension four, the full packing function for many rational and ruled surfaces is known, exhibiting a staircase pattern related to the Fibonacci numbers. These results illustrate how capacities translate global symplectic topology into concrete numerical obstructions.

Contact Geometry and its Symplectic Fillings

Contact geometry is the odd‑dimensional counterpart of symplectic geometry. A contact manifold (Y, ξ) of dimension 2n‑1 carries a hyperplane field ξ = ker α where α is a 1‑form with α ∧ (dα)ⁿ⁻¹ ≠ 0. The Reeb vector field R is defined by α(R)=1, dα(R,·)=0. A symplectic filling of (Y, ξ) is a compact symplectic manifold (W, ω) with ∂W = Y such that ω|_ξ > 0 and a Liouville vector field points outward along the boundary. Weak, strong, and Stein fillings form a hierarchy: every Stein filling is strong, every strong filling is weak.

Eliashberg’s classification of tight contact structures on S³ (1992) showed that the standard contact structure is the unique tight one, while overtwisted structures are classified by homotopy classes of plane fields. The existence of a Stein filling implies tightness, but the converse fails in higher dimensions. Giroux’s correspondence (2000) establishes a bijection between contact structures on a closed 3‑manifold up to isotopy and open book decompositions up to positive stabilization, providing a combinatorial handle on contact topology.

Symplectic field theory (SFT), introduced by Eliashberg, Givental, and Hofer (2000), constructs invariants of contact manifolds by counting punctured pseudoholomorphic curves in the symplectization ℝ × Y. The resulting algebraic structure — a differential graded algebra generated by Reeb orbits — yields contact homology, a powerful invariant that distinguishes many contact manifolds with the same underlying smooth topology. SFT also provides a framework for defining Gromov–Witten invariants of symplectic cobordisms, linking closed and open symplectic topology.

Worked Example: Computing the Gromov Width of an Ellipsoid
Let E(a,b) = { (z₁,z₂) ∈ ℂ² | π|z₁|²/a + π|z₂|²/b < 1 } with 0 < a ≤ b. Determine its Gromov width c_G(E(a,b)).
The Gromov width of a four‑dimensional ellipsoid equals the smaller symplectic area a. Proof: the inclusion B⁴(√(a/π)) E(a,b) given by scaling the first coordinate shows c_G ≥ a. For the upper bound, assume a ball of capacity > a embeds. By monotonicity of the Ekeland–Hofer capacities c_k, the first capacity of the ball is its Gromov width, while the first capacity of E(a,b) is a. Since capacities are monotone, the ball’s capacity cannot exceed a. Hence c_G(E(a,b)) = a.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a symplectic capacity of a domain, first identify whether the domain is a ball, cylinder, ellipsoid, or polydisk. Recall the normalization values: c_G(B²ⁿ(r)) = πr², c_G(Z²ⁿ(r)) = πr². For ellipsoids E(a,b) the answer is min(a,b). For polydisks P(a,b) the Gromov width is min(a,b) as well, but higher Ekeland–Hofer capacities differ. Write down the relevant monotonicity property to justify any inequality.

Geometric Quantization and the Role of Polarizations

Geometric quantization provides a systematic procedure to associate a Hilbert space to a symplectic manifold (M, ω) equipped with a prequantum line bundle L → M whose curvature equals −i ω. The prequantum Hilbert space consists of square‑integrable sections of L, but it is too large; a polarization — an integrable Lagrangian distribution P ⊂ TM ⊗ ℂ — selects a subspace of “quantum states”. Real polarizations correspond to Lagrangian foliations (e.g., fibers of a Lagrangian fibration), while Kähler polarizations use a compatible complex structure J and take holomorphic sections.

The Bohr–Sommerfeld condition characterizes which leaves of a real polarization support non‑zero covariantly constant sections: a leaf F is Bohr–Sommerfeld if the holonomy of the connection around any loop in F is trivial. In the case of a torus fibration, this recovers the classical action‑angle quantization ∮ p dq = 2πℏ (n + ½). For Kähler polarizations, the quantum Hilbert space is the space of holomorphic sections H⁰(M, L), and its dimension is given by the Riemann–Roch formula, which in the symplectic setting becomes the index of a Spinc Dirac operator.

Quantization commutes with reduction (the “Guillemin–Sternberg conjecture”, proved by Meinrenken and by Tian–Zhang in the 1990s) states that the quantization of the symplectic quotient M//G equals the G‑invariant part of the quantization of M. This theorem links representation theory of compact Lie groups (via the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem) with symplectic geometry of coadjoint orbits, and it underlies the modern approach to the geometric Langlands program.

Lagrangian Intersection Theory and the Arnold Conjecture Beyond the Classical Setting

The Arnold conjecture asserts that a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of a closed symplectic manifold has at least as many fixed points as the sum of Betti numbers of the manifold. Floer’s original proof (1988) used Lagrangian Floer homology for the diagonal Δ ⊂ M × M and its image under the graph of the diffeomorphism. Later developments extended the result to degenerate fixed points, to non‑contractible periodic orbits, and to symplectic manifolds with non‑trivial π₂ via the use of Novikov rings and virtual fundamental cycles.

In the setting of Lagrangian submanifolds L₀, L₁ with clean intersection, the Floer complex is generated by intersection points graded by the Maslov index. The differential counts pseudoholomorphic strips with boundary on L₀ ∪ L₁. When L₀ and L₁ are Hamiltonian isotopic, the Floer homology is isomorphic to the singular homology of L₀ (the Piunikhin–Salamon–Schwarz isomorphism). This provides a Morse‑theoretic interpretation of the Arnold conjecture: the number of intersection points is bounded below by the rank of H*(L₀).

Recent work by Abouzaid, Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono, and others has established the conjecture for all closed symplectic manifolds using Kuranishi structures or polyfold theory to handle transversality issues. Moreover, the “nearby Lagrangian” conjecture (proved by Abouzaid–Kragh for cotangent bundles) states that any exact Lagrangian in T*Q is Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section, linking symplectic topology with smooth topology of the base.

Symplectic Field Theory and Contact Homology

Symplectic field theory (SFT) is a functorial invariant of contact manifolds and symplectic cobordisms built from counts of punctured pseudoholomorphic curves in the symplectization ℝ × Y and in completed cobordisms. The algebraic structure is a differential graded algebra (A, ∂) generated by good Reeb orbits, with differential defined by counting rigid curves with positive punctures at the input orbit and negative punctures at output orbits. The homology of this complex is the contact homology HC*(Y).

For a contact manifold that bounds a Stein domain, the contact homology vanishes (Bourgeois–Oancea). This vanishing theorem provides obstructions to the existence of Stein fillings. Conversely, non‑vanishing contact homology distinguishes contact structures that are homotopic as plane fields but not contactomorphic. The theory also yields the “cylindrical contact homology” when one restricts to curves of genus zero with one positive puncture, which is often computable via combinatorial methods (e.g., for prequantization bundles).

SFT satisfies a gluing axiom: a symplectic cobordism (W, ω) from (Y₋, ξ₋) to (Y₊, ξ₊) induces a chain map Φ_W : HC*(Y₊) → HC*(Y₋). Composition of cobordisms corresponds to composition of maps, making SFT a (1+1)‑dimensional topological quantum field theory with additional algebraic structure. This functoriality underlies the proof of the Weinstein conjecture for many contact manifolds and the classification of tight contact structures on lens spaces.

  • Confusing the Gromov width with the Hofer–Zehnder capacity; they coincide for balls and cylinders but differ for ellipsoids and polydisks.
  • Assuming every tight contact structure admits a Stein filling; counterexamples exist in dimension five and higher.
  • Neglecting the Novikov ring when defining Floer homology on manifolds with non‑zero π₂; without it the differential may not square to zero.
  • Treating the Maslov index as an integer without specifying a trivialization of the determinant line bundle; the grading is only well‑defined modulo the minimal Maslov number.
  • Overlooking the distinction between weak, strong, and Stein fillings when applying Eliashberg’s classification results.
  • Applying the Arnold conjecture lower bound to non‑Hamiltonian symplectomorphisms; the conjecture is false for general symplectomorphisms.
  • Forgetting that contact homology is defined only for non‑degenerate contact forms; one must perturb the form or use a Morse–Bott version.
