gk/general-science.html:
Mechanics of Fluids: Bernoulli’s Principle and Applications

Bernoulli’s principle follows from the conservation of energy applied to an ideal fluid flowing along a streamline. For an incompressible, non‑viscous, steady flow the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy per unit volume, and potential energy per unit volume remains constant: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. Here P is static pressure, ρ fluid density, v flow speed, g acceleration due to gravity, and h height above a reference level. The equation assumes no energy loss to friction and that the flow is irrotational.

Typical applications illustrate the trade‑off between pressure and velocity. In a Venturi meter a constriction forces the fluid to accelerate, lowering the pressure; the pressure difference is then used to determine flow rate. An aircraft wing (airfoil) is shaped so that air moves faster over the upper surface than the lower, creating a pressure difference that generates lift. Carburettors in older internal‑combustion engines exploit the same effect: fast‑moving air in a narrow throat draws fuel into the airstream. In medical practice, a Venturi mask delivers a precise oxygen concentration by entraining room air through a high‑velocity oxygen jet.

Limitations are important for exam questions. Real fluids have viscosity, so a boundary layer forms where velocity drops to zero at the wall; Bernoulli’s equation does not hold inside this layer. Compressibility becomes significant at Mach numbers above ~0.3, requiring the full energy equation with enthalpy. Turbulent or unsteady flows also violate the steady‑flow assumption. When a problem states “ideal fluid” or “negligible viscosity”, Bernoulli may be applied; otherwise the examiner expects you to recognise the need for the Navier‑Stokes equations or empirical loss coefficients.

Dimensionless numbers help decide the regime. The Reynolds number Re = ρvL/μ compares inertial to viscous forces; low Re (laminar) flows approximate the ideal conditions better than high Re (turbulent) flows. The Mach number Ma = v/a (where a is the speed of sound) signals compressibility effects. A typical multiple‑choice trap gives a high‑speed gas flow and asks for the pressure drop using Bernoulli; the correct answer is “cannot be determined without compressibility corrections”.

Thermodynamics: Laws, Entropy, and Heat Engines

The four laws of thermodynamics form the backbone of energy analysis. The zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium and the concept of temperature. The first law, ΔU = Q – W, states that the change in internal energy U of a closed system equals heat Q added to the system minus work W done by the system. Sign conventions vary; in physics W is work done by the system, while in chemistry it is often work done on the system. The second law introduces entropy S, a measure of energy dispersal: for any spontaneous process in an isolated system ΔS ≥ 0. The Clausius inequality ∮ δQ/T ≤ 0 quantifies this for cyclic processes. The third law asserts that the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero.

Heat engines convert heat into work by operating between a hot reservoir at temperature Tₕ and a cold reservoir at T𝒸. The Carnot cycle, consisting of two isothermal and two adiabatic reversible steps, defines the maximum possible efficiency: ηCarnot = 1 – T𝒸/Tₕ (temperatures in kelvin). No real engine can exceed this limit. Practical engines (Otto, Diesel, Brayton) have lower efficiencies due to irreversibilities such as friction, finite temperature differences during heat transfer, and non‑ideal gas behaviour. Refrigerators and heat pumps are reverse heat engines; their coefficient of performance (COP) for a Carnot refrigerator is COPR = T𝒸/(Tₕ – T𝒸) and for a heat pump COPHP = Tₕ/(Tₕ – T𝒸).

Entropy change for a reversible process is ΔS = ∫ δQrev/T. For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal expansion, ΔS = nR ln(V₂/V₁). In irreversible processes the actual entropy increase is larger than ∫ δQ/T. The concept of availability (exergy) combines the first and second laws to assess the maximum useful work obtainable from a system as it comes to equilibrium with the environment.

Common exam twists include: (i) asking for the efficiency of a cycle described by a PV diagram — you must identify the heat input and work output from the area enclosed; (ii) giving a real‑engine efficiency and asking whether it violates the second law — compare with Carnot efficiency at the same reservoir temperatures; (iii) mixing units (Celsius instead of kelvin) in the Carnot formula — a frequent source of arithmetic errors.

Dimensional Analysis Check
A student writes the efficiency of a Carnot engine as η = (Tₕ – T𝒸)/Tₕ. Verify whether the expression is dimensionally consistent.
Both numerator and denominator are temperatures, so their ratio is dimensionless. Efficiency is defined as a pure number (or percentage), therefore the expression is dimensionally correct. The same check would fail if the student wrote η = (Tₕ – T𝒸) because the result would have units of temperature.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the Carnot efficiency formula η = 1 – T𝒸/Tₕ and the COP expressions. When a question gives a claimed efficiency, instantly compute the Carnot limit using the reservoir temperatures in kelvin; any value higher than the Carnot limit is automatically impossible, allowing you to eliminate options quickly.

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure: VSEPR, Hybridisation, and Intermolecular Forces

The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) model predicts molecular geometry by minimising repulsion between electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs) around a central atom. The sequence of electron‑domain geometries for 2 to 6 domains is: linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), trigonal bipyramidal (90°/120°), and octahedral (90°). Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, so they compress adjacent bond angles; for example, water (two bonding pairs, two lone pairs) has a bent shape with an H–O–H angle of about 104.5°, less than the tetrahedral angle.

Hybridisation provides an orbital picture consistent with VSEPR geometries. sp hybridisation (one s + one p) yields two linear orbitals (e.g., BeCl₂). sp² (one s + two p) gives three trigonal planar orbitals (e.g., BF₃). sp³ (one s + three p) forms four tetrahedral orbitals (e.g., CH₄). For five domains, sp³d (one s + three p + one d) produces trigonal bipyramidal orbitals (e.g., PCl₅). Six domains use sp³d² (one s + three p + two d) for octahedral geometry (e.g., SF₆). The number of hybrid orbitals always equals the number of electron domains.

Intermolecular forces (IMFs) govern physical properties such as boiling point, viscosity, and solubility. The weakest are London dispersion forces, present in all molecules, arising from instantaneous dipoles; their magnitude increases with polarisability (larger electron clouds). Dipole‑dipole forces act between permanent dipoles (e.g., HCl). Hydrogen bonding is a special, strong dipole‑dipole interaction occurring when hydrogen is covalently bonded to N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F. It explains the anomalously high boiling points of water, ammonia, and hydrogen fluoride.

Relative strength order: hydrogen bonding > dipole‑dipole > London dispersion. However, for large non‑polar molecules (e.g., I₂) dispersion forces can outweigh dipole‑dipole forces in small polar molecules. This nuance appears in questions comparing boiling points of isomers: n‑pentane (linear, larger surface area) boils higher than neopentane (spherical) despite both being non‑polar. Solubility follows “like dissolves like”: polar solvents dissolve polar/ionic solutes via ion‑dipole or hydrogen‑bonding interactions; non‑polar solvents dissolve non‑polar solutes via dispersion forces.

Electrochemistry: Redox Reactions, Electrochemical Cells, and Applications

Redox (reduction‑oxidation) reactions involve electron transfer. Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number), reduction is gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). The half‑reaction method balances redox equations in acidic or basic media: separate into oxidation and reduction half‑reactions, balance atoms other than O and H, balance O with H₂O, balance H with H⁺ (acidic) or H₂O/OH⁻ (basic), balance charge with electrons, equalise electron count, and add half‑reactions. The oxidising agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidised.

A galvanic (voltaic) cell converts spontaneous redox energy into electrical work. The anode is the site of oxidation (negative electrode), the cathode the site of reduction (positive electrode). Cell notation writes the anode on the left, cathode on the right, with phase boundaries indicated by a single vertical line and a salt bridge by a double line, e.g., Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s). The standard cell potential E°cell = E°cathode – E°anode. The Nernst equation relates the instantaneous cell potential to reaction quotient Q: E = E° – (RT/nF) ln Q. At 298 K, RT/F ≈ 0.0257 V, so E = E° – (0.0591/n) log₁₀ Q.

Standard electrode potentials are tabulated relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, defined as 0 V). A more positive reduction potential indicates a stronger oxidising agent. The electrochemical series predicts spontaneity: a redox reaction is spontaneous if E°cell > 0. Electrolytic cells drive non‑spontaneous reactions using external voltage; the minimum voltage required is the decomposition potential, slightly higher than the thermodynamic E°cell due to overpotential.

Faraday’s laws quantify electrolysis: (1) mass of substance liberated is proportional to charge passed (m = ZIt, where Z is electrochemical equivalent); (2) masses liberated by the same charge are proportional to their equivalent weights. Applications include rechargeable batteries (lead‑acid: PbO₂ + Pb + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; lithium‑ion: LiCoO₂ + C₆ ⇌ LiC₆ + CoO₂), corrosion (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ at anode, O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ at cathode), and electroplating (e.g., Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) on cathode).

Optics: Wave‑Particle Duality, Interference, Diffraction, and Polarisation

Light exhibits both wave and particle characteristics. The photon energy is E = hν = hc/λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The de Broglie wavelength for matter is λ = h/p, but for light the wave description suffices for interference and diffraction phenomena.

Young’s double‑slit experiment produces bright fringes where the path difference equals an integer multiple of the wavelength: d sinθ = mλ (m = 0, ±1, ±2…). For small angles, fringe width on a screen at distance D is β = λD/d. Coherence (constant phase relationship) and monochromaticity are essential; white light yields coloured fringes with a central white maximum.

Single‑slit diffraction minima occur at a sinθ = mλ (m = ±1, ±2…), where a is slit width. The central maximum is twice as wide as the secondary maxima. The intensity distribution follows I(θ) = I₀ (sinα/α)² with α = (πa sinθ)/λ. A diffraction grating with N slits produces principal maxima at the same angles as double‑slit but with much sharper peaks; the resolving power is R = mN.

Polarisation restricts the electric‑field vector to a single plane. Unpolarised light passing through a polariser emerges with intensity I = I₀/2. For a second polariser (analyser) at angle θ to the first, Malus’s law gives I = I₀ cos²θ. Brewster’s angle θB satisfies tanθB = n₂/n₁; at this angle reflected light is perfectly s‑polarised. Applications include polarising sunglasses (reduce glare), LCDs (twisted nematic cells rotate polarisation), and optical activity measurements (sugar solutions rotate plane of polarisation).

  • Confusing the sign convention in the first law (ΔU = Q – W vs ΔU = Q + W) leads to incorrect efficiency calculations.
  • Applying Bernoulli’s equation to compressible or viscous flows without correction factors.
  • Using Celsius temperatures in the Carnot efficiency formula instead of kelvin.
  • Misidentifying the anode and cathode in electrolytic versus galvanic cells.
  • Forgetting that lone pairs compress bond angles more than bonding pairs in VSEPR predictions.
  • Treating hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond rather than a strong intermolecular force.
  • Remember to review these traps before the exam.

hand/subfactor-theory.html:
The Standard Invariant and Its Reconstruction Theorems

The standard invariant of a subfactor N ⊂ M is the lattice of relative commutants N′ ∩ Mk together with the inclusion maps and the trace‑preserving conditional expectations. It can be packaged as a planar algebra, a C*-tensor category of N–N, N–M, M–N, and M–M bimodules, or as a λ‑lattice in the sense of Popa. The fundamental reconstruction theorem of Popa (1995) states that a finite‑depth subfactor is completely determined by its standard invariant up to isomorphism. Later, Guionnet, Jones, and Shlyakhtenko (2010) proved that every subfactor planar algebra arises from a subfactor of the hyperfinite II1 factor, establishing a bijective correspondence between subfactor planar algebras and subfactors of the hyperfinite II1 factor. This means that the combinatorial data of a planar algebra — the vector spaces Pk,± and the action of planar tangles — encodes the entire analytic structure of the inclusion. The reconstruction proceeds by first building a tower of finite‑dimensional algebras from the planar algebra, then taking the GNS completion with respect to the canonical trace, and finally verifying that the resulting inclusion has the prescribed standard invariant. The theorem also clarifies why exotic subfactors such as the Haagerup subfactor can exist: they correspond to planar algebras that do not come from any known group or quantum group construction, yet satisfy all axioms.

Key Steps in the Reconstruction

  1. From the planar algebra P construct the sequence of finite‑dimensional algebras Ak = Pk,+ with multiplication given by the tangle that connects two internal disks.
  2. Define a trace on each Ak using the spherical structure of the planar algebra (the “closing” tangle).
  3. Form the inductive limit A = ∪k Ak and complete in the GNS Hilbert space to obtain a II1 factor M.
  4. Identify the subfactor N as the relative commutant of the first step; the inclusion N ⊂ M then has standard invariant isomorphic to P.

The reconstruction is functorial: a morphism of planar algebras induces an isomorphism of the corresponding subfactors. This categorical equivalence is the backbone of modern classification programmes, because it reduces analytic problems to combinatorial ones that can be tackled with computer‑assisted enumeration of planar algebras.

Bimodule Categories and Fusion Rules of Subfactors

The standard invariant can be equivalently described as a unitary fusion category generated by the N–M bimodule X = NL2(M)M. The tensor product of bimodules corresponds to Connes fusion, and the decomposition of tensor powers X ⊗N X ⊗M … into irreducible bimodules yields the fusion rules. The principal graph of the subfactor is precisely the Bratteli diagram of the inclusion of the even part of the tower, and its vertices label the simple objects in the fusion category. The Frobenius‑Perron dimension of the category equals the Jones index [M:N]. For index < 4 the fusion category is known to be the representation category of a quantum group at a root of unity (e.g. SU(2)q with q = eπi/(k+2)), and the fusion rules coincide with the Verlinde formulas of the associated conformal field theory. At index ≥ 4 the category can be non‑modular, and exotic fusion categories such as the Haagerup category appear. The Ocneanu compactness theorem guarantees that for a fixed principal graph there are only finitely many inequivalent fusion categories, which makes a systematic classification possible. The pentagon and hexagon equations for the associator and braiding in the bimodule category translate into polynomial equations for the 6j‑symbols; solving these equations is the core of the “connection” approach to subfactor classification.

Fusion Rules for the Jones–Wenzl Subfactors

For the subfactor coming from quantum SU(2) at level k, the simple bimodules are labelled by spins j = 0, ½, 1, …, k/2. The fusion rule is j₁ ⊗ j₂ = ⊕|j₁−j₂| ≤ j ≤ min(j₁+j₂, k−j₁−j₂) j. The principal graph is the Ak+1 Dynkin diagram, and the index is 4 cos²(π/(k+2)). The same fusion rules appear in the SU(2)k Wess–Zumino–Witten model, illustrating the deep link between subfactors and rational conformal field theory.

Technique: Computing the Principal Graph from the Standard Invariant
Given a subfactor planar algebra with P0,+ = ℂ, P1,+ = ℂ, P2,+ of dimension 2, and the multiplication tangle yielding a commutative algebra with minimal projections e₁, e₂ satisfying e₁e₂ = 0, e₁ + e₂ = 1, and trace(e₁) = trace(e₂) = ½, determine the principal graph up to depth 2.
The even part at depth 2 is P2,+ ≅ ℂ ⊕ ℂ. The inclusion P1,+ ⊂ P2,+ sends 1 to (1,1). The Bratteli diagram has one vertex at level 0 (the trivial bimodule), one vertex at level 1 (the generating N–M bimodule), and two vertices at level 2 corresponding to the two minimal central projections. Edges are given by the multiplicities of the inclusion: each level‑1 vertex connects to both level‑2 vertices with multiplicity 1. Hence the principal graph up to depth 2 is a “V” shape: a single edge from level 0 to level 1, then two edges from level 1 to two distinct vertices at level 2. This matches the A₃ Dynkin diagram, confirming index = 4 cos²(π/4) = 2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the principal graph from algebraic data, first identify the dimensions of the relative commutants Pk,+. The number of minimal central projections at each depth equals the number of vertices at that level. Use the inclusion map to read off edge multiplicities. Remember that the index is the square of the Frobenius‑Perron eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix; for small graphs you can compute it directly.

The Temperley–Lieb Algebra and Index Quantization

The Temperley–Lieb algebra TLn(δ) is generated by idempotents e₁,…,en−1 satisfying ei² = δ ei, eiei±1ei = ei, and eiej = ejei for |i−j| > 1. In the Jones basic construction, the Jones projection eN generates a copy of TL∞(δ) with δ = [M:N]⁻¹ᐟ². The representation theory of TLn(δ) controls the structure of the relative commutants: N′ ∩ Mk is isomorphic to the centralizer algebra of the TL action on the k‑th tensor power of the fundamental bimodule. When δ = 2 cos(π/n) with integer n ≥ 3, the Temperley–Lieb algebra is semisimple and its irreducible representations are labelled by the Jones–Wenzl projectors. The quantization of the index follows from the requirement that the Markov trace on TL be positive definite; this forces δ ≥ 2 or δ = 2 cos(π/n). The case δ = 2 corresponds to index = 4, the threshold where the principal graph becomes affine Ã∞. For δ > 2 the index is > 4 and the principal graph can be any bipartite graph with norm ≤ δ. The Temperley–Lieb picture also explains the appearance of the ADE classification at index < 4: the only bipartite graphs with norm < 2 are the simply‑laced Dynkin diagrams A, D, E. This diagrammatic approach underlies the original proof of Jones’ index theorem and remains the most accessible route to the quantization result.

Jones–Wenzl Projectors

The Jones–Wenzl projector f(k) ∈ TLk(δ) is the unique idempotent that annihilates all ei and has trace equal to the quantum dimension [k+1]q where q + q⁻¹ = δ. These projectors categorify the fusion rules of SU(2)q and appear as the minimal central projections in the relative commutants. Their recursive definition f(k) = f(k−1) − ( [k−1]q / [k]q ) f(k−1) ek−1 f(k−1) is a standard tool in computations of the standard invariant.

Exotic Subfactors Beyond Haagerup: Extended Haagerup, Asaeda–Haagerup, and the 2221 Subfactor

After the Haagerup subfactor (index (5+√13)/2 ≈ 4.302, principal graph with three‑fold symmetry), the next exotic examples were discovered by extending the classification programme to higher indices. The extended Haagerup subfactor, constructed by Grossman, Jones, and Peters (2011), has index (5+√17)/2 ≈ 4.562 and a principal graph with a 4‑valent vertex and a 2‑valent tail. Its planar algebra was obtained by solving the pentagon equations for a fusion category with the same fusion rules as the Haagerup category but with a different associator. The Asaeda–Haagerup subfactor (index ≈ 4.377) and its dual have principal graphs that are mirror images; they were found by a computer‑assisted search of bipartite graphs with norm < √(5+√13)/2. The 2221 subfactor (index ≈ 5.048) has a principal graph shaped like a “T” with four branches of lengths 2,2,2,1. All these subfactors are finite depth, have no group‑theoretic or quantum‑group origin, and their planar algebras are not known to arise from any conformal field theory. Their existence demonstrates that the landscape of subfactors is far richer than the ADE series. Recent work by Morrison, Penneys, and others has pushed the classification up to index 5.25, revealing a handful of further exotic candidates, but a complete classification remains open. The techniques involve a blend of graph‑norm bounds, numerical solutions of the pentagon equations, and rigorous verification of positivity of the Markov trace.

Key Properties of the Extended Haagerup Subfactor

  • Index = (5+√17)/2.
  • Principal graph: a central vertex of degree 4 connected to four chains of lengths 1,1,1,2.
  • Depth = 4 (the highest relative commutant appears at M3).
  • Planar algebra dimension sequence: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, … (Catalan‑like growth).
  • No known braided tensor category realization; the fusion category is non‑modular.

Subfactors in Topological Quantum Computation and Knot Invariants

The representation of the braid group on the higher relative commutants of a subfactor yields unitary braid group representations that can be used for topological quantum computation. For the Jones–Wenzl subfactors (quantum SU(2) at root of unity), the braid group representation factors through the Temperley–Lieb algebra and coincides with the Jones polynomial evaluation at the corresponding root of unity. The anyonic model based on the Fibonacci category (the SU(2)₃ subfactor, index = (3+√5)/2 ≈ 2.618) is universal for quantum computation: braiding of Fibonacci anyons can approximate any unitary operation on the logical qubit. The Haagerup and extended Haagerup subfactors give rise to braid group representations that are not known to be universal, but they provide new knot invariants beyond the Jones polynomial. The planar algebra formalism makes the construction of these invariants systematic: a planar tangle with one external disk and several internal disks corresponds to a multilinear map on the standard invariant; closing the external disk yields a scalar invariant of the tangle, which can be interpreted as a knot invariant when the tangle represents a braid closure. The Ocneanu trace on the planar algebra provides the Markov trace needed for invariance under Reidemeister moves. Recent work by Freedman, Larsen, and Wang shows that any unitary modular tensor category arising from a subfactor yields a topological quantum field theory in 2+1 dimensions, and the associated anyon model can be simulated by a quantum computer. This circle of ideas — subfactors → planar algebras → braid group representations → knot invariants → topological quantum computation — is a vibrant research frontier that connects operator algebras, low‑dimensional topology, and quantum information.

Fibonacci Anyons from the SU(2)₃ Subfactor

The SU(2)₃ subfactor has principal graph A₄, index = φ² where φ = (1+√5)/2. Its fusion category has two simple objects: the trivial object 1 and the Fibonacci anyon τ with fusion rule τ ⊗ τ = 1 ⊕ τ. The braiding eigenvalues are e±4πi/5. The resulting braid group representation on τ⊗n is dense in the unitary group of the fusion space, establishing universality. The Jones polynomial at q = e2πi/5 evaluates to the Fibonacci trace, providing a concrete link between the subfactor index and a computable knot invariant.

  • Confusing the standard invariant with the principal graph alone; the standard invariant includes the full planar algebra structure, not just the graph.
  • Assuming all subfactors of index < 4 come from quantum groups; the Haagerup subfactor is a counterexample at index ≈ 4.302 > 4, but there are also exotic subfactors at index < 4 that are not quantum group subfactors (none known, but the statement must be qualified).
  • Misapplying the Jones index formula [M:N] = δ⁻² without checking that δ is the loop parameter of the Temperley–Lieb algebra in the basic construction.
  • Treating the Jones–Wenzl projectors as ordinary projections in the von Neumann algebra; they live in the relative commutants and are only idempotents in the planar algebra sense.
  • Overlooking the role of the spherical structure in the reconstruction theorem; without sphericity the trace on the planar algebra does not match the canonical trace on the reconstructed factor.
  • Believing that every finite‑depth subfactor yields a modular tensor category; only those with a braiding that satisfies the modularity condition (non‑degenerate S‑matrix) do.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the even and odd parts of the planar algebra; the odd part Pk,− encodes the N–M bimodules and is essential for the full standard invariant.

The advanced sections above complete the deep dive into subfactor theory beyond the introductory material.

hand/combinatorial-game-theory.html:
Misère Play and the Theory of Misère Quotients

In normal play the player who makes the last move wins; in misère play the player who makes the last move loses. This simple reversal dramatically changes the algebraic structure of impartial games. Bouton’s 1901 solution for misère Nim shows that the P‑positions are exactly those where every heap has size one and the number of heaps is odd, or where at least one heap exceeds one and the Nim‑sum (xor) of all heap sizes is zero. For general impartial games the Sprague‑Grundy theory no longer applies directly because the mex rule assumes normal play.

The modern framework for misère impartial games is the theory of misère quotients, developed by Plambeck and Siegel in the early 2000s. A misère quotient is a finite commutative monoid equipped with a distinguished subset of “P‑elements” that captures the misère equivalence classes of a given game. Two positions are misère equivalent if they have the same outcome when added to any other position from the same game. The quotient construction replaces the infinite set of Grundy values with a finite algebraic object, making it possible to compute misère outcomes for many games that are intractable under normal‑play analysis.

A game is called tame if its misère quotient is a group; otherwise it is wild. Nim is tame: its misère quotient is the two‑element group {0,1} with 1+1=0, reflecting the parity of heaps larger than one. Dawson’s Kayles, by contrast, is wild; its misère quotient has order 34 and exhibits a periodic structure that was only uncovered with extensive computer search. The distinction between tame and wild games explains why some misère games admit simple closed forms while others require case‑by‑case analysis.

The quotient method also extends to partizan misère play, where Left and Right have different options. In that setting the outcome classes are four: L (Left wins regardless of who starts), R (Right wins regardless), N (next player wins), and P (previous player wins). The misère quotient becomes a monoid with a designated subset of P‑elements, and the same algebraic machinery applies. Recent work by Siegel and others has produced misère quotients for several partizan games, including certain Hackenbush strings and Domineering boards.

From an examiner’s perspective, the key points are: (1) misère Nim is not solved by the normal‑play xor rule; (2) the misère quotient provides a uniform algebraic language for all impartial misère games; (3) tame games have group quotients, wild games do not; (4) the quotient of Dawson’s Kayles has order 34 and period 34, a classic result that often appears in advanced problem sets.

Loopy Games and the Etheridge–Siegel Theory

Standard combinatorial game theory assumes that every game terminates; the game graph is well‑founded. Many natural games, however, contain cycles. The most famous example is the ko rule in Go, where a capture can be immediately recaptured, creating a potential infinite loop. Other examples include certain positions in Chess (threefold repetition) and the game of Geography on directed graphs.

Etheridge’s 1990s work introduced a rigorous framework for loopy games by assigning each position a value in an extended surreal‑like structure that includes “loopy” infinitesimals. The central idea is to treat a cycle as a game that can be “unrolled” a finite number of times, with the players’ preferences encoded by a temperature parameter. Siegel later refined this into a general theory of loopy games using the concept of a “thermograph” for cyclic positions. The cooling operator G_t = {G^L_t − t | G^R_t + t} still applies, but the thermograph may now contain horizontal segments that correspond to the temperature at which the cycle becomes inactive.

A crucial result is the “loopy thermograph theorem”: for any finite loopy game, the thermograph stabilises after a finite tax t, and the mean value m(G) is well defined. The mean represents the long‑term average gain per move when the cycle is played repeatedly. In Go endgame theory, this mean corresponds to the “miai value” of a ko threat. The theory also yields a notion of “atomic weight” for loopy infinitesimals, extending the atomic weight theory of all‑small games.

Practical computation of loopy game values often uses the “Norton multiplication” to scale a game by a positive integer n, effectively playing n copies in parallel. This allows the analysis of large cyclic positions by reducing them to a sum of simpler components. The combination of cooling, thermographs, and Norton multiplication forms the algorithmic backbone of modern Go endgame engines.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between well‑founded and loopy games, the definition of the cooling operator for cyclic positions, and the interpretation of the thermograph’s horizontal segments. A typical trap is to assume that the Sprague‑Grundy theorem applies to loopy impartial games; it does not, because the mex definition requires a well‑founded option set.

Worked Example: Misère Quotient of a Small Impartial Game
Consider the impartial game G where a move consists of removing either 1 or 2 tokens from a single heap. Heaps of size 0 are terminal. Determine the misère quotient of G for heap sizes up to 4.

Step 1: List positions. Heap sizes: 0,1,2,3,4. In misère play, the player who takes the last token loses.

Step 2: Compute outcome classes (N/P) for each heap size by exhaustive analysis.

  • Size 0: no moves → previous player wins → P.
  • Size 1: only move to 0 (P) → next player wins → N.
  • Size 2: moves to 1 (N) or 0 (P). Moving to 0 gives opponent a P position, so current player can force a win? Wait: if you move to 0, you took the last token and lose immediately. In misère, moving to 0 is a losing move. So the only legal move that does not lose immediately is to 1. Since 1 is N, the opponent wins. Thus size 2 is P.
  • Size 3: moves to 2 (P) or 1 (N). Moving to 2 gives opponent a P position, so you win. Thus size 3 is N.
  • Size 4: moves to 3 (N) or 2 (P). Moving to 2 gives opponent P, so you win. Thus size 4 is N.

Step 3: Build the misère quotient monoid. The equivalence classes are determined by the outcome of sums. Compute sums of heaps up to size 4. The distinct misère equivalence classes are represented by the outcomes of single heaps: [0] (P), [1] (N), [2] (P), [3] (N), [4] (N). However, [0] and [2] are both P but may behave differently in sums. Check sum [1]+[1]: two heaps of size 1. Moves: reduce one heap to 0 (lose immediately) or reduce to 0? Actually from size 1 you can only move to 0, which loses. So any move from [1]+[1] loses immediately, so the position is P. Thus [1]+[1] = [0] in the quotient. Similarly [1]+[2]: heap 1 (N) and heap 2 (P). The only safe move from heap 1 is to 0 (lose), from heap 2 you can move to 1 (N) or 0 (lose). Moving heap 2 to 1 yields [1]+[1] which is P, so the player who moves wins. Hence [1]+[2] is N. Continuing this process yields a monoid of order 4: elements {a,b,c,d} with addition table reflecting the outcomes. The misère quotient is the four‑element monoid where a is the identity (P class of empty heap), b = [1], c = [2], d = [3] = [4]. The P‑elements are {a,c}. This quotient is not a group (b+b=a but c+c≠a), so the game is wild.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a misère analysis, first check whether the game is a known tame game (Nim, certain subtraction games). If it is tame, recall the group structure of its misère quotient; if wild, look for a small finite quotient that can be computed by hand. For loopy games, identify the cycle and apply the cooling operator symbolically; the thermograph’s horizontal segment indicates the temperature at which the cycle becomes dormant. Always distinguish normal‑play mex from misère outcome classes.

Atomic Weights and the Structure of Infinitesimals

Infinitesimal games are those that are positive but smaller than any positive number, or negative but larger than any negative number. The simplest infinitesimal is ∗ = {0|0}, a first‑player win in normal play. Conway introduced the “up” game ↑ = {0|∗} and its negative ↓ = {∗|0}. These games are not numbers because their left option is not strictly less than their right option; they are “hot” in the sense that the first player gains an advantage by moving.

The atomic weight of an infinitesimal, denoted aw(G), measures how many “up” moves are needed to balance the game. Formally, for an all‑small game G (every option is also all‑small), the atomic weight is the integer n such that G is equivalent to n·↑ plus a game of atomic weight zero. The atomic weight theorem states that for all‑small games, the outcome of a sum is determined by the sum of atomic weights: if the total atomic weight is positive, Left wins; if negative, Right wins; if zero, the outcome depends on the “remainder” infinitesimals of atomic weight zero.

Key examples: aw(∗) = 0, aw(↑) = 1, aw(↑↑) = 2, aw(↑+∗) = 1 (since ∗ has weight 0). The game tiny = ↑+∗ has atomic weight 1 but is not equal to ↑; it is a distinct infinitesimal that appears in Domineering and Hackenbush. The game miny = ↓+∗ has atomic weight −1. The set of infinitesimals of atomic weight zero forms a group under addition, known as the “infinitesimal group”. This group contains ∗, ↑+↓, and many other games that are “confused” with zero in the sense of the ordering but not equal to zero.

The theory of atomic weights extends to “hot” games that are not all‑small via the concept of “temperature”. A game with temperature t > 0 can be cooled to a game of lower temperature; the atomic weight of the cooled game gives information about the urgency of moves. In Go endgame analysis, the atomic weight of a ko threat corresponds to the number of free moves a player can make before the ko must be resolved.

Examiners often ask for the atomic weight of a given Hackenbush string or a sum of infinitesimals. The standard technique: reduce each component to its canonical form using the simplicity rule, then count the number of ↑ moves. A common trap is to confuse atomic weight with the “mean” of a game; the mean is a real number (or surreal) representing long‑term value, while atomic weight is an integer measuring the leading infinitesimal term.

Algorithmic Complexity and Outcome Classes

Determining the outcome of a combinatorial game under optimal play is a central computational problem. For impartial games given by a set of moves (e.g., subtraction games), the Grundy numbers can be computed in polynomial time using dynamic programming. However, for partizan games represented as game trees, the problem is PSPACE‑complete. This result, due to Fraenkel, Lichtenstein, and others, holds even for very restricted classes such as Geography on directed graphs or certain Hackenbush positions.

The four outcome classes for partizan games are L (Left wins regardless of who starts), R (Right wins regardless), N (next player wins), and P (previous player wins). For impartial games only N and P occur. The outcome class of a sum G+H can be deduced from the outcome classes of G and H using the “outcome matrix”. For example, N+N = N, N+P = N, P+P = P, L+R = N, L+L = L, etc. This matrix is the basis for the “disjunctive sum” algebra used in combinatorial game theory.

For specific games, the complexity varies. Nim is in P (xor computation). Dawson’s Kayles has a periodic Grundy sequence of period 34, so its outcome can be decided in constant time after precomputation. Domineering on rectangular boards is PSPACE‑complete in general, but for fixed width the problem is in P. Hackenbush on trees reduces to evaluating surreal numbers, which can be done in polynomial time using the colon principle. However, Hackenbush on general graphs is PSPACE‑complete.

Misère play adds another layer of complexity. Computing the misère quotient of a game is often harder than the normal‑play analysis; for many games the quotient is not known to be computable in polynomial time. The “taming” theory shows that for tame games the misère quotient is a group and can be found by solving a system of equations over the group, which is often tractable.

In examinations, typical questions ask: (1) Given a small game tree, compute its outcome class. (2) Prove that a game is PSPACE‑complete by reduction from a known hard game. (3) Use the outcome matrix to determine the class of a sum. The key is to recognise the representation of the game (explicit tree vs. succinct description) because complexity classes refer to the input size.

The Colon Principle and Hackenbush Evaluation

Hackenbush is a partizan game played on a rooted graph with edges coloured Blue (Left), Red (Right), or Green (either). The value of a Hackenbush position is a surreal number when the graph is a tree (no cycles). The colon principle, discovered by Conway, provides a direct method to compute the value of a Hackenbush string (a path) by reading the colours as binary digits.

For a string of edges attached to the ground, assign 1 to a Blue edge and 0 to a Red edge, reading from the ground upward. The resulting binary fraction (with the first edge as the most significant bit) gives a dyadic rational. The value of the string is the simplest number between the values of its left and right options, which coincides with the binary interpretation. For example, a single Blue edge has value 1 = {0|}; a Blue edge above a Red edge gives the string “10” which equals 1/2 = {0|1}. A string “110” equals 3/4, and so on. Green edges are treated as both Blue and Red, contributing a ∗ (star) component; a Green string reduces to an impartial game whose Grundy number is the xor of the Grundy numbers of its branches.

The fusion principle extends the colon principle to arbitrary trees: any Hackenbush tree can be simplified by “fusing” vertices that are connected by a single edge of a given colour, without changing the game’s value. This allows the reduction of complex trees to a sum of strings, each evaluated by the colon principle. The overall value is the surreal sum of the string values.

For graphs with cycles (loopy Hackenbush), the value may be a loopy game requiring thermography. The Norton multiplication can be used to analyse multiple copies of a cyclic component. In Go, the colon principle underlies the evaluation of “corridor” endgames, where a linear sequence of empty points corresponds to a Hackenbush string of alternating colours.

Examiners frequently test the colon principle by giving a coloured string and asking for its surreal value. The steps: write the binary sequence, convert to a dyadic rational, then apply the simplicity rule if the string is not a simple binary fraction (e.g., when the string ends with a Green edge). A common error is to treat Green edges as 1/2 instead of as an impartial ∗ component; the correct treatment is to separate the Green part and compute its Grundy value independently.

Common Traps

  • Assuming the Sprague‑Grundy theorem applies to misère or loopy games; it only applies to well‑founded impartial games under normal play.
  • Confusing atomic weight with mean value; atomic weight is an integer counting leading infinitesimal terms, while mean is a surreal number representing long‑term average gain.
  • Treating Green Hackenbush edges as numeric 1/2 instead of as impartial ∗ components; Green edges contribute to the Grundy value, not to the surreal value.
  • Believing that every partizan game has a numeric value; only cold games (where all left options are less than all right options) are numbers.
  • Using the normal‑play outcome matrix for misère sums; the misère outcome classes follow a different algebra captured by the misère quotient.
  • Overlooking the distinction between tame and wild misère games; wild games do not have group quotients and cannot be analysed by simple parity arguments.
  • Assuming PSPACE‑completeness results apply to all representations; some games are polynomial when the board width is fixed or the game tree is given explicitly.

Mastering these advanced topics requires careful attention to the algebraic structures that underlie each variant of play.

hand/tropical-geometry.html:
Tropical Intersection Theory and the Balanced Condition

Tropical intersection theory, developed by Allermann and Rau and later refined by Katz, provides a rigorous framework for intersecting tropical cycles inside a tropical variety. A tropical cycle is a weighted rational polyhedral complex satisfying the balancing condition at every codimension‑one face: the sum of the primitive integer normal vectors of the adjacent maximal cells, each multiplied by its weight, equals zero. This condition is the tropical analogue of the algebraic fact that the divisor of a rational function has degree zero. The intersection product of two tropical cycles of complementary dimension is defined by first refining the polyhedral structures so that the cycles intersect transversely, then assigning to each intersection point a multiplicity equal to the absolute value of the determinant of the lattice generated by the direction vectors of the intersecting cells. The resulting zero‑cycle is independent of the refinement, yielding a well‑defined intersection number. The tropical Bézout theorem follows immediately: two tropical plane curves of degrees d₁ and d₂ intersect in exactly d₁·d₂ points counted with these multiplicities. This theorem mirrors the classical Bézout theorem but is proved by a purely combinatorial argument using the Newton polygons of the defining tropical polynomials. The balancing condition also guarantees that tropical cycles form a ring under the intersection product, and the projection formula holds for morphisms of tropical varieties. These results allow one to compute Gromov‑Witten invariants of toric surfaces by counting tropical curves with prescribed incidence conditions, because Mikhalkin’s correspondence theorem identifies the tropical counts with the corresponding algebraic invariants.

Tropical Moduli Spaces and the Boundary of M_g

The moduli space of tropical curves M_gtrop is a generalized cone complex whose cones correspond to combinatorial types of stable metric graphs of genus g. A point in a cone represents a graph with fixed topology and positive edge lengths; the faces of the cone are obtained by collapsing edges of length zero, which corresponds to the formation of nodes in the algebraic setting. The space M_gtrop is connected, rational polyhedral, and of pure dimension 3g−3 for g≥2. Its natural compactification adds boundary strata indexed by stable graphs, exactly mirroring the Deligne‑Mumford compactification M̅_g of the moduli space of algebraic curves. The tropical Torelli map sends a metric graph to its Jacobian, a principally polarized tropical abelian variety, and this map is a morphism of cone complexes. The image of M_gtrop under the Torelli map is the tropical Schottky locus, a proper subcone complex of the moduli space of tropical principally polarized abelian varieties A_gtrop. The combinatorial structure of M_gtrop has been used to compute the rational cohomology of M_g and to prove that the tautological ring of M_g is generated by kappa classes. Moreover, the tropical boundary strata provide a concrete description of the limit mixed Hodge structures on the cohomology of degenerating families of curves, linking tropical geometry to the weight filtration in Hodge theory.

Worked Example: Computing a Tropical Intersection Multiplicity
Let C₁ be the tropical line defined by min(x, y, 0) and C₂ the tropical conic defined by min(2x, 2y, x+y, 0). Determine the intersection points of C₁ and C₂ in ℝ² and compute the multiplicity at each point.
The tropical line C₁ consists of three rays: x = y ≤ 0, x = 0 ≤ y, and y = 0 ≤ x, meeting at the vertex (0,0). The tropical conic C₂ has Newton polygon with vertices (2,0), (0,2), (1,1), (0,0). Its corner locus is a balanced graph with four unbounded rays in directions (−1,0), (0,−1), (1,−1), (−1,1) and a bounded edge connecting the vertices (−1,0) and (0,−1) after appropriate translation. By drawing both curves one finds three intersection points: (0,0), (−1,0), and (0,−1). At (0,0) the line has direction vectors (1,0) and (0,1); the conic has direction vectors (−1,0) and (0,−1). The lattice generated by (1,0) and (0,1) has determinant 1, so multiplicity = 1. At (−1,0) the line direction is (1,0) (the ray x=0) and the conic direction is (−1,0) (the ray (−1,0)). The two vectors are opposite, generating a lattice of index 1, multiplicity = 1. Similarly at (0,−1) multiplicity = 1. The sum of multiplicities is 3, which equals the product of degrees 1·2 = 2? Wait, the tropical Bézout theorem states the total intersection number equals d₁·d₂ = 2. The discrepancy arises because the conic as written has degree 2 but its Newton polygon contains the interior lattice point (1,1), giving genus 1; the tropical Bézout theorem for curves of genera g₁,g₂ requires counting with multiplicities that sum to d₁·d₂. Re‑examining the conic: the correct tropical conic of degree 2 has Newton polygon with vertices (2,0),(0,2),(0,0) and no interior points, giving a rational curve. Its corner locus has three unbounded rays and one bounded edge. Intersecting with the line yields exactly two points each of multiplicity 1, total 2, matching Bézout. The earlier conic included an extra term x+y which raises the degree. Thus the correct intersection count is 2.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for tropical intersection numbers, first write down the Newton polygons of the defining tropical polynomials. The mixed volume of the Newton polygons equals the total intersection number (Bernstein‑Kushnirenko theorem). Use this as a quick check: if your point‑by‑point multiplicities do not sum to the mixed volume, you have missed an intersection point or miscomputed a multiplicity.

Tropical Hodge Theory for Matroids and the Adiprasito‑Huh‑Katz Theorem

In 2018 Adiprasito, Huh, and Katz proved the Hodge‑Riemann relations for the Chow ring of a matroid, thereby establishing the long‑standing Rota‑Heron‑Welsh conjecture on the log‑concavity of the characteristic polynomial. The proof constructs a tropical Hodge theory on the Bergman fan of a matroid, which is the tropicalization of the linear subspace defined by the matroid over a valued field. The Chow ring A^*(M) of a matroid M is generated by variables x_F for each non‑empty proper flat F, subject to linear relations ∑F∋i x_F = ∑F∋j x_F for all i,j and quadratic relations x_F x_G = 0 when F and G are incomparable. The degree map sends the top‑degree monomial corresponding to a maximal chain of flats to 1. The key step is to define a strictly convex piecewise‑linear function on the Bergman fan, which serves as an ample class ℓ. One then verifies the hard Lefschetz property: multiplication by ℓd−k gives an isomorphism A^k(M) → Ad−k(M), and the Hodge‑Riemann bilinear form (−1)^k ℓd−2k is positive definite on the primitive subspace. The tropical proof uses the fact that the Bergman fan is a rational polyhedral fan satisfying the balancing condition, and the convex function is obtained by pulling back a strictly convex function on the tropical projective space. This machinery has since been extended to valuated matroids and to the tropical Hodge theory of arbitrary tropical varieties, providing a combinatorial framework for Hodge theory that does not require complex geometry.

Tropical Mirror Symmetry: SYZ Fibrations and Tropical Calabi‑Yau

Mirror symmetry predicts an equivalence between the symplectic geometry of a Calabi‑Yau manifold X and the complex geometry of its mirror X̂. The Strominger‑Yau‑Zaslow (SYZ) conjecture proposes that this equivalence is realized by dual torus fibrations: X and X̂ admit special Lagrangian torus fibrations over the same base B, with generic fibers dual tori. In the tropical limit, the base B becomes an integral affine manifold with singularities, and the fibrations are replaced by their tropicalizations. The tropical manifold Trop(X) is a polyhedral complex equipped with an integral affine structure away from a codimension‑two discriminant locus. The mirror tropical manifold Trop(X̂) is obtained by taking the fiberwise dual of the torus fibration, which at the tropical level corresponds to the Legendre transform of the affine structure. Gross and Siebert developed a program to reconstruct the mirror pair from a tropical manifold with a polarization, using scattering diagrams to correct the affine structure across walls. The tropical vertex, introduced by Kontsevich and Soibelman, encodes the wall‑crossing automorphisms that ensure the consistency of the scattering diagram. For toric Calabi‑Yau threefolds, the tropical mirror is described by a consistent scattering diagram on ℝ² whose walls are tropical curves counted by open Gromov‑Witten invariants. The resulting tropical geometry computes the generating functions of both closed and open Gromov‑Witten invariants, providing a combinatorial algorithm for mirror symmetry that has been verified in numerous examples, including the resolved conifold and local ℙ².

Tropicalization of Cluster Algebras and the Fock‑Goncharov Conjecture

Cluster algebras, introduced by Fomin and Zelevinsky, are commutative algebras generated by clusters of variables related by mutations. Fock and Goncharov associated to each cluster variety a tropical space, the tropicalization of the cluster variety, which carries a natural piecewise‑linear structure. The tropical points of a cluster variety correspond to valuations on the field of rational functions that are compatible with the cluster structure. The Fock‑Goncharov conjecture asserts that the tropical points of a cluster variety are in bijection with the set of generic bases of the associated upper cluster algebra, and that the tropicalization map induces an isomorphism between the tropical variety and the space of valuations. This conjecture has been proved for cluster varieties arising from surfaces (by Goncharov and Shen) and for acyclic cluster algebras (by Gross, Hacking, Keel, and Kontsevich). The proof uses the tropicalization of the cluster scattering diagram, which is a collection of walls in the tropical space where the cluster coordinates undergo piecewise‑linear transformations. The consistency of the scattering diagram is equivalent to the tropical version of the cluster mutation relations. The tropical cluster variety also carries a natural symplectic form, the tropicalization of the canonical Poisson structure on the cluster variety, making it a tropical symplectic manifold. This structure has applications to the study of Donaldson‑Thomas invariants, where the tropical scattering diagram computes the wall‑crossing of BPS invariants, and to the theory of higher Teichmüller spaces, where the tropical points parametrize positive representations of surface groups.

  • Confusing the tropical semiring (min‑plus) with the max‑plus convention; the sign change flips the balancing condition and intersection multiplicities.
  • Assuming every tropical curve is a planar graph; higher‑dimensional tropical varieties can have cells of dimension greater than one and are not graphs.
  • Neglecting the weight on each maximal cell when checking the balancing condition; unweighted graphs do not satisfy the tropical cycle definition.
  • Applying the classical Bézout theorem directly without using the mixed volume of Newton polygons; the tropical count equals the mixed volume, not the product of degrees unless the Newton polygons are standard simplices.
  • Overlooking the role of the discriminant locus in tropical mirror symmetry; the affine structure is singular there and the Legendre transform must be performed on each chamber separately.
  • Treating the tropical moduli space M_gtrop as a smooth manifold; it is a cone complex with non‑trivial orbifold structure at the boundary strata.
  • Forgetting that the Ronkin function is only piecewise‑linear at infinity; its strict convexity fails precisely on the spine, which is the tropical skeleton.

hand/teichmuller-dynamics.html:
Kontsevich–Zorich Cocycle and the Lyapunov Spectrum

The Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle is the linear cocycle over the Teichmüller geodesic flow obtained by the action of the mapping class group on the real first homology H₁(S, ℝ) of a translation surface (S, ω). It preserves the symplectic intersection form, so its Lyapunov exponents come in symmetric pairs λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … ≥ λ_g ≥ −λ_g ≥ … ≥ −λ₁. The top exponent λ₁ equals 1 for every ergodic SL(2, ℝ)-invariant measure, reflecting the expansion of the horizontal direction under the flow g_t = diag(e^t, e-t). The remaining exponents are strictly between −1 and 1 and encode the deviation of ergodic averages for the vertical flow. For the Masur–Veech measure on a stratum ΩM_g(κ) with zero orders κ = (k₁, …, k_m), the sum of the positive exponents is given by the Kontsevich–Zorich formula Σi=1^g λ_i = 1/12 Σj=1^m k_j(k_j+2)/(k_j+1). This formula was proved by Eskin, Kontsevich, and Zorich using the relation between Lyapunov exponents and the Siegel–Veech constant of cylinders. The individual exponents have been computed explicitly for low genus: for genus 2 the non‑trivial exponent is 1/3; for genus 3 the two positive exponents are 2/3 and 1/3 in the principal stratum, while other strata exhibit different spectra. The simplicity of the spectrum (λ₁ > λ₂ > … > λ_g > 0) was established by Avila and Viana for the Masur–Veech measure, and later extended to all ergodic SL(2, ℝ)-invariant measures by Eskin, Mirzakhani, and Mohammadi. The cocycle also governs the diffusion rate of the Zorich renormalization of interval exchange transformations, linking the Lyapunov exponents to the polynomial deviation of ergodic integrals for typical IETs.

Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi Measure Classification

The landmark theorem of Eskin, Mirzakhani, and Mohammadi (2015) classifies all ergodic SL(2, ℝ)-invariant probability measures on the moduli space of translation surfaces. The result states that any such measure is the Lebesgue measure on an affine invariant submanifold — a closed, SL(2, ℝ)-invariant subset locally cut out by linear equations in period coordinates with real coefficients. These submanifolds are complex algebraic varieties in the sense of the period mapping, and their tangent spaces are defined over ℚ. The proof combines the measure rigidity technique of Ratner for unipotent flows with the polynomial growth of the SL(2, ℝ) action on the moduli space, using the fact that the Teichmüller flow is partially hyperbolic. A key ingredient is the “magic wand” theorem, which shows that the conditional measures on unstable leaves are either atomic or Lebesgue. This classification implies that the closure of any SL(2, ℝ) orbit is a finite union of affine invariant submanifolds, and that the set of periodic SL(2, ℝ) orbits (Teichmüller curves) is dense in each such submanifold. As a corollary, the Veech dichotomy holds for every direction on almost every surface in an affine invariant submanifold, and the Lyapunov spectrum of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle is constant on each ergodic component. The theorem also provides a framework for computing Masur–Veech volumes by integrating Siegel–Veech constants over the space of invariant measures.

Worked Example: Identifying an Affine Invariant Submanifold
Consider the stratum ΩM2(1,1) of genus‑2 translation surfaces with two simple zeros. Let M be the subset of surfaces admitting an involution that exchanges the two zeros and acts as −1 on homology. Show that M is an affine invariant submanifold and determine its dimension.
The involution condition is linear in period coordinates: if the relative periods are (z₁, z₂, z₃, z₄) with Σ z_i = 0, the involution forces z₁ = −z₂ and z₃ = −z₄. These are two independent real linear equations, so the real codimension is 2. The ambient stratum has complex dimension 2g + m − 1 = 4 + 2 − 1 = 5, hence real dimension 10. Subtracting 2 gives real dimension 8, i.e. complex dimension 4. The subset is clearly SL(2, ℝ)-invariant because the involution commutes with the linear action on periods. It is closed and the equations have rational coefficients, so by the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi theorem M is an affine invariant submanifold of complex dimension 4.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the dimension of an affine invariant submanifold defined by linear constraints in period coordinates, count the number of independent real linear equations, subtract from the real dimension of the ambient stratum (2 × (2g + m − 1)), and halve to obtain the complex dimension. Remember that the equations must be defined over ℚ for the submanifold to be affine invariant.

Square‑Tiled Surfaces, Origamis, and Lattice Surfaces

A square‑tiled surface (or origami) is a translation surface obtained by gluing finitely many unit squares along their edges by translations. Equivalently, it is a branched covering π: S → 𝕋² = ℝ²/ℤ² of the standard torus, ramified only over the origin. The Veech group of a square‑tiled surface is a finite‑index subgroup of SL(2, ℤ), hence a lattice in SL(2, ℝ); therefore every square‑tiled surface is a Veech surface. The degree of the covering equals the number of squares, and the combinatorial data of the gluing can be encoded by a pair of permutations (σ_h, σ_v) in the symmetric group S_N describing the horizontal and vertical identifications. The stratum of a square‑tiled surface is determined by the cycle structure of the commutator [σ_h, σ_v]; each cycle of length k corresponds to a zero of order k−1. Counting square‑tiled surfaces of a given degree in a fixed stratum is a classical problem in enumerative geometry. Eskin and Okounkov (2001) expressed the generating function for these numbers in terms of characters of the symmetric group and the Kontsevich–Witten τ‑function, leading to the exact formula for Masur–Veech volumes. The set of square‑tiled surfaces is dense in every affine invariant submanifold, and the SL(2, ℝ) orbit of a square‑tiled surface projects to a closed Teichmüller curve in the moduli space. The Lyapunov exponents of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle on a Teichmüller curve can be computed via the decomposition of the Hodge bundle into irreducible representations of the Veech group, a method pioneered by Möller and extended by Eskin, Kontsevich, and Zorich.

Rauzy–Veech Induction, Zorich Acceleration, and Deviation of Ergodic Averages

The Rauzy–Veech induction is a renormalization operator on the space of interval exchange transformations (IETs) that records the first‑return map to a subinterval obtained by removing the rightmost subinterval of the longer of the two extremal intervals. It produces a sequence of IETs with the same permutation but rescaled lengths, and the associated matrices in SL(d, ℤ) encode the cocycle over the induction. Zorich’s acceleration groups several Rauzy steps into a single step whenever the same “winner” (top or bottom interval) occurs consecutively, yielding a faster algorithm with better convergence properties. The Zorich cocycle is the restriction of the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle to the subspace of absolute homology, and its Lyapunov exponents coincide with the non‑trivial exponents of the full cocycle. For a typical IET, the deviation of ergodic averages for a smooth observable f is governed by the Lyapunov spectrum: if λ₂ > 0 is the second exponent, then the ergodic integral ∑k=0n-1 f(T^k x) − n∫ f grows like nλ₂ for almost every x. This polynomial deviation was proved by Zorich (1997) and later refined by Forni, who gave a geometric interpretation in terms of the Hodge norm on the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle. The exponential mixing of the Teichmüller flow (Avila–Forni, 2007) implies that the Zorich induction has exponential decay of correlations, which in turn yields quantitative bounds on the speed of convergence of the Rauzy–Veech matrices to the Oseledets subspaces.

Weil–Petersson Geometry, Mirzakhani’s Recursion, and Intersection Theory

The Weil–Petersson metric on the moduli space M_g of Riemann surfaces is a Kähler metric with negative sectional curvature, incomplete but geodesically convex. Its volume form integrates to the Weil–Petersson volume Vg,n(L₁, …, L_n) of the moduli space of bordered Riemann surfaces with geodesic boundaries of lengths L_i. Mirzakhani (2007) derived a recursive formula for these volumes by integrating the McShane identity over Mg,n, expressing Vg,n in terms of volumes of lower‑genus and lower‑boundary moduli spaces. The recursion involves integrals of polynomials in the boundary lengths against the Weil–Petersson symplectic form, and its solution yields polynomials in π² with rational coefficients. For example, V1,1(L) = (π² + L²)/24. These volumes are central to Mirzakhani’s proof that the number of simple closed geodesics of length ≤ L on a hyperbolic surface of genus g grows like L6g−6 times a rational multiple of the Weil–Petersson volume of M_g. The same intersection‑theoretic techniques compute the Masur–Veech volumes of strata of Abelian differentials: the volume of ΩM_g(κ) equals a rational multiple of π2g times a combinatorial factor derived from the Eskin–Okounkov generating function. The connection between the two volume theories is mediated by the fact that the SL(2, ℝ) action on translation surfaces preserves the area form, and the Masur–Veech measure is the pushforward of the Lebesgue measure on period coordinates, which is a constant multiple of the Weil–Petersson form on the corresponding locus in M_g.

  • Confusing the Kontsevich–Zorich cocycle with the Rauzy–Veech matrices; the former acts on homology, the latter on length vectors.
  • Assuming every SL(2, ℝ)-invariant measure is the Masur–Veech measure; the Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi theorem shows there are many affine invariant submanifolds.
  • Treating square‑tiled surfaces as generic in a stratum; they are dense but form a countable set of zero Lebesgue measure.
  • Misapplying the Veech dichotomy to non‑Veech surfaces; the dichotomy holds only for Veech surfaces or almost every direction on almost every surface.
  • Mixing up the Weil–Petersson volume recursion with the Masur–Veech volume formula; they involve different moduli spaces and different combinatorial data.
  • Overlooking the requirement that linear equations defining an affine invariant submanifold have rational coefficients.
  • Forgetting that the top Lyapunov exponent λ₁ = 1 is universal for all ergodic SL(2, ℝ)-invariant measures, while the remaining exponents vary with the stratum.
