hand/geometric-group-theory.html:
Quasi-isometric Rigidity and Classification of Lattices

Quasi-isometric rigidity asks whether the large‑scale geometry of a group determines its algebraic structure up to finite extensions. For lattices in semisimple Lie groups, the answer is largely affirmative. Mostow’s strong rigidity theorem (1968) shows that any isomorphism between lattices in higher‑rank simple Lie groups extends to an isomorphism of the ambient groups. In the quasi‑isometric setting, Kleiner and Leeb (1997) proved that any group quasi‑isometric to a higher‑rank symmetric space is virtually a lattice in the same Lie group. Eskin and Farb (1997) extended this to rank‑one spaces of non‑compact type, showing that quasi‑isometries of complex hyperbolic and quaternionic hyperbolic spaces are at bounded distance from isometries. The Euclidean case is different: groups quasi‑isometric to ℝⁿ are virtually ℤⁿ by Gromov’s polynomial growth theorem. For products of trees and hyperbolic planes, the quasi‑isometry classification is more subtle; work of Whyte and others shows that certain right‑angled Artin groups are quasi‑isometrically rigid while others admit non‑trivial quasi‑isometries. The general program seeks a dictionary linking quasi‑isometry invariants — such as asymptotic dimension, Dehn functions, and boundaries — to algebraic properties like virtual nilpotence, virtual specialness, or the existence of a non‑trivial splitting.

A key tool is the notion of a quasi‑action: a group acts quasi‑isometrically on a metric space if each element moves points a uniformly bounded distance from an isometric action. The Schwartz–Moser lemma guarantees that a quasi‑action on a proper geodesic space is quasi‑conjugate to an isometric action on a possibly different space. This reduces many rigidity problems to the study of isometric actions on CAT(0) spaces or buildings. For example, a group quasi‑isometric to a product of trees must act properly and cocompactly on a product of trees, which forces a virtual splitting as a direct product of groups acting on trees. The classification of lattices in products of rank‑one groups (Burger–Mozes, 2000) shows that irreducible lattices are quasi‑isometrically rigid, while reducible lattices decompose as products. These results illustrate how coarse geometry can recover fine algebraic information, a theme that continues to drive research in geometric group theory.

Applications extend beyond pure group theory. Quasi‑isometric rigidity of mapping class groups (Behrstock–Kleiner–Minsky–Mosher, 2012) implies that any group quasi‑isometric to a mapping class group is virtually a mapping class group. Similar statements hold for Out(Fₙ) (Bestvina–Feighn–Handel) and for certain graph‑of‑groups constructions. The techniques involve the analysis of hierarchical hyperbolic spaces, projection complexes, and the geometry of curve graphs. Understanding these invariants equips the aspirant to recognise when a problem about an unknown group can be reduced to a known rigid class, a frequent pattern in advanced examinations.

Boundaries of Hyperbolic Groups and Conformal Dimension

The Gromov boundary ∂G of a hyperbolic group G captures its asymptotic geometry. It is a compact metrizable space defined up to homeomorphism by the quasi‑isometry class of G. For a hyperbolic group, the boundary carries a family of visual metrics: for a basepoint o and a parameter ε > 0 small enough, the metric d_ε(ξ,η) ≈ exp(−ε·(ξ|η)_o) where (ξ|η)_o is the Gromov product. Different ε give bi‑Lipschitz equivalent metrics, so the boundary has a well‑defined quasi‑symmetric structure. The conformal dimension of ∂G is the infimum of Hausdorff dimensions over all metrics quasi‑symmetric to a visual metric. This invariant, introduced by Pansu and studied by Bourdon and Pajot, distinguishes many hyperbolic groups. For example, the boundary of a uniform lattice in real hyperbolic space Hⁿ is a sphere Sⁿ⁻¹ with conformal dimension n−1. In contrast, the boundary of a free group is a Cantor set of conformal dimension 0. Bourdon and Pajot (1999) showed that for a hyperbolic group whose boundary is a Sierpiński carpet, the conformal dimension is strictly greater than 1 but less than 2, and it is attained by a unique (up to quasi‑symmetry) metric. This rigidity of the conformal gauge has strong algebraic consequences: if a hyperbolic group has boundary of conformal dimension 1, then the group is virtually a free group or a surface group (by a theorem of Kapovich and Kleiner).

Computing conformal dimension often involves constructing explicit quasi‑symmetric maps or using the combinatorial Loewner property. A metric space satisfies the combinatorial Loewner property if the modulus of curve families is controlled by discrete approximations. Bourdon and Pajot proved that the boundary of a hyperbolic group with a planar Cayley graph (e.g., a hyperbolic 3‑manifold group) satisfies this property, which forces the conformal dimension to be realized by a visual metric. For groups acting on CAT(0) cube complexes, the boundary is a median space; recent work of Hagen and others relates the conformal dimension to the rank of the cube complex. In examinations, a typical question asks to explain why the conformal dimension is a quasi‑isometry invariant and how it can be used to rule out certain groups being quasi‑isometric to each other. The answer hinges on the fact that a quasi‑isometry induces a quasi‑symmetric homeomorphism of boundaries, and quasi‑symmetric maps preserve the conformal gauge.

Technique
Explain why the Gromov boundary of a hyperbolic group is a quasi‑isometry invariant and how the conformal dimension of the boundary can be used to distinguish two hyperbolic groups that are not quasi‑isometric.
A quasi‑isometry f: G → H between hyperbolic groups extends continuously to a homeomorphism ∂f: ∂G → ∂H because quasi‑geodesic rays in G map to quasi‑geodesic rays in H, and the fellow‑traveller property guarantees a well‑defined limit point. Moreover, ∂f is quasi‑symmetric: there exists a homeomorphism η: [0,∞) → [0,∞) such that for any distinct ξ,η,ζ ∈ ∂G, the ratio d(∂f(ξ),∂f(η)) / d(∂f(ξ),∂f(ζ)) is bounded by η of the corresponding ratio in ∂G. Since conformal dimension is defined as the infimum of Hausdorff dimensions over all metrics in the quasi‑symmetric gauge, it is invariant under quasi‑symmetric homeomorphisms. Therefore, if two hyperbolic groups have boundaries with different conformal dimensions, they cannot be quasi‑isometric. For instance, a free group has boundary a Cantor set of conformal dimension 0, while a uniform lattice in H³ has boundary S² of conformal dimension 2; these groups are not quasi‑isometric.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks for a quasi‑isometry invariant, first list the standard ones: growth type, Dehn function, asymptotic dimension, boundary homeomorphism type, and conformal dimension. Then match the invariant to the specific groups mentioned. If the groups are given by presentations, check whether they are hyperbolic (linear Dehn function) and compute or recall their boundaries. A quick mental table — free groups → Cantor set (dim 0), surface groups → circle (dim 1), hyperbolic 3‑manifold groups → Sierpiński carpet or S² (dim >1) — often yields the answer without heavy computation.

Random Groups and Generic Properties

Gromov’s density model provides a probabilistic framework for studying “typical” finitely presented groups. Fix a free group Fₘ of rank m ≥ 2 and a length ℓ. Choose each reduced word of length ℓ independently with probability p = (2m−1)−dℓ where d ∈ (0,1) is the density parameter. The resulting random presentation ⟨S | R⟩ defines a random group G(d). Gromov showed that for d < 1/2 the group is infinite, hyperbolic, and torsion‑free with overwhelming probability as ℓ → ∞, while for d > 1/2 the group is trivial (or finite) with overwhelming probability. The threshold d = 1/2 is sharp: at density exactly 1/2 the behaviour is more delicate and depends on the number of generators. Ollivier (2005) refined the model and proved that at densities d < 1/3 the random group satisfies a linear isoperimetric inequality with an explicit constant, and that the first ℓ²‑Betti numbers vanish. Žuk (2003) established property (T) for random groups at densities d > 1/3, showing that property (T) appears generically in this range. These results demonstrate a phase transition: low density yields free‑like hyperbolic groups, intermediate density yields hyperbolic groups with property (T), and high density yields trivial groups.

The generic properties of random groups have become a benchmark for conjectures. For instance, the Baum–Connes conjecture with coefficients is known for all hyperbolic groups (Lafforgue, 2002), and random groups provide a plentiful supply of test cases. The fact that random groups at density d < 1/2 are hyperbolic and have trivial first ℓ²‑Betti numbers supports the Singer conjecture for hyperbolic groups. Moreover, the existence of random groups with property (T) but without finite subgroups (for d ∈ (1/3, 1/2)) gives counterexamples to the conjecture that every group with property (T) has a finite subgroup. In examinations, a typical problem asks to state the density thresholds for hyperbolicity, property (T), and triviality, and to explain why the model is useful for producing groups with prescribed combinations of properties. The answer should reference the independence of relators at large length, the use of small cancellation theory at low density, and the spectral gap arguments of Žuk at higher density.

Beyond the density model, other random group models include the Gromov–Misha model (fixed number of relators) and the triangular model (relators chosen from a triangular region). These variants exhibit similar phase transitions but with different critical densities. The study of random groups also connects to the theory of expanders: the Cayley graphs of random groups at density d > 1/3 form a family of expanders with high probability, as shown by Żuk and later by Alon and Roichman. This link provides a geometric source of expander graphs, which are central in theoretical computer science and the study of property (τ). Understanding these connections equips the aspirant to discuss how probabilistic methods produce explicit families of groups with desired geometric and analytic features.

Higher Dehn Functions and Filling Invariants

The classical Dehn function measures the difficulty of filling loops in the Cayley complex. Higher Dehn functions, introduced by Gromov and developed by Alonso, Wang, Pride, and others, measure the difficulty of filling spheres of higher dimension. For a finitely presented group G = ⟨S | R⟩, the k‑th Dehn function δ_k(n) is the maximal minimal volume of a (k+1)‑chain filling a k‑cycle of volume ≤ n in the universal cover of the presentation complex. When k = 1 this recovers the usual Dehn function. For k = 2, δ2(n) captures the complexity of filling 2‑spheres, which is related to the second homotopy group of the presentation complex. A group is of type F_k if it admits a classifying space with finite k‑skeleton; the finiteness of δ_k(n) for all n is equivalent to the group being of type Fk+1 and having a polynomial (or linear) filling function. For example, hyperbolic groups have linear Dehn functions in all dimensions (Gromov, 1987). Automatic groups have quadratic Dehn functions in dimension 1, but their higher Dehn functions can be exponential. The Baumslag–Solitar group BS(1,2) has exponential Dehn function in dimension 1 and its higher Dehn functions grow even faster.

Filling invariants are closely tied to the isoperimetric profile of the group. The isoperimetric function of degree k, IP_k(n), is the supremum of minimal (k+1)‑volumes needed to fill k‑cycles of volume ≤ n in a contractible complex on which the group acts properly and cocompactly. For CAT(0) groups, the Euclidean isoperimetric inequality holds: IP_k(n) ≤ C n(k+1)/k. This is a consequence of the fact that CAT(0) spaces admit cone constructions with controlled volume. For groups acting on buildings, the isoperimetric profile can be computed using the combinatorics of apartments. The work of Young (2013) on the Dehn functions of SL_n(ℤ) shows that the k‑th Dehn function grows like n(k+1)/k for k < n−1, reflecting the rank of the symmetric space. These results illustrate how higher filling functions encode the large‑scale geometry of the group and its associated symmetric spaces or buildings.

In examinations, a common question asks to compare the Dehn function and the second Dehn function of a given group, or to explain why a linear isoperimetric inequality in all dimensions characterizes hyperbolic groups. The key points are: (1) hyperbolicity implies a linear isoperimetric inequality for all k because the Cayley graph is δ‑thin and the cone construction yields linear filling; (2) conversely, if a group has linear Dehn functions in all dimensions, its asymptotic cones are simply connected and have trivial higher homotopy, forcing the group to be hyperbolic (by a theorem of Gromov). The aspirant should be able to sketch the cone argument: a linear filling function gives a uniform bound on the volume of fillings, which passes to the ultralimit and yields contractibility of asymptotic cones, a hallmark of hyperbolicity.

Coarse Embeddability, Property A, and the Novikov Conjecture

A metric space X coarsely embeds into a Hilbert space if there exist non‑decreasing functions ρ₁, ρ₂: [0,∞) → [0,∞) with ρ₁(r) → ∞ such that ρ₁(d(x,y)) ≤ ‖f(x)−f(y)‖ ≤ ρ₂(d(x,y)) for some map f: X → ℋ. For finitely generated groups equipped with a word metric, coarse embeddability into Hilbert space is a quasi‑isometry invariant. Yu (2000) proved that if a discrete group coarsely embeds into Hilbert space, then the coarse Baum–Connes conjecture holds for that group, which in turn implies the Novikov conjecture on the homotopy invariance of higher signatures. This result provides a geometric sufficient condition for the Novikov conjecture that applies to a wide class of groups, including all hyperbolic groups (which embed via the Gromov boundary), all amenable groups (by a construction of Higson and Kasparov), and all groups acting properly on CAT(0) cube complexes (by a theorem of Guentner, Higson, and Weinberger).

Property A, introduced by Yu (2000), is a weaker, combinatorial condition that implies coarse embeddability into Hilbert space. A discrete metric space X has Property A if for every ε > 0 and R > 0 there exists a map ξ: X → ℓ¹(X) with ‖ξ(x)‖₁ = 1, support of ξ(x) contained in B(x, S) for some S, and ‖ξ(x)−ξ(y)‖₁ < ε whenever d(x,y) ≤ R. For groups, Property A is equivalent to the existence of a sequence of almost invariant means (Reiter’s condition) and to the exactness of the reduced C*‑algebra. All amenable groups have Property A, and so do all hyperbolic groups (by a construction using the Gromov boundary). However, there exist groups that coarsely embed into Hilbert space but do not have Property A (e.g., certain expanders with property (T) constructed by Gromov). The distinction is important: coarse embeddability is sufficient for the Novikov conjecture, while Property A is sufficient for the coarse Baum–Connes conjecture with coefficients.

Recent work has extended these ideas to the Farrell–Jones conjecture. Bartels and Lück (2012) proved the Farrell–Jones conjecture for groups acting properly on CAT(0) spaces and for hyperbolic groups, using controlled algebra and the existence of finite asymptotic dimension. Asymptotic dimension, introduced by Gromov, is another coarse invariant: a metric space has asymptotic dimension ≤ n if for every R > 0 there is a uniformly bounded cover with multiplicity ≤ n+1 and Lebesgue number ≥ R. Groups with finite asymptotic dimension coarsely embed into Hilbert space (by a theorem of Guentner, Higson, and Weinberger), and thus satisfy the Novikov conjecture. In examinations, a typical question asks to state Yu’s theorem and to give examples of groups that satisfy its hypothesis. The answer should list hyperbolic groups, amenable groups, groups acting on CAT(0) cube complexes, and groups with finite asymptotic dimension, and briefly explain why each class coarsely embeds (e.g., hyperbolic groups via the boundary embedding, amenable groups via the Folner sequence construction).

  • Confusing quasi‑isometric rigidity with commensurability: rigidity concerns large‑scale geometry, while commensurability is an algebraic finite‑index relation.
  • Assuming all hyperbolic groups have conformal dimension 1: only those with circle or Sierpiński carpet boundaries have dimension 1; free groups have dimension 0, and many 3‑manifold groups have dimension >1.
  • Misstating the density thresholds for random groups: hyperbolicity holds for d < 1/2, property (T) for d > 1/3, triviality for d > 1/2.
  • Equating the Dehn function with the second Dehn function: they measure filling of loops versus spheres and can have drastically different growth rates.
  • Believing Property A is equivalent to coarse embeddability: Property A implies coarse embeddability, but the converse fails (expanders with property (T) provide counterexamples).
  • Overlooking that the Novikov conjecture follows from coarse embeddability, not directly from hyperbolicity: hyperbolicity gives embeddability, which then yields the conjecture via Yu’s theorem.
  • Neglecting the role of asymptotic dimension: finite asymptotic dimension implies coarse embeddability, but many groups (e.g., certain hyperbolic groups) have infinite asymptotic dimension yet still embed.

hand/thermodynamics.html:
Thermodynamic Stability Criteria and Phase Transitions

Stability of a thermodynamic equilibrium state is governed by the convexity properties of the appropriate potential. For a simple compressible system at fixed temperature and pressure the Gibbs free energy G(T,P) must be a minimum; equivalently the matrix of second derivatives of the internal energy U(S,V) with respect to its extensive variables must be positive‑definite. This yields the familiar mechanical stability condition (∂P/∂V)_T ≤ 0 and the thermal stability condition C_V ≥ 0. When one of these inequalities is violated the homogeneous phase becomes unstable and the system separates into coexisting phases. The spinodal line, defined by (∂P/∂V)_T = 0, marks the limit of metastability; the binodal (coexistence) curve is obtained from the common‑tangent construction on the G‑versus‑V isotherm or, equivalently, from equality of chemical potentials μ₁ = μ₂ and pressures P₁ = P₂ of the two phases.

First‑order transitions exhibit a discontinuity in the first derivatives of G (entropy S = −(∂G/∂T)_P and volume V = (∂G/∂P)_T), giving latent heat L = TΔS and a volume change ΔV. The Clausius–Clapeyron equation dP/dT = L/(TΔV) follows directly from the equality of Gibbs potentials along the coexistence line. Second‑order (continuous) transitions, classified by Ehrenfest, show continuous first derivatives but discontinuities in second derivatives such as heat capacity C_P, compressibility κ_T, and thermal expansion α_P. Modern classification uses the concept of critical exponents and universality classes; the Ising model provides the paradigmatic example where the order parameter (magnetisation) vanishes continuously at the critical point.

In multicomponent systems the Gibbs phase rule F = C − P + 2 (where C is the number of components and P the number of phases) determines the number of intensive variables that can be varied independently. For a binary alloy the lever rule gives the relative amounts of coexisting phases from the overall composition. The chemical potential of each component μ_i = (∂G/∂N_i)T,P,Nj≠i must be equal in all phases at equilibrium. This condition underlies the construction of phase diagrams such as the eutectic, peritectic, and miscibility‑gap diagrams that are standard material‑science tools.

Metastable states (supercooled liquids, supersaturated vapours) persist because nucleation of the stable phase requires the formation of a critical nucleus whose free‑energy barrier ΔG* = (16πγ³)/(3Δμ²) (for a spherical nucleus with interfacial tension γ and chemical‑potential difference Δμ) must be overcome. Classical nucleation theory predicts the nucleation rate J ∝ exp(−ΔG*/k_B T). In practice, heterogeneous nucleation on impurities or container walls dramatically reduces the barrier, explaining why perfectly pure substances can be supercooled far below their equilibrium freezing point.

Non‑Equilibrium Thermodynamics and Onsager Reciprocal Relations

When a system is driven slightly away from equilibrium, the fluxes J_i (heat flow, particle diffusion, electrical current, etc.) are linearly related to the thermodynamic forces X_j (temperature gradient, chemical‑potential gradient, electric field) by J_i = Σ_j Lij X_j. The phenomenological coefficients Lij form a symmetric matrix Lij = Lji — the Onsager reciprocal relations — provided the forces and fluxes are chosen such that the entropy production rate σ = Σ_i J_i X_i is a bilinear form and microscopic reversibility holds. The symmetry follows from the time‑reversal invariance of the underlying microscopic equations of motion and the regression hypothesis that spontaneous fluctuations decay according to the same linear laws as macroscopic irreversible processes.

A classic example is thermoelectricity: the Seebeck effect (voltage generated by a temperature gradient) and the Peltier effect (heat carried by an electric current) are described by the same off‑diagonal coefficient L12 = L21. The Kelvin relations Π = ST (Peltier coefficient Π equals Seebeck coefficient S times absolute temperature T) are a direct consequence of Onsager symmetry. Similarly, the Soret effect (mass flux driven by a temperature gradient) and the Dufour effect (heat flux driven by a concentration gradient) are coupled through reciprocal coefficients.

The entropy production σ must be non‑negative for any admissible process, which imposes positive‑definiteness on the matrix Lij. This leads to inequalities such as the thermal conductivity κ ≥ 0, the diffusion coefficient D ≥ 0, and the determinant condition L11L22 − L12² ≥ 0. These constraints are routinely used to check the consistency of experimentally measured transport coefficients.

Beyond the linear regime, extended irreversible thermodynamics introduces higher‑order fluxes (e.g., the heat‑flux vector itself as a state variable) leading to hyperbolic heat‑conduction equations (Cattaneo–Vernotte) that avoid the infinite propagation speed paradox of Fourier’s law. The GENERIC framework (General Equation for Non‑Equilibrium Reversible‑Irreversible Coupling) provides a unified geometric structure that separates reversible Hamiltonian dynamics from irreversible gradient‑flow dynamics, guaranteeing compliance with both the first and second laws.

Worked Example: Onsager Symmetry in a Thermoelectric Element
A thermoelectric rod of length L connects two reservoirs at temperatures T₁ and T₂ (T₁ > T₂) and is open‑circuit (no net electric current). The linear relations are J_q = L11 (−∇T/T²) + L12 (∇μ_e/T) and J_e = L21 (−∇T/T²) + L22 (∇μ_e/T), where J_q is heat flux, J_e is electric current density, and μ_e is the electrochemical potential. Given L12 = L21, derive the open‑circuit voltage V = ∫ E·dx in terms of the Seebeck coefficient S and the temperature difference ΔT = T₁ − T₂.
Open circuit means J_e = 0 ⇒ L21(−∇T/T²) + L22(∇μ_e/T) = 0 ⇒ ∇μ_e = (L21/L22) (∇T/T). The electric field E = −∇μ_e/e (e is elementary charge). The Seebeck coefficient is defined as S = E/(−∇T) = (L21/eL22)(1/T). Using Onsager symmetry L21=L12 and the Kelvin relation Π = ST, one finds S = (1/eT)(L12/L22). Integrating E = −S∇T from T₂ to T₁ gives V = ∫T₂T₁ S(T) dT. For constant S, V = S ΔT.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sign of an off‑diagonal Onsager coefficient, remember that the entropy‑production inequality forces the determinant of the L‑matrix to be non‑negative. If the diagonal coefficients are known positive, the off‑diagonal term can be either sign but its magnitude is bounded by √(L11L22). Use this bound to eliminate impossible answer choices quickly.

Advanced Heat‑Engine Cycles: Stirling, Ericsson, and Combined Cycles

The Carnot cycle sets the absolute efficiency ceiling η_C = 1 − T_C/T_H, but its two isothermal and two adiabatic steps are impractical for real machines because isothermal heat transfer requires infinite time. The Stirling cycle replaces the adiabats with two constant‑volume (isochoric) processes and retains the two isotherms. A perfect regenerator stores the heat rejected during the constant‑volume cooling and returns it during the constant‑volume heating, making the net heat exchange occur only during the isotherms. With an ideal regenerator the Stirling efficiency equals the Carnot efficiency. Real regenerators have effectiveness ε < 1, so the efficiency becomes η = η_C − (1−ε)C_V(T_H−T_C)/Q_H, where Q_H is the heat absorbed on the hot isotherm.

The Ericsson cycle uses two isobars and two isotherms, again with a regenerator. Its ideal efficiency also reaches η_C. Both Stirling and Ericsson cycles are external‑combustion cycles; they can run on any heat source (solar, nuclear, waste heat) and are the basis for modern Stirling cryocoolers and solar‑thermal generators. The regenerator is the critical component: its matrix must have high heat capacity, low flow resistance, and minimal axial conduction. Practical designs use stacked metal screens, random‑fiber matrices, or porous ceramics.

Combined cycles couple a high‑temperature gas‑turbine (Brayton) topping cycle with a low‑temperature steam‑turbine (Rankine) bottoming cycle. The exhaust gases from the Brayton turbine (≈ 600 °C) generate steam in a heat‑recovery steam generator (HRSG). The overall efficiency η_comb = η_B + η_R − η_B η_R can exceed 60 % in modern combined‑cycle power plants, far above the 40 % typical of simple cycles. The analysis uses the same first‑law balance on each component but adds the second‑law constraint that the entropy generation in the HRSG must be minimised by matching the gas‑side and steam‑side temperature profiles (pinch‑point analysis).

For any real cycle the exergy (availability) destruction I = T₀ Σ ΔS_gen quantifies the lost work potential, where T₀ is the environment temperature. Minimising I across all components — compressors, turbines, combustors, heat exchangers — is the guiding principle of thermodynamic optimisation. The Gouy–Stodola theorem links exergy destruction directly to entropy generation, providing a common metric for comparing cycles with different working fluids and temperature ranges.

Fluctuation Theorems, Jarzynski Equality, and the Thermodynamics of Small Systems

Classical thermodynamics assumes the thermodynamic limit (N → ∞) where relative fluctuations vanish as 1/√N. For nanoscale systems, single‑molecule experiments, and molecular‑dynamics simulations, fluctuations are dominant and the second law must be reformulated as a statistical statement. The Jarzynski equality ⟨e−βW⟩ = e−βΔF holds for any protocol that drives a system from an initial equilibrium state (temperature T, free energy F_i) to a final state (free energy F_f), where W is the work performed on the system during a single realisation and β = 1/k_B T. The average is over an ensemble of repetitions of the same protocol. Because the exponential average is dominated by rare low‑work trajectories, the equality provides a practical method to extract equilibrium free‑energy differences from non‑equilibrium pulling experiments (e.g., optical‑tweezer unfolding of RNA).

The Crooks fluctuation theorem refines this: P_F(W)/P_R(−W) = eβ(W−ΔF), where P_F and P_R are the work distributions for the forward and time‑reversed protocols. It implies the second‑law inequality ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF (by Jensen’s inequality) and gives a direct route to ΔF by locating the crossing point of the forward and reverse work histograms. The integral fluctuation theorem ⟨e−Σ⟩ = 1, where Σ = ΔS_tot/k_B is the total entropy production (system plus reservoirs), is a universal statement valid for any Markovian dynamics satisfying local detailed balance.

These theorems have been verified experimentally in colloidal particles dragged through water, in single‑molecule RNA folding, and in superconducting qubits. They also underpin the thermodynamic uncertainty relations that bound the precision of any current (particle, heat, or charge) by the entropy production rate: Var(J)/⟨J⟩² ≥ 2k_B/⟨Σ⟩. This trade‑off between speed, accuracy, and dissipation is a central design principle for molecular machines and nanoscale heat engines.

In the quantum regime, the two‑point measurement scheme defines work as the difference of energy eigenvalues measured at the beginning and end of the protocol. The Tasaki–Crooks relation and the quantum Jarzynski equality retain the same form provided the initial state is thermal and the measurements are projective. Recent work extends fluctuation theorems to systems with feedback control (Maxwell’s demon), where the mutual information I between system and controller appears as an additional term: ⟨e−β(W−ΔF)−I⟩ = 1, leading to the generalized second law ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF − k_B T ⟨I⟩.

  • Confusing the spinodal line (limit of metastability) with the coexistence curve (binodal) — the spinodal is inside the two‑phase region, not on its boundary.
  • Assuming Onsager reciprocity holds for any choice of forces and fluxes; it requires the entropy production to be a bilinear form with forces that are even under time reversal.
  • Treating the regenerator in Stirling/Ericsson cycles as perfect without accounting for its finite effectiveness, leading to over‑estimated efficiencies.
  • Applying the Carnot efficiency formula to combined cycles without recognising that the bottoming cycle operates between a lower temperature range, so the overall efficiency is not simply 1−T_C/T_H of the topping cycle.
  • Using the Jarzynski equality with insufficient sampling — the exponential average converges slowly because it is dominated by rare trajectories; importance‑sampling or bidirectional methods (Crooks) are often needed.
  • Neglecting the mutual‑information term in feedback‑controlled nanoscale engines, which can apparently violate the conventional second law if omitted.
  • Misidentifying the chemical potential in multicomponent phase equilibria; each component’s μ must be equal across phases, not just the total Gibbs energy per mole.

hand/nonlinear-dynamics.html:
Routes to Chaos: Period-Doubling, Quasiperiodicity, and Intermittency

The transition from regular to chaotic dynamics follows a few universal scenarios that are independent of the specific equations governing a system. The most celebrated is the period‑doubling cascade, first described by Feigenbaum for one‑dimensional maps such as the logistic map xn+1 = r xn(1 − xn). As the control parameter r increases, a stable fixed point loses stability and a period‑2 orbit appears; further increase yields period‑4, period‑8, and so on, accumulating at a finite parameter value r∞ ≈ 3.5699456. The ratio of successive bifurcation intervals converges to the Feigenbaum constant δ ≈ 4.6692, a universal number for a broad class of unimodal maps.

A second route is the quasiperiodic (or torus) route, described by the Ruelle–Takens–Newhouse scenario. Here a stable limit cycle undergoes a Hopf bifurcation, creating a two‑torus with two incommensurate frequencies. A third Hopf bifurcation can produce a three‑torus; according to the theory, a three‑torus typically breaks down into a strange attractor, giving rise to chaos. This route is common in fluid dynamics, for example in the transition to turbulence in Rayleigh–Bénard convection.

The third major route is intermittency, identified by Pomeau and Manneville. Near a saddle‑node or subcritical Hopf bifurcation, a trajectory alternates between long laminar phases (near the remnant of a stable orbit) and chaotic bursts. The average laminar length scales as a power law of the distance from the bifurcation point, with exponent −1/2 for type‑I intermittency (saddle‑node) and −1 for type‑III (subcritical Hopf). Intermittency is observed in laser dynamics, chemical reactions, and cardiac tissue models.

Each route leaves distinct signatures in the power spectrum and in the Lyapunov spectrum. Period‑doubling yields a cascade of subharmonic peaks; quasiperiodicity produces a set of incommensurate peaks that broaden at the transition; intermittency shows a broadband background with narrow peaks corresponding to the laminar frequency. Recognising these signatures in experimental time series is a core skill for identifying the underlying bifurcation mechanism.

Numerical Computation of Lyapunov Exponents: Algorithms and Pitfalls

Accurate estimation of the Lyapunov spectrum from numerical simulations or experimental data requires careful handling of the tangent‑space dynamics. The standard algorithm for flows integrates the variational equations dδx/dt = DF(x)·δx alongside the trajectory, periodically re‑orthonormalising the set of perturbation vectors using the Gram–Schmidt procedure (or QR decomposition). The logarithms of the norm growth factors, averaged over the integration time, converge to the Lyapunov exponents λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … ≥ λm. For maps, the Jacobian Df(xn) is multiplied iteratively, with the same re‑orthonormalisation step.

Several practical issues affect reliability. First, the integration time must be long enough for convergence; the maximal exponent typically converges faster than the smaller ones. A rule of thumb is to integrate for at least 10⁴–10⁵ characteristic times (e.g., 10⁴ periods of the dominant oscillation). Second, the choice of re‑orthonormalisation interval matters: too frequent re‑orthonormalisation suppresses the growth of subdominant directions, while too infrequent intervals lead to overflow and loss of orthogonality. Adaptive schemes that monitor the condition number of the perturbation matrix are recommended.

Third, for experimental data the Jacobian is not directly available. One must reconstruct the attractor in an embedding space using delay coordinates (Takens’ theorem) and then apply algorithms such as the Rosenstein–Kantz method for the maximal exponent or the Sano–Sawada algorithm for the full spectrum. These methods rely on nearest‑neighbour tracking and are sensitive to noise, embedding dimension, and data length. Surrogate data testing is essential to distinguish genuine chaos from coloured noise.

Fourth, the sum of Lyapunov exponents for a dissipative flow equals the average phase‑space contraction rate, i.e., the trace of the Jacobian averaged over the attractor. This provides a valuable consistency check: Σ λi = ⟨div F⟩. For the Lorenz system with classic parameters, div F = −(σ + 1 + β) = −13.666…, and the numerically computed spectrum (≈ 0.906, 0, −14.57) satisfies the relation within numerical error.

Worked Example: Maximal Lyapunov Exponent of the Logistic Map
Compute the maximal Lyapunov exponent λ for the logistic map xn+1 = r x_n (1 − x_n) at r = 4 using the analytical formula λ = ∫01 ln|r(1−2x)| ρ(x) dx, where ρ(x) = 1/(π√(x(1−x))) is the invariant density.
At r = 4 the map is fully chaotic on [0,1]. The invariant density is ρ(x) = 1/(π√(x(1−x))). The derivative is f'(x) = 4(1−2x). Then λ = ∫01 ln|4(1−2x)| ρ(x) dx. Substitute x = sin²θ, dx = 2 sinθ cosθ dθ, √(x(1−x)) = sinθ cosθ, ρ(x) dx = (2/π) dθ. The integral becomes λ = (2/π) ∫0π/2 ln|4 cos 2θ| dθ. Using symmetry and known integrals, ∫0π/2 ln|cos 2θ| dθ = −(π/2) ln 2. Hence λ = (2/π)[ (π/2) ln 4 − (π/2) ln 2 ] = ln 2 ≈ 0.6931. This positive value confirms chaos and matches numerical estimates.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Lyapunov exponent of a one‑dimensional map at a specific parameter, first check whether the map is conjugate to a known solvable case (e.g., logistic map at r = 4, tent map, Bernoulli shift). If an analytical invariant density is known, use the integral formula; otherwise, describe the numerical QR algorithm and mention the need for long transients and re‑orthonormalisation. Always state the convergence criterion (e.g., exponent stabilises within 1 % over the last decade of integration time).

Fractal Dimensions: Box‑Counting, Correlation, and Information Dimensions

Strange attractors are characterised by non‑integer fractal dimensions that quantify their geometric complexity. The box‑counting (capacity) dimension D₀ is defined as D₀ = limε→0 log N(ε) / log(1/ε), where N(ε) is the minimum number of ε‑side boxes needed to cover the attractor. In practice, one plots log N(ε) versus log(1/ε) over a scaling range and fits a straight line; the slope gives D₀. For the Lorenz attractor, D₀ ≈ 2.06, reflecting its slightly folded two‑dimensional surface.

The correlation dimension D₂, introduced by Grassberger and Procaccia, is more accessible from experimental time series. It is defined via the correlation integral C(ε) = limN→∞ (2/(N(N−1))) Σi<j</sub> Θ(ε − ||x_i − x_j||), where Θ is the Heaviside step function. For a fractal set, C(ε) ∼ εD₂ for small ε, so D₂ = d log C(ε) / d log ε. D₂ ≤ D₁ ≤ D₀, where D₁ is the information dimension, which weights boxes by their natural measure (probability of visitation). The Kaplan–Yorke conjecture gives an estimate D_KY = k + (Σi=1^k λ_i)/|λk+1|, where k is the largest integer with Σi=1^k λ_i ≥ 0. For the Lorenz system, λ ≈ (0.906, 0, −14.57) yields D_KY ≈ 2.06, in excellent agreement with direct box‑counting.

Estimating dimensions from finite, noisy data requires careful selection of the scaling region. Too large ε saturates the box count; too small ε enters the noise floor where C(ε) scales with the embedding dimension rather than the attractor dimension. The Theiler window (excluding temporally close points) avoids spurious correlations from the time‑series sampling. Surrogate data with the same power spectrum but randomised phases provide a baseline for significance testing.

Hyperchaos, defined by at least two positive Lyapunov exponents, implies a Kaplan–Yorke dimension greater than three and requires a minimum phase‑space dimension of four. The Rössler hyperchaotic system (four variables) and the coupled Lorenz systems are standard examples. In such systems, the correlation dimension can exceed three, and the attractor exhibits a richer folding structure.

Control and Synchronization of Chaotic Systems: OGY Method and Pecora–Carroll

Chaos control aims to stabilise an unstable periodic orbit (UPO) embedded in a chaotic attractor by applying small, time‑dependent perturbations. The Ott–Grebogi–Yorke (OGY) method linearises the Poincaré map near a chosen UPO and computes a control law that adjusts a system parameter once per crossing of a Poincaré section. The perturbation magnitude is proportional to the distance from the UPO, ensuring that the control remains within a predefined small bound. Successful OGY control has been demonstrated in magneto‑elastic ribbons, diode resonators, and cardiac tissue models.

Synchronization of chaos exploits the fact that two identical chaotic systems, when coupled appropriately, can evolve identically despite sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Pecora and Carroll showed that if a drive system transmits a scalar signal to a response system that replicates a subsystem of the drive, the response can synchronise provided the conditional Lyapunov exponents (exponents of the response subsystem with the drive signal as input) are all negative. This principle underlies chaotic secure communication: the message is added to the chaotic carrier at the transmitter and recovered at the receiver by subtracting the synchronised chaotic signal.

Generalised synchronization extends the concept to non‑identical systems, where a functional relationship Φ(x_drive) = x_response emerges. The auxiliary system approach tests for generalised synchronization by duplicating the response system and checking whether the two responses converge. Applications include laser arrays, neuronal networks, and power‑grid stability analysis.

Both control and synchronization rely on the existence of a dense set of UPOs within the attractor and on the ability to measure or estimate the relevant Jacobians. In experimental settings, model‑free control schemes such as time‑delayed feedback (Pyragas control) apply a perturbation proportional to the difference between the current state and its state one period earlier, stabilising UPOs without explicit model knowledge. The method succeeds when the target orbit’s Floquet multipliers satisfy certain conditions, but it can fail for orbits with odd‑number real multipliers greater than one.

  • Confusing the Feigenbaum constant δ (ratio of bifurcation intervals) with the universal scaling constant α (ratio of orbit widths) — they are distinct numbers (δ ≈ 4.669, α ≈ 2.503).
  • Assuming a positive maximal Lyapunov exponent alone proves chaos; a positive exponent can also arise from stochastic noise if the embedding and noise‑reduction steps are inadequate.
  • Using the box‑counting dimension D₀ as a substitute for the correlation dimension D₂ without verifying the scaling range; D₀ is more sensitive to noise and often overestimates the fractal dimension.
  • Neglecting the Theiler window when computing the correlation integral, leading to artificial saturation at small ε due to temporal correlations.
  • Believing the OGY method can stabilise any UPO with arbitrarily small perturbations; the required perturbation grows as the target orbit’s instability (Floquet multiplier) increases, and there is a practical bound set by actuator limits.
  • Thinking that identical drive and response systems guarantee synchronization; the conditional Lyapunov exponents must be negative, which depends on the coupling configuration and the specific signal transmitted.
  • Overlooking that hyperchaos requires at least four dimensions; a three‑dimensional flow cannot have two positive Lyapunov exponents because the sum of exponents equals the average divergence, which is negative for dissipative systems.

hand/yamabe-problem.html:
Blow‑up Analysis and the Bubbling Phenomenon in the Yamabe Problem

The lack of compactness of the Sobolev embedding H¹ Lp (with p = 2n/(n−2)) is the central analytic difficulty of the Yamabe problem. When a minimizing sequence for the Yamabe functional approaches the infimum, it may concentrate energy at isolated points, producing “bubbles” conformally equivalent to the standard sphere. Blow‑up analysis, developed by Schoen (1984) and refined by Li‑Zhu (1995), shows that any sequence of solutions uk with bounded energy either converges smoothly or, after rescaling around concentration points, converges to the extremal functions for the Euclidean Sobolev inequality: Uε,y(x) = cn ε(n−2)/2 ( ε² + |x−y|² )(2−n)/2. These bubbles carry exactly the Yamabe energy of the round sphere Y(Sn). Bubble interaction is governed by the Green’s function of the conformal Laplacian; the leading-order interaction energy is expressed through the mass of the asymptotically flat metric obtained by removing the concentration point. This mass equals the ADM mass from the positive mass theorem, linking analytic bubbling to the geometric argument that rules out Y(M) = Y(Sn) unless M is conformal to the sphere.

In dimensions n ≥ 6 the Weyl curvature contributes negatively to the interaction energy, allowing Aubin’s test functions to push the Yamabe quotient below Y(Sn). In lower dimensions or the locally conformally flat case the Weyl term vanishes, and the next-order term involves the scalar curvature and its derivatives; this is why n = 3,4,5 and locally conformally flat manifolds required Schoen’s global argument using the positive mass theorem. The blow‑up profile also yields quantization of the loss of compactness: the total energy of a Palais‑Smale sequence splits into the limit solution’s energy plus an integer multiple of Y(Sn). This quantization underpins the compactness theory of Yamabe metrics and the study of prescribed scalar curvature.

Compactness of Yamabe Metrics and the Schoen Compactness Theorem

Once existence of a constant scalar curvature metric in each conformal class is established, a natural question is whether the set of all such metrics (Yamabe metrics) is compact in the smooth topology. Schoen (1991) proved that for a fixed compact manifold M of dimension 3 ≤ n ≤ 24, the space of unit‑volume Yamabe metrics is compact in C∞. The proof combines blow‑up analysis with study of the linearized Yamabe operator. If a sequence of Yamabe metrics gk = uk4/(n−2) g were to degenerate, the conformal factors uk would develop bubbles. The linearized operator around a bubble is the conformal Laplacian on the sphere, whose kernel consists of conformal Killing fields. Projecting the equation onto the kernel and using the Pohozaev identity yields a balancing condition forcing bubbles to be isolated and non‑interacting. In dimensions ≤ 24 the positive mass theorem (Schoen‑Yau, extended by Lohkamp) guarantees positive mass for each bubble, contradicting the balancing condition unless no bubbles form. Hence the sequence converges smoothly.

In dimensions n ≥ 25 compactness fails: Khuri, Marques and Neves (2009) constructed sequences of Yamabe metrics on certain manifolds that develop bubbles without a smooth limit. This relates to non‑trivial solutions of the linearized problem on the sphere with negative eigenvalues, which appear only in high dimensions. The compactness theorem implies the Yamabe invariant Y(M) is attained by a smooth metric, the set of constant scalar curvature metrics in a given conformal class is finite up to diffeomorphism (for generic metrics), and the moduli space of Yamabe metrics is a finite‑dimensional orbifold. These facts are used in the prescribed scalar curvature problem and Yamabe flow analysis.

Worked Example: Blow‑up Quantization
Let (M³, g) be a compact three‑manifold and {uk} a Palais‑Smale sequence for the Yamabe functional with energy bounded by Y(S³) + δ, δ > 0 small. Show that after passing to a subsequence either uk converges strongly in H¹ or there exists a point p ∈ M such that uk concentrates at p and the loss of energy is exactly Y(S³).
By the concentration‑compactness principle of Lions, the sequence of measures μk = |∇uk|² + Rguk² dVg converges weakly to a measure μ. If no concentration occurs, the embedding H¹ L⁶ is compact on bounded domains away from the concentration set, yielding strong convergence. If concentration occurs at p, rescale around p using conformal normal coordinates: define vk(x) = λk(n−2)/2 uk(expp(λkx)) with λk → 0 chosen so that the maximum of vk is 1. The rescaled metrics converge to the Euclidean metric, and vk converges to the standard bubble U(x) = (1+|x|²)(2−n)/2. The energy of the bubble is exactly the Yamabe energy of the round sphere, Y(S³). Since the total energy is bounded by Y(S³)+δ, at most one bubble can form, and the loss of energy equals Y(S³).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about compactness of Yamabe metrics, first state the dimension range (3 ≤ n ≤ 24) and cite Schoen’s 1991 theorem. Then outline the two‑step proof: (1) blow‑up analysis reduces degeneration to bubbling, (2) the positive mass theorem forces the mass of each bubble to be positive, which contradicts the Pohozaev balancing condition. For dimensions ≥ 25 mention the Khuri‑Marques‑Neves counterexample. This structure shows you understand both the analytic and geometric ingredients.

The Yamabe Problem on Manifolds with Boundary: Escobar’s Theorem

The Yamabe problem extends to compact manifolds with boundary. Given (M, g) with ∂M ≠ ∅, one seeks a conformal metric g̃ = u4/(n−2) g with constant scalar curvature in the interior and constant mean curvature on the boundary. The Euler‑Lagrange system is Lgu = λ u(n+2)/(n−2) in M, and Bgu = μ un/(n−2) on ∂M, where Lg = −4(n−1)/(n−2) Δg + Rg is the conformal Laplacian and Bg = ∂/∂ν + (n−2)/2 Hg is the conformal boundary operator (Hg is the boundary mean curvature). The variational functional is the Yamabe‑Escobar quotient Q(u) = (∫M (a|∇u|² + Rgu²) dV + 2∫∂M Hgu² dS) / (∫M |u|p dV)2/p with p = 2n/(n−2). Escobar (1992) proved existence of a minimizer for all n ≥ 3 assuming the boundary is not umbilic or the Sobolev quotient is strictly below that of the half‑sphere. The proof uses a test function from the Green’s function of the conformal Laplacian with Neumann boundary condition, together with a positive mass theorem for asymptotically flat manifolds with boundary (the Shi‑Tam mass). When the boundary is umbilic and the quotient equals that of the half‑sphere, the manifold is conformal to a spherical cap and the minimizer is the first eigenfunction of the conformal Laplacian.

Escobar’s theorem yields a conformal invariant, the Yamabe‑Escobar invariant Y(M, ∂M), classifying conformal classes by the sign of the invariant. It also gives a sharp Sobolev trace inequality on manifolds with boundary, with extremals given by conformal factors of constant scalar curvature metrics. The boundary Yamabe problem relates to prescribed scalar and mean curvature problems; Kazdan‑Warner type obstructions appear as integrals of boundary mean curvature against conformal Killing fields. Recent work by Marques (2005) and Almaraz‑Barbosa‑do Carmo (2012) extended compactness theory to the boundary setting, showing the space of unit‑volume Yamabe‑Escobar metrics is compact in dimensions ≤ 24, with similar non‑compactness in higher dimensions.

The Yamabe Invariant, Exotic Smooth Structures, and the Positive Mass Theorem

The Yamabe invariant Y(M) = inf[g] Y([g]) is a diffeomorphism invariant. Its sign classifies: Y(M) > 0 iff M admits a metric of positive scalar curvature; Y(M) = 0 iff M admits zero scalar curvature but no positive scalar curvature metric; Y(M) < 0 otherwise. The connection with the positive mass theorem appears in the study of exotic spheres. In dimensions n ≥ 5, Gromov‑Lawson, Schoen‑Yau, and Stolz showed a simply connected spin manifold admits positive scalar curvature iff its Â‑genus vanishes. Exotic spheres bounding spin manifolds have vanishing Â‑genus, so they admit positive scalar curvature metrics and Y(M) > 0. However, the exact value of Y(M) can distinguish exotic smooth structures. Petean (1999) proved that for n ≥ 5, Y(M) = Y(Sn) iff M is conformally diffeomorphic to the standard sphere. For exotic spheres not conformally equivalent to the round sphere, 0 < Y(M) < Y(Sn). The proof uses the positive mass theorem for asymptotically flat manifolds with boundary (Shi‑Tam mass) applied to the Green’s function of the conformal Laplacian at a point where the Yamabe metric is not locally conformally flat; the mass is positive unless the manifold is conformal to the sphere, giving a strict inequality.

Bray‑Neves (2004) and Akutagawa‑Botvinnik (2003) relate the Yamabe invariant to minimal hypersurface structure. In dimension three, it connects to Heegaard genus and incompressible tori. In higher dimensions, the invariant for connected sums satisfies Y(M # N) = min(Y(M), Y(N)) when both are non‑positive; for positive invariants the formula is more subtle and involves the positive mass theorem. These results illustrate how the Yamabe invariant bridges conformal geometry, global analysis, and high‑dimensional topology.

The Yamabe Flow: Parabolic Approach and Convergence Results

The Yamabe flow, introduced by Hamilton (1989), is the gradient flow of the Yamabe functional restricted to unit-volume metrics. It evolves g(t) by ∂t g = (r − R) g, where R is the scalar curvature and r = (∫M R dV)/Vol(M) is the average scalar curvature (constant along the flow). In conformal gauge g(t) = u(t)4/(n−2) g0, the flow reduces to ∂t u = −(n−2)/4 u (Lg0u − r u(n+2)/(n−2)). The flow preserves the conformal class and volume, and the Yamabe functional is non‑increasing. Ye (1994) proved that for locally conformally flat manifolds with positive Yamabe invariant, the flow exists globally and converges smoothly to a constant scalar curvature metric. Schwetlick‑Struwe (2003) extended global existence to all n ≥ 3 assuming initial Yamabe energy below Y(Sn). Above this threshold singularities can form; Brendle (2005) showed that in dimension three the flow can develop Type‑II singularities modeled on the ancient solution on S³. Singularity analysis uses the same blow‑up techniques as the elliptic problem, plus Harnack inequalities for the linearized flow.

Convergence results have been refined. For n ≤ 5 the flow converges for any initial metric with positive Yamabe invariant (Brendle‑Marques‑Neves, 2011). In higher dimensions convergence holds for generic initial metrics, but non‑convergence examples exist due to non‑trivial ancient solutions. The Yamabe flow provides a dynamical perspective on the Yamabe problem and proves existence of constant scalar curvature metrics where variational methods are difficult. It also connects to the prescribed scalar curvature problem: adding a potential term yields a flow whose stationary points are metrics with given scalar curvature. Long‑time behavior is governed by the same compactness and bubbling phenomena as the elliptic theory.

  • Confusing the Yamabe invariant Y(M) with the Yamabe constant of a conformal class Y([g]); the former is a global infimum over all conformal classes, the latter is the infimum within a fixed class.
  • Assuming the positive mass theorem holds in all dimensions without the spin or dimension ≤ 7 hypothesis; Schoen‑Yau proved it for n ≤ 7, Witten’s spinor proof works for spin manifolds in any dimension, and Lohkamp extended it to all dimensions but with additional technical assumptions.
  • Overlooking the role of the Weyl tensor in Aubin’s test function; the negative contribution of the Weyl curvature is essential for dimensions ≥ 6 and non‑locally‑conformally‑flat manifolds.
  • Stating that the Yamabe flow always converges; convergence fails in high dimensions or for energies above Y(Sn) where bubbling singularities occur.
  • Neglecting the boundary term in the Escobar problem; the boundary operator Bg and the mean curvature H are crucial for the variational structure and for the positive mass theorem with boundary.
  • Claiming that the Yamabe invariant distinguishes all exotic smooth structures; it distinguishes some but not all — there exist exotic spheres with the same Yamabe invariant.
  • Misapplying the compactness theorem of Schoen to dimensions ≥ 25; the Khuri‑Marques‑Neves counterexamples show compactness fails in high dimensions.

hand/atomic-structure.html:
Fine Structure, Spin-Orbit Coupling, and the Lamb Shift

The Bohr model and the Schrödinger equation for hydrogen predict that energy levels depend only on the principal quantum number n. High-resolution spectroscopy reveals additional splittings. Fine structure arises from two relativistic corrections: the kinetic energy correction (p⁴ term) and the spin-orbit interaction. The spin-orbit coupling Hamiltonian is H_SO = ξ(r) L·S, where ξ(r) = (1/2m²c²r)(dV/dr) for a central potential V(r). For a hydrogen-like atom, the first-order energy shift is ΔE_fs = (Z⁴α²/n³)[1/(j+½) − 3/(4n)] × 13.6 eV, where α ≈ 1/137 is the fine-structure constant and j = ℓ ± ½ is the total angular momentum quantum number. This splits each ℓ > 0 level into two components (e.g., 2p splits into 2p₁/₂ and 2p₃/₂). The 2s₁/₂ and 2p₁/₂ levels remain degenerate in the Dirac theory. The Lamb shift, discovered in 1947 by Lamb and Retherford, lifts this degeneracy: the 2s₁/₂ level lies about 1057 MHz (4.37 × 10⁻⁶ eV) above 2p₁/₂. The shift originates from quantum electrodynamics — the interaction of the bound electron with the quantized electromagnetic field (vacuum fluctuations and self-energy). For multi-electron atoms, fine-structure splitting scales roughly as Z⁴ and becomes large for heavy elements; in lead (Z=82) the 6p splitting exceeds 1 eV. Total angular momentum J = L + S couples individual electron momenta. In LS coupling (Russell-Saunders), valid for light atoms (Z < 30), fine-structure splitting within a term follows the Landé interval rule: ΔE(J, J−1) = A·J, where A is the spin-orbit coupling constant. In jj coupling, dominant for heavy atoms, each electron's j is coupled individually. The transition between coupling schemes is continuous; intermediate coupling requires diagonalization of the full Hamiltonian matrix.

Term Symbols, Russell-Saunders Coupling, and Hund's Rules for Ground States

A term symbol ²ˢ⁺¹L_J encodes the total spin S, total orbital angular momentum L (S, P, D, F, G, H... for L = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...), and total angular momentum J of an atomic state. For a given electron configuration, possible terms are found by coupling individual ℓ and s values. For two equivalent p electrons (p²), allowed terms are ¹S, ¹D, and ³P. The Pauli principle forbids ³S, ³D, and ¹P because their spatial-spin symmetry combinations would require symmetric total wavefunctions for fermions. Hund's rules determine the ground-state term: (1) Maximum multiplicity (2S+1) — the term with the largest S lies lowest. (2) For a given multiplicity, the term with the largest L lies lowest. (3) For less-than-half-filled shells, the level with the smallest J lies lowest; for more-than-half-filled, the largest J lies lowest. Applied to carbon (1s² 2s² 2p²): the p² configuration gives terms ³P, ¹D, ¹S. Rule 1 selects ³P (S=1). Rule 2 is satisfied (only one triplet term). Rule 3: p² is less than half-filled (half-filled is p³), so J = |L−S| = |1−1| = 0. The ground state is ³P₀. For nitrogen (p³), the ground term is ⁴S₃/₂ (S=3/2, L=0). For oxygen (p⁴), equivalent to two holes in p⁶, the ground term is ³P₂ (more than half-filled, J = L+S = 2). The Landé g-factor for a level is g_J = 1 + [J(J+1) + S(S+1) − L(L+1)] / [2J(J+1)]. In a weak magnetic field, the Zeeman splitting is ΔE = μ_B g_J M_J B, where μ_B = eℏ/2m_e = 9.274 × 10⁻²⁴ J/T. The number of Zeeman components is 2J+1. For ³P₁ (J=1), g_J = 1.5, giving three equally spaced components. For ³P₀ (J=0), no splitting occurs. For ³P₂ (J=2), g_J = 1.5, giving five components. In strong fields (Paschen-Back regime), LS coupling breaks down and M_L, M_S become good quantum numbers; the splitting becomes ΔE = μ_B (M_L + 2M_S)B.

Worked Example: Ground-State Term Symbol and Zeeman Pattern
Determine the ground-state term symbol for a vanadium atom (Z=23) and predict the number of Zeeman components for the ground level in a weak magnetic field.
Vanadium electron configuration: [Ar] 3d³ 4s². The valence electrons are 3d³ (4s² is a closed subshell with L=0, S=0). For d³ (less than half-filled; half-filled is d⁵), Hund's rules give: Maximum S: three parallel spins give S = 3/2 (multiplicity 4). Maximum L for S=3/2: electrons occupy m_ℓ = +2, +1, 0 to maximize M_L = 3, giving L = 3 (F). The term is ⁴F. Since the shell is less than half-filled, J = |L−S| = |3 − 3/2| = 3/2. Ground-state term symbol: ⁴F₃/₂. In a weak field, Zeeman splitting yields 2J+1 = 4 components (M_J = ±3/2, ±1/2). The Landé g-factor: g_J = 1 + [J(J+1) + S(S+1) − L(L+1)] / [2J(J+1)] = 1 + [(15/4) + (15/4) − 12] / [2(15/4)] = 1 + [(30/4 − 48/4)] / (30/4) = 1 + (−18/4) / (30/4) = 1 − 18/30 = 0.4. The splitting is ΔE = μ_B g_J M_J B = 0.4 μ_B M_J B.
Exam Strategy: Term Symbols and Hund's Rules
Memorize ground-state term symbols for dⁿ (n=1–10) and fⁿ (n=1–14). For dⁿ: d¹/d⁹ → ²D, d²/d⁸ → ³F, d³/d⁷ → ⁴F, d⁴/d⁶ → ⁵D, d⁵ → ⁶S. The J value follows Hund's third rule: less than half-filled (n ≤ 5) takes J = |L−S|; more than half-filled (n > 5) takes J = L+S. For fⁿ, the pattern is analogous but with larger L values. In multiple-choice questions, check whether the configuration is less or more than half-filled before selecting J. A common trap: 4s electrons in transition metals are paired (S=0, L=0) and do not contribute to the neutral atom's term symbol; only the incomplete d or f shell matters. For ions, remove 4s electrons first, then 3d.

Photoelectron Spectroscopy and Koopmans' Theorem

Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) measures the kinetic energy of electrons ejected from a sample by monochromatic photons. The binding energy (ionization energy) is BE = hν − KE − φ, where φ is the spectrometer work function. X-ray PES (XPS, hν ≈ 1–1.5 keV) probes core levels; ultraviolet PES (UPS, hν ≈ 10–100 eV) probes valence orbitals. Koopmans' theorem states that in the Hartree-Fock approximation, the ionization energy from a specific orbital equals the negative of its orbital energy: IE_i = −ε_i. This assumes frozen orbitals (no relaxation). For first ionization of closed-shell species, Koopmans' theorem typically overestimates IE by 1–2 eV due to orbital relaxation. For core levels, relaxation energies are larger (5–10 eV for 1s in second-period elements). The difference between experimental IE and −ε_i is the relaxation energy. Electron correlation (neglected in HF) also contributes. In open-shell systems, Koopmans' theorem applies to α and β spin orbitals separately; ionization energy to a specific final state is better given by ΔSCF (difference in total HF energies), which includes relaxation. Photoelectron spectra show vibrational fine structure when the ion geometry differs from the neutral; the Franck-Condon principle governs intensities. For atoms, spin-orbit splitting appears as doublets for p, d, f core levels (e.g., Cl 2p₃/₂ and 2p₁/₂ separated by 1.6 eV). The intensity ratio of spin-orbit components equals the statistical weight ratio (2j+1): for p levels, 2p₃/₂ : 2p₁/₂ = 4:2 = 2:1; for d levels, 5:3; for f levels, 7:5. Chemical shifts in XPS arise from changes in effective nuclear charge due to bonding; electronegative ligands increase the binding energy of core electrons. The Auger effect — a radiationless transition where a core hole is filled by a higher electron, ejecting another — appears as extra peaks in XPS; Auger kinetic energies are photon-energy independent, distinguishing them from photoelectrons.

Relativistic Effects in Heavy Atoms and the Inert Pair Effect

For heavy elements (Z > 50), relativistic corrections to the Schrödinger equation become chemically significant. The Dirac equation predicts that s and p₁/₂ orbitals contract and stabilize, while p₃/₂, d, and f orbitals expand and destabilize. Direct relativistic contraction of s and p₁/₂ orbitals increases electron density near the nucleus, raising effective nuclear charge for outer electrons. This indirect effect further expands d and f orbitals. The mass-velocity correction lowers kinetic energy for high-momentum (core) electrons; the Darwin term affects only s orbitals (non-zero probability at nucleus). For gold (Z=79), the 6s orbital contracts by ~20% and stabilizes by ~2 eV; the 5d orbitals expand. This explains gold's yellow color (5d→6s transition shifted to visible), high electronegativity (2.54, close to iodine), and Au(I) stability (5d¹⁰). The inert pair effect — the reluctance of ns² electrons in post-transition metals (Tl, Pb, Bi, Po) to participate in bonding — is largely a relativistic phenomenon. In thallium, the 6s orbital is so stabilized that Tl(I) (6s²) is more stable than Tl(III) (6s⁰); the promotion energy 6s² → 6s¹6p¹ is too high. For lead, Pb(II) (6s²) is more stable than Pb(IV); for bismuth, Bi(III) (6s²) dominates over Bi(V). Spin-orbit splitting of the 6p orbital into 6p₁/₂ (stabilized) and 6p₃/₂ (destabilized) further enhances the effect: the 6p₁/₂ orbital is lowered, but the gap to 6s remains large. Relativistic effects also contract the 7s orbital in superheavy elements (Z > 100); calculations suggest element 112 (copernicium) may behave like a noble gas with a closed-shell 7s² configuration. Relativity shapes the periodic table's bottom: without it, 7p elements would be more reactive and the 6d series would resemble the 5d series more closely. Quantitative relativistic calculations use the Dirac-Coulomb-Breit Hamiltonian or scalar relativistic pseudopotentials (e.g., Douglas-Kroll-Hess, ZORA).

Selection Rules, Atomic Spectra, and the Zeeman Effect

Electric dipole transitions between atomic states obey strict selection rules derived from the Wigner-Eckart theorem and parity conservation. For LS coupling: ΔS = 0 (spin conservation), ΔL = 0, ±1 (but L=0 L=0 forbidden), ΔJ = 0, ±1 (but J=0 J=0 forbidden), and parity must change (even odd). Parity is (−1)^Σℓ_i; configurations with an odd number of odd-ℓ electrons (p, f, h...) have odd parity. The Laporte rule forbids transitions between states of the same parity (e.g., d-d transitions in free ions are forbidden; they gain intensity in complexes via vibronic coupling). For jj coupling: Δj = 0, ±1 for the jumping electron, ΔJ = 0, ±1 (J=0 J=0 forbidden), parity change. Intercombination lines (ΔS ≠ 0) are weakly allowed due to spin-orbit mixing of singlet and triplet states; the classic example is the ³P₁ → ¹S₀ transition in mercury (253.7 nm) and the ³P₁ → ¹S₀ in zinc (213.9 nm). In a magnetic field, the Zeeman effect splits levels according to M_J. The normal Zeeman effect (observed only for singlet states, S=0) gives three components: ΔM_J = 0 (π, polarized parallel to B) and ΔM_J = ±1 (σ, polarized perpendicular). The anomalous Zeeman effect (S ≠ 0) gives more components with unequal spacing determined by g_J. For the sodium D-lines (3p ²P₁/₂,₃/₂ → 3s ²S₁/₂), the ²P₃/₂ (g=4/3) splits into 4 levels, ²P₁/₂ (g=2/3) into 2, and ²S₁/₂ (g=2) into 2. Allowed transitions (ΔM_J = 0, ±1) produce 10 components (6 for D₂, 4 for D₁). In strong fields (Paschen-Back effect), LS coupling decouples; M_L and M_S become good quantum numbers. The selection rules become ΔM_L = 0, ±1, ΔM_S = 0. The splitting pattern reverts to a triplet (normal Zeeman) for each spin component, but the two spin components (M_S = ±1/2) are separated by 2μ_B B. The Stark effect (electric field) splits levels with permanent dipole moments; for hydrogen, the linear Stark effect splits n=2 into three components (2s and 2p₀ mix). For non-hydrogenic atoms, the quadratic Stark effect dominates (ΔE ∝ E²).

  • Confusing the fine-structure splitting formula (ΔE ∝ Z⁴/n³) with the gross energy scaling (E ∝ Z²/n²); the Z⁴ dependence makes fine structure dominant in heavy elements.
  • Applying Hund's third rule incorrectly: for less-than-half-filled shells, J = |L−S| (minimum J); for more-than-half-filled, J = L+S (maximum J). The half-filled shell (d⁵, f⁷) has L=0, so J=S.
  • Assuming Koopmans' theorem gives exact ionization energies; it neglects orbital relaxation and electron correlation, typically overestimating IE by 1–2 eV for valence and 5–10 eV for core levels.
  • Forgetting that the 4s electrons in transition metals are paired and do not contribute to the term symbol of the neutral atom; only the incomplete d shell determines the ground term.
  • Misidentifying the parity of a configuration: parity = (−1)^Σℓ_i. A configuration with an odd number of p, f, h... electrons has odd parity; even number gives even parity. Transitions require parity change.
  • Confusing the normal Zeeman effect (three equally spaced lines, S=0) with the anomalous Zeeman effect (multiple unequally spaced lines, S≠0). The normal effect is a special case of the anomalous effect when g_J = 1.
  • Overlooking that the inert pair effect is relativistic in origin: s and p₁/₂ orbital contraction stabilizes the ns² pair, making lower oxidation states more favorable for Tl, Pb, Bi, and Po.

hand/donaldson-thomas.html:
Virtual Fundamental Class and Obstruction Theory

The virtual fundamental class is the cornerstone of Donaldson–Thomas theory on a Calabi–Yau threefold X. Because the moduli space of ideal sheaves or stable pairs is typically singular and of the wrong dimension, one constructs a perfect obstruction theory in the sense of Behrend–Fantechi. The obstruction theory is a two‑term complex of vector bundles E⁻¹ → E⁰ on the moduli stack whose cohomology sheaves are the tangent and obstruction spaces. For the Hilbert scheme of curves, the tangent space at an ideal sheaf I is Ext¹(I, I)₀ and the obstruction space is Ext²(I, I)₀, where the subscript 0 denotes trace‑free part. The Calabi–Yau condition gives a Serre duality isomorphism Ext²(I, I)₀ ≅ Ext¹(I, I)₀∨, making the obstruction theory symmetric. The virtual dimension is then χ(I, I)₀ = 0, so the virtual fundamental class lives in degree zero and the DT invariant is an integer obtained by integrating 1 against this class. The construction uses the intrinsic normal cone and the Behrend function ν, which assigns to each point a weighted Euler characteristic; the DT invariant equals the weighted Euler characteristic of the moduli space. This approach works for any proper moduli space with a symmetric obstruction theory, including Pandharipande–Thomas stable pairs and the moduli of sheaves with fixed Chern character.

In practice, computing the virtual class requires a global presentation of the obstruction theory. For toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, the torus action localizes the virtual class to fixed points, which are described by combinatorial data such as plane partitions. The localization formula expresses the DT invariant as a sum over fixed points of contributions involving the equivariant Euler class of the virtual tangent bundle. This reduces the problem to a combinatorial sum that can be evaluated by the topological vertex. For non‑toric geometries, one often deforms to a toric situation or uses wall‑crossing to relate the invariant to a known chamber. The obstruction theory also underlies the definition of the reduced DT invariants for local curves, where one removes a trivial factor coming from the motion of the curve in the threefold. The reduced theory yields invariants that satisfy the same wall‑crossing formulas but with a simpler generating function.

Generating Functions and the Topological Vertex

The generating functions of DT and PT invariants are formal series in variables q and v^β that encode the entire tower of invariants for all curve classes β and Euler characteristics n. The DT partition function Z_DT(q, v) = Σn,β DTn,β q^n v^β and the PT partition function Z_PT(q, v) = Σn,β PTn,β q^n v^β are related by the DT/PT correspondence Z_DT = Z_PT · Z_DTdeg 0, where the degree‑zero factor is the MacMahon function M(q)χ(X). For toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, the topological vertex provides a closed combinatorial formula for Z_PT. The vertex assigns to each trivalent vertex of the toric diagram a sum over three‑dimensional partitions λ, μ, ν weighted by products of Schur functions and the quantum parameter q. The full partition function is obtained by gluing vertices along edges, summing over partitions on internal edges with a framing factor (−q)|λ|/2 and a weight v^β determined by the Kähler parameters. This algorithm computes the PT invariants for toric threefolds and, via the DT/PT correspondence, the DT invariants as well. The topological vertex also makes manifest the integrality of the Gopakumar–Vafa BPS invariants ng,β, because the vertex expansion can be reorganized into the Gopakumar–Vafa form Σg,β ng,β (2 sin(u/2))2g−2 with q = −eiu. The vertex formalism has been extended to open invariants, where branes are inserted along legs of the toric diagram, and to refined invariants that depend on two parameters q, t, capturing the motivic refinement of DT theory.

Worked Example: Topological Vertex for the Resolved Conifold
Compute the PT partition function for the resolved conifold using the topological vertex. The toric diagram has two vertices connected by a single internal edge. Assign partitions λ, μ to the two external legs of the first vertex and ν, ρ to the second. Write the vertex sum and perform the gluing sum over the internal partition.
The topological vertex for a single vertex is Cλ μ ν(q) = q(κ(λ)+κ(μ)+κ(ν))/2 Ση sλ^t/η(q-ρ) sμ/η(q-ρ) sν(q-ρ) where κ(λ)=Σ_i λ_i(λ_i−2i+1) and q-ρ = (q1/2, q3/2, …). For the resolved conifold, the two vertices are glued along an internal edge with partition α. The gluing sum is Σα (−Q)|α| C∅ ∅ α(q) C∅ ∅ α^t(q) where Q = v^β is the Kähler parameter. Using the identity C∅ ∅ α(q) = qκ(α)/2 sα^t(q-ρ) and the Cauchy identity Σα sα^t(x) sα(y) = ∏i,j (1 + x_i y_j), the sum evaluates to ∏k≥1 (1 − Q q^k)−k. This is precisely the MacMahon function M(Q q) with a shift, matching the known PT partition function for the conifold. The DT partition function follows by multiplying with the degree‑zero factor M(q)χ(X).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the topological vertex computation, first identify the toric diagram and the number of vertices. Write the vertex function for each vertex, then set up the gluing sum over internal partitions. Remember the framing factor (−Q)|α| and the transpose on one side of the edge. Use the Cauchy identity to evaluate the sum; the final answer is usually an infinite product of the form ∏ (1 − Q q^k)±k. Practice the conifold and local P² cases, as they appear frequently.

Quiver Representations and the Cohomological Hall Algebra

Quiver DT invariants provide a combinatorial laboratory where the full machinery of wall‑crossing and the Cohomological Hall Algebra (CoHA) can be tested. A quiver Q consists of vertices and arrows; a representation assigns a vector space to each vertex and a linear map to each arrow. The moduli space of representations with fixed dimension vector d is a quotient of the representation space by the product of general linear groups. When Q arises from a Calabi–Yau threefold via a tilting bundle, the DT invariants of the threefold are conjecturally equal to the quiver DT invariants with a suitable stability condition. The CoHA, introduced by Kontsevich and Soibelman, is the cohomology of the moduli stack of representations equipped with a convolution product defined by the correspondence stack of short exact sequences. This product is associative and graded by the dimension vector. The CoHA carries a natural action of the quantum torus algebra, and its Drinfeld double encodes the wall‑crossing formula. The categorification of DT invariants means lifting the numerical invariant Ω(γ) to the cohomology of the moduli space; the CoHA provides the algebraic structure whose graded dimension recovers the DT generating series. For the Jordan quiver (one vertex, one loop), the CoHA is isomorphic to the algebra of symmetric functions, and its Hilbert series is the MacMahon function. For the Kronecker quiver (two vertices, two arrows), the CoHA is related to the elliptic Hall algebra. The Kac conjecture, proved by Hausel–Letellier–Rodriguez‑Villegas using the CoHA, states that the number of absolutely indecomposable representations over a finite field is given by a polynomial in the field size whose coefficients are the multiplicities of the roots of the associated Kac–Moody algebra. This result connects the arithmetic of quiver varieties to the representation theory of infinite‑dimensional Lie algebras.

Bridgeland Stability Conditions and the Space of Stability

Bridgeland stability conditions on the derived category D^b(Coh(X)) form a complex manifold Stab(X) of dimension equal to the rank of the numerical Grothendieck group. A stability condition consists of a central charge Z: K(X) → ℂ, a group homomorphism, and a slicing P(φ) of semistable objects of phase φ, satisfying the Harder–Narasimhan property and the support property. For a Calabi–Yau threefold, the central charge is often taken as Z(E) = −∫_X e−(B+iω) ch(E) √{td(X)} where B+iω is a complexified Kähler class. Varying (B, ω) moves the stability condition in Stab(X). Walls are real codimension‑one loci where a strictly semistable object appears; crossing a wall changes the set of stable objects and hence the DT invariants. The Kontsevich–Soibelman wall‑crossing formula describes the transformation of the DT generating function as a product of quantum dilogarithms E(x; q) = ∏k≥0 (1 + qk+1/2 x)−1 over the charges γ of objects that become stable or unstable. The formula lives in the quantum torus algebra with commutation e_γ e_δ = q⟨γ,δ⟩ eγ+δ, where ⟨·,·⟩ is the Euler form. The Joyce–Song approach uses the Hall algebra of the abelian category of coherent sheaves and defines generalized DT invariants via a logarithmic map on the stack function algebra. Both frameworks produce the same wall‑crossing transformations and have been verified in many examples, including local curves and quiver representations. The space of stability conditions also admits a natural action of the autoequivalence group of D^b(Coh(X)), which can be used to relate different chambers and to establish the DT/PT correspondence by moving from the large volume chamber (where ideal sheaves are stable) to the non‑commutative chamber (where stable pairs are stable).

Applications to String Theory and Mirror Symmetry

Donaldson–Thomas invariants count BPS states in type IIA string theory compactified on a Calabi–Yau threefold X. The DT partition function computes the indexed degeneracies of D‑brane bound states, which are protected by supersymmetry and depend only on the topological class of the brane. The MNOP conjecture identifies the DT partition function with the topological string partition function of the A‑model on X, after the change of variables q = −eiu. This is a precise mathematical formulation of the OSV conjecture relating black hole entropy to topological strings. Mirror symmetry exchanges the A‑model on X with the B‑model on the mirror threefold Y. On the B‑model side, the topological string partition function is computed by the holomorphic anomaly equations of Bershadsky–Cecotti–Ooguri–Vafa, which determine the higher genus amplitudes recursively from the genus‑zero prepotential. The DT side provides a non‑perturbative definition of the topological string that is invariant under mirror symmetry. The wall‑crossing formula for DT invariants corresponds to the crossing of walls of marginal stability in the moduli space of the B‑model, where BPS states decay. The Cohomological Hall Algebra is expected to be isomorphic to the algebra of BPS operators in the four‑dimensional N=2 theory obtained by compactifying M‑theory on X. The refined DT invariants, depending on two parameters q, t, capture the spin content of BPS states and are related to the Nekrasov partition function of the five‑dimensional gauge theory engineered by the same geometry. These connections make DT theory a central tool for testing string dualities and for computing exact non‑perturbative quantities in quantum gravity.

  • Confusing the virtual fundamental class with the ordinary fundamental class; the virtual class lives in the expected dimension even when the moduli space is singular.
  • Forgetting the degree‑zero MacMahon factor when converting between DT and PT partition functions.
  • Misapplying the topological vertex by omitting the framing factor or using the wrong transpose on glued edges.
  • Assuming wall‑crossing formulas are identical for all stability conditions; the KS and Joyce–Song formulas agree but are derived in different algebraic frameworks.
  • Neglecting the support property when checking whether a given central charge defines a Bridgeland stability condition.
  • Treating refined DT invariants as a simple substitution q → q, t without adjusting the quantum dilogarithm in the wall‑crossing formula.
  • Mastering these pitfalls ensures accurate answers on DT theory questions.
